1a3e4777f7a048bc: SHAH ALAM: A decision regarding the Confidence and Supply Agreement (CSA) between the Selangor government and Bersatu is expected to be announced soon, once negotiations are finalised.

Selangor Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Amirudin Shari said negotiations with Bersatu were ongoing, with an understanding reached on the fundamental principles, although several sensitive matters still needed to be ironed out.
He said the cooperation established at the federal level had facilitated efforts to implement a similar arrangement in Selangor to ensure stability in the state administration.

"There are indeed negotiations with Bersatu, and if successful, they will provide en bloc support while remaining as the opposition. The fundamental principles are already in place; it is just that there are a few slightly sensitive details that need to be considered," he told reporters.
He was speaking after the appreciation ceremony in conjunction with the 22nd Malaysia Games (Sukma) and 2026 Para Sukma at Dewan Raja Muda Musa.
Amirudin said he was ready to finalise the agreement once all related matters had been resolved with the party leadership.

"Wait a moment; it is already in place at the federal level, making it easier for us to implement at the Selangor level. That is indeed the way to ensure cooperation or mutual understanding. Therefore, I am ready for this at any time," he said.
The proposed CSA in Selangor was previously mooted to ensure the smooth running of the state administration, including matters related to the budget, through cooperation across party lines.

c7bced1d6613a201: KLANG: Former Universiti Putra Malaysia (UPM) vice-chancellor Prof Emeritus Datuk Dr Aini Ideris was named National Academic Figure at the 17th National Academic Awards ceremony.
The award was presented by Higher Education Minister Datuk Seri Dr Zambry Abd Kadir with Dr Aini receiving a trophy, certificate and RM200,000 in prize money.

Dr Aini, 73, has contributed to avian medicine, animal biotechnology and vaccine development, including the development of the Newcastle disease vaccine (NDV4UPM) and a fowlpox vaccine, which have entered international markets.

She also made history as the first woman appointed UPM vice-chancellor, serving from 2016 to 2020, and previously received the 2010 National Academic Award in the Innovation and Product Commercialisation category.
She was also awarded the 2026 Merdeka Award in the Outstanding Contribution to Science, Technology and Innovation category.
The 17th National Academic Awards recognised the excellence and contributions of nine academics from higher education institutions in various fields.
The Promising Academic Award went to Prof Dr Ong Wee Jun of Xiamen University Malaysia (XMUM) and Associate Prof Dr Serene Lock Sow Mun of Universiti Teknologi Petronas (UTP).

The Innovation and Product Commercialisation Award went to Associate Prof Dr Mohd Khairi Abu Husain of Universiti Teknologi Malaysia (UTM), while the Book Publication Award was presented to Dr Siti Noor Hafizah Mohamed Sharif of Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM).
The Teaching Award (Arts and Social Sciences) went to Associate Prof Dr Saipolbarin Ramli of Universiti Pendidikan Sultan Idris (UPSI).

Other recipients were Associate Prof Dr Jayanthi Arasan of UPM for the Teaching Award (Pure Sciences); Dr Ooi Say Keat of USM for the Journal Article Publication Award (Social Sciences and Arts); and Prof Dr Yong Wai Fen of XMUM for the Journal Article Publication Award.
Recipients in the respective categories received RM50,000 in prize money, a trophy and a certificate, while the Promising Academic Award recipients received RM25,000.

In his speech, Zambry said the ceremony represented the nation's highest honour for scholars and academics who had dedicated their lives to advancing knowledge and contributing to society and the country.
"This recognition is not merely an acknowledgement of past achievements, but also a responsibility to continue exploring knowledge, producing quality work and inspiring future generations.
"We want to produce scholars who not only achieve excellence for themselves but also build the greatness of their nation. Scholars can reach for the sky while remaining rooted to the earth," he said.
The awards is an annual programme organised by the Higher Education Ministry since 2002.

This year's edition was managed by the Academic Excellence Division of the Department of Higher Education, in collaboration with USM and Universiti Tenaga Nasional, which served as the programme's committee and secretariat.
2606285fce47d9a7: MONTREAL: EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa held talks with Canada's Mark Carney in Montreal Friday to finalise a new partnership in a world dominated by the United States and China.

The two parties are set to unveil a series of deals – from critical minerals to artificial intelligence – and lay the groundwork for a broader alliance open to other democracies seeking to better navigate global trade tensions.

"It means affordability, more competition, more choice, and easier access. It means opportunity," Carney, the Canadian prime minister, said of closer cooperation with the EU, as he arrived at the talks.
"And it means, at its base, sovereignty, greater resilience, and the ability to withstand shocks together."

Already sharing a free trade agreement, Canada and the EU have sought to move closer together since President Donald Trump's return to the White House upended relations with Washington's traditional allies.
Both Canada and the EU have been hit with US tariffs and territorial threats.

Von der Leyen, the European Commission president, said Canada could not become a "full-fledged" EU member due to its geographical location, but said the bloc wanted to bring it "as close as possible".
A senior EU official explained the new relationship would be unique to Canada.
It entails aligning policies, such as on climate and artificial intelligence, Canada joining some EU programmes, and creating a stable governance framework, the official said.
The partners are expected to kick off with a series of deals on Friday.
Critical minerals are a key focus of the two-day summit which officially began Thursday evening.
They are needed for green technologies such as batteries and wind turbines that Europe sources mostly from China but are also in plentiful stock in Canada.
But Canada needs massive infrastructure investment to jump-start its mining industry.
An agreement allowing the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects is expected to be unveiled at the summit.
'Alliance for the Future'
Brussels and Ottawa also want to collaborate on AI, a field where they are playing catch-up with the US and China.
Europe is ready to open its supercomputing infrastructure to Canadian researchers, industry and start-ups, von der Leyen said.

On Thursday, Ottawa announced a C$1.6 billion (US$1.1 billion) investment in the Canadian AI firm Cohere. The company has recently partnered with Germany's Aleph Alpha in a move that Carney said was an example of what Europe and Canada could do together.
"We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don't know or by those we don't trust," Carney said.
A digital trade deal allowing faster and cheaper online transactions is also in the offering.

The two parties should also work towards Canada's participation in EU initiatives like the Erasmus programme, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad, and the Galileo satellite programme – an alternative to the American Global Positioning System (GPS).
The summit will additionally establish the basis for a larger "Alliance for the Future" open to other "trusted partners" such as Japan, South Korea or Australia, the senior EU official said.
This idea is to form a "common space for economic prosperity" and better coordinate trade policies such as tariffs to avoid mutual harm, the official said.
"There is always a risk that inadvertently you hit one of your partners with your economic measures," the official noted.

157a2f7bf88b26d3: KUALA LUMPUR: Global air passenger demand fell 0.5 per cent in September from the same month last year, reflecting weakness in the Middle East and North America.
The International Air Transport Association (IATA) said demand grew 0.3 per cent when the Middle East was excluded.

In a statement issued in Geneva, Switzerland, the association said total capacity, measured in available seat kilometres (ASK), declined 0.2 per cent year-on-year, while the passenger load factor stood at 83.2 per cent, down 0.3 percentage points from a year earlier.

IATA senior vice-president (sustainability) and chief economist Marie Owens Thomsen said the figures nevertheless marked an improvement from August, with most international markets returning to growth.
"These patterns have more-or-less repeated themselves throughout much of the year, and we can expect this to continue amid geopolitical uncertainty and volatile fuel prices.
"Global scheduled seat capacity is expected to remain above 2025 levels in October and November, but the rates of growth remain weak and highly unbalanced between regions," she added.
IATA said international passenger demand grew 0.4 per cent in September compared with the same month last year, rising to 1.7 per cent when the Middle East was excluded.
International capacity increased 0.5 per cent year-on-year, while the load factor stood at 83.6 per cent.
In its regional breakdown, IATA said most key international routes showed a general improvement from August, with some returning to growth while others recorded slower rates of decline.
"Asia-Pacific airlines saw a 0.7 per cent y-o-y increase in demand. Capacity increased 0.4 per cent y-o-y, and the load factor was 83.1 per cent (up 0.3 ppt compared to September 2025).

"Traffic increased on four of the six largest international route areas serving Asia-Pacific. On routes within Asia, traffic declined by 0.9 per cent, though this was a slower rate of decline than in August," said IATA, which represents over 370 airlines accounting for some 85 per cent of global air traffic.

139db0e5e00c5498: KLANG: Growing reliance on artificial intelligence (AI) risks weakening critical thinking and producing a generation with access to vast amounts of information but lacking the ability to engage meaningfully with knowledge.

Speaking at the 17th National Academic Awards (AAN17) here tonight, Higher Education Minister Datuk Seri Dr Zambry Abd Kadir said academics and universities must ensure technological advances, including generative AI, do not undermine education and intellectual development.
"Students no longer regard professors as their primary source of knowledge. They have a new teacher," he said, referring to AI tools such as ChatGPT.
Zambry said academics must go beyond lecture halls and research laboratories to shape public thinking and address national and global challenges.
He said academic excellence should not be measured merely by publications, research grants and international rankings, but also by how far knowledge and expertise benefited society.
He also urged academics to challenge existing assumptions, offer constructive criticism and have the courage to speak truth to power, while upholding intellectual integrity and moral responsibility.

At the ceremony, Universiti Putra Malaysia (UPM) Professor Emeritus Datin Dr Aini Ideris received the Tokoh Akademik Negara award for her contributions to poultry science, biotechnology and vaccine production.

Aini, UPM's first woman vice-chancellor, serving from 2016 to 2020, was recognised for developing the Newcastle disease vaccine (NDV4-UPM) and fowl pox vaccine, which have reached international markets.
She received RM200,000, a trophy, plaque and certificate.
The Anugerah Ahli Akademik Harapan went to Xiamen University Malaysia's Professor Dr Ong Wee Jun and Universiti Teknologi Petronas Associate Professor Dr Serene Lock Sow Mun.

Other recipients included UPM's Associate Professor Dr Jayanthi Arasan, who was recognised for excellence in science teaching and received a full scholarship to pursue further studies at Oxford University, and Universiti Sains Malaysia's Dr Ooi Sya Keat, who was recognised for journal publication.
A total of nine awards were presented at the ceremony.
The awards also recognised achievements in innovation and commercialisation, book publishing, and teaching in the arts and social sciences.

Zambry said Malaysian academics had also made their mark internationally, with researchers from local universities featuring among the world's top 200 scientists in a database developed by researchers from Stanford University in the United States.
He said the presence of international students at Malaysian universities also reflected confidence in the country's higher education standards.
Congratulating the recipients, he said the awards carried a responsibility to advance knowledge, produce quality research and inspire future generations.
"We want scholars who do not merely pursue excellence for themselves, but build greatness for their nation," he said.
Introduced in 2002, the annual awards recognise outstanding contributions by academics from higher education institutions in advancing knowledge and enhancing Malaysia's standing internationally.

50a3ffbcf81f32b5: PETALING JAYA: Tiga kanak-kanak warga Myanmar dibenarkan ikat jamin selepas Mahkamah Tinggi hari ini membatalkan keputusan Mahkamah Majistret sebelum ini yang menolak permohonan tersebut susulan tuduhan menakut-nakutkan seorang warga emas secara jenayah.

342909a1099acd6e: LONDON: Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta warned Max Dowman he was "not in Disneyland" after the teenage rising star was sent off in the Gunners' shock League Cup defeat by lowly Fleetwood.

The Premier League champions suffered one of the most embarrassing losses in their history when, after the fourth-round tie ended 1-1 in normal time, they lost 5-3 on penalties away to fourth-tier Fleetwood on Tuesday.
To make matters worse for the Gunners, Dowman saw red five minutes before the end of normal time.
Although it looked a harsh decision to send off Dowman for aiming a kick towards Harrison Neal, Arteta was unimpressed with the 16-year-old, giving him a stern word as the midfielder trudged off.

Arteta's reaction on the touchline was criticised by some pundits, who felt he should have been more sympathetic towards Dowman, who is now starting an immediate three-game ban for violent conduct after Arsenal lost an appeal against his red card and punishment.
And an unpretenient Arteta defended his response to Dowman's red card in a pre-match press conference on Friday ahead of Arsenal's trip to Liverpool.
"This is the environment, this is the reality," he said. "We are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League."
Dowman has been carefully nurtured by Arsenal since making his debut when he was just 15.

"We look after him so much, but at the same time we're going to be demanding because he needs to earn the right to play, just like everybody else," said the Spaniard, whose side are level on points with Premier League leaders Manchester City.
"The other boys, what are they going to say to me? You need to be fair.
"My reaction comes from a moment of heat and extreme frustration because I know the consequences of that, especially for Max.
"It is not the first time it has happened, it happened another time this month with England (under-19s)."
"And it will continue to happen because of the way he plays and the way he attracts opponents, and that's it.

"We have to be able to tell each other what we think because he is 16 and we have to be very protective of him, but at the same time very straight with him about what we expect of him towards the team, individuals and the club."
Arteta, himself a former Arsenal midfielder, insisted all was well in his relationship with Dowman.
"There are no issues. We had a talk yesterday. I have done it. It's not the first time it has happened, so we need to put an end to it very, very quickly."
1182f881ed18e30b: Voyager 1 gave controllers the silent treatment for a few days this month before resuming communication weeks before the spacecraft reaches the one-light-day milestone.

The incident happened on October 18: NASA's Deep Space Network (DSN) couldn't detect a signal from the probe. On October 19, on the next scheduled communication attempt, there was still nothing. Was this it? Had the decades-long galactic venture finally ended?

Things are operating on a knife's edge for the two veteran spacecraft, which will reach their half-century next year. Voyager 2 suffered an antenna pointing issue in 2023, and a low power condition caused Voyager 1 to unexpectedly turn off one of its two radio transmitters.
The good news is that on October 20, the signal reappeared, leaving engineers wondering why Voyager 1 temporarily went silent.
Thus far, it seems a group of thrusters went offline and their backups were turned on. This could indicate onboard computers detected a problem and put the spacecraft into a safe mode.

Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, said: "This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected.
"We're relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened."
The Register spoke to Badaruddin in 2024, where he described the challenges of working with the veteran spacecraft, but he reckoned the work was the "best job at JPL."

The twin Voyager spacecraft have recently been through a procedure dubbed the "Big Bang," where controllers turned off onboard devices and switched to lower power alternatives. The result will extend the lifetime of the spacecraft by a few more years and postpone further instrument deactivation. It was completed first on Voyager 2, and then Voyager 1, six weeks later in September.

However, the brief lapse in communication highlights that despite the ingenuity of the team that keep the spacecraft running, the project must eventually come to an end. In 2026, Suzanne Dodd, Project Manager for the Voyager project, told The Register what the end would look like.
She said, "We're just going to one day not hear the signal from the DSN, and we're going to rush around and make sure that it's not something on the ground."
Months of listening will follow, before engineers throw in the towel and declare the mission over. And then? Maybe a farewell message sent to the last known location.
Thankfully, in this case, the signal returned, so no need for a goodbye transmission just yet.
In a few weeks, Voyager 1 will be so far away that it will take a full 24 hours for commands to reach it and another 24 hours for a response to reach Earth.

Communications blip notwithstanding, there is every chance both Voyager spacecraft will still be operational as they pass their half-century milestone next year and, technology and funding permitting, continue sending data to Earth for a good few years yet. ®

269e82b33d053c9a: MAYA Gourdel, a 19-year-old student in Brussels, sits at a desk writing slogans against those running her country: "If we burn, you burn with us!"

The slogan, taken from the 2012 film The Hunger Games that has been adopted as a symbol by many youth movements globally, reflects the anger, frustration and desire for change driving Gen Z-led protests around Europe.
From the suburbs of Paris to the squares of Belgrade, thousands have taken to the streets.
At times those protests triggered violence — with thousands of shops in France alone being damaged or looted in recent weeks — and police firing stun grenades and water cannons.

Last weekend they also brought real change — student-led protests culminated in the toppling in an election of Serbia's long-time leader Aleksandar Vucic after nearly two years of demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism.
"Waking up, the first thing we felt was certainly a sense of relief and freedom," said student protester Stasa Piletic.
"I feel that we finally moved from protests to responsibility."
Meanwhile, Chiara, a 21-year-old student in protest-hit Milan, said: "I think the worst damage this ruling class has done to my generation is stealing even the ability to imagine a future, to dream.

"And all of this with the prospect of an underpaid job which we didn't qualify for and the prospect of living in a tiny, overpriced house, probably away from our city, which we didn't want to live in."
Protests led by Gen Z have caused ructions globally as the generation born roughly between 1997 and 2012 found its voice, from Bangladesh in 2024 and Nepal in 2025, to India this year.
Now Europe has become a focal point.
Rising prices and the cost of living are a concern for 40 per cent of 16 to 30-year-olds, according to a European Union survey published last year.
Among the 92.7 million people in the European Union who faced the risk of poverty or social exclusion last year, the highest risk was recorded for young adults aged 18 to 24 years, at 26.3 per cent.
Younger people are also wary of shouldering the financial burden of an older generation that tends to vote in greater numbers.
People over 60 in France make up a quarter of the population but own 60 per cent of France's wealth.
French pensions are by far the biggest public expense, on track to reach 14 per cent of economic output, as the population ages and voters resist raising the retirement age or reducing benefits.

That is still less than Greece or Italy, which spend the largest proportion of national income on public pensions among Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries, at around 16 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), according to OECD figures last year.
But it is much more than Australia, Chile, Iceland, Ireland or South Korea, which spent less than four per cent of GDP on public pensions, according to the OECD.

Protests showed "that young people in Europe are united", said Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris, adding that "we all agree on one point: that young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren't listened to enough".
Gourdel, too, has been protesting for better conditions in schools in Belgium.
"We tried to do it passively. Nobody heard us. It's only when people started to burn trash or that kind of stuff that the media and cameras started showing us," she said.
The protests are still spreading, with a demonstration planned in Germany this weekend over cost of living, inequality, war and the state of schools.

Unrest has also hit Albania, where student-led demonstrations against Prime Minister Edi Rama's government, fuelled by anger over perceived corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, engulfed Tirana and spread to other cities.
"Our prime minister spent 130 days not listening to us," said Xyke Kurti, a 19-year-old architecture student.

"If you ask a student in Albania, 'where do you see your future?' Everyone says 'outside this country'," she said, arguing that at home, even if you have talent, someone with "connections is always going to beat you".
The writers are from Reuters

b5b1d0f8b9b2331d: United States President Donald Trump has touted billions of dollars in new factories, energy projects and jobs while campaigning for Republicans in competitive races before the Nov 3 midterm elections, but several projects remain uncertain or years from delivering economic benefits, a Reuters review found.

Stop after stop, Trump has pointed to the projects as evidence that his economic policies are paying off, including an Alaska liquefied natural gas LNG pipeline, an Iowa steel mill, a Texas power plant, a Kentucky pharmaceutical project and a North Carolina quartz mine.

US presidents typically spend the final stretch before the midterms highlighting legislative victories and their economic records. Trump has gone further, dangling cash payments, federal investments and other benefits, some explicitly tied to Republican victories.
It is a bet that voters will reward Republicans at the ballot box, even as many remain frustrated by the cost of living, Reuters/Ipsos opinion polls show.
But some of the projects Trump is promoting are far from done deals, said the companies and governments involved.

After Trump heralded a US$54 billion South Korean investment for the Alaska pipeline late last month, part of a broader US$200 billion pledge, Seoul said no decision had been made on whether to invest or how much.

Financing and the construction timeline for the Texas power plant, included in the South Korean package, also remain uncertain, according to South Korean media reports citing unresolved questions over ownership, power-purchase agreements and permitting.

Mesabi Metallics, the company behind the Iowa steel complex, said production would not begin until 2030. Sibelco, the quartz producer involved in the North Carolina project, said its agreement was subject to "further negotiations".

The announcements underscore Republicans' urgency to show economic progress before Tuesday's elections, especially around jobs and energy prices. Inflation has begun to outpace wages just as voters cast ballots, while rising energy prices from the US-Iran war are straining household budgets.

"It starts to feel pretty theatrical when you're this close to an election and you've spent the last year and a half creating chaos with your tariff policies," said Todd Tucker, director of industrial policy and trade at the left-leaning Roosevelt Institute.
"It's crucial for the country that these investments work out, so it's tragic that we'd be throwing fake Monopoly money across the country in the days before an election."
Beyond the investment announcements, Trump has made election-year promises of payments and policy changes, some tied to Republican wins.

One of the most high-profile was Trump's Sept 9 promise of a US$5,000 "dividend" to all US adults if Republicans retain control of Congress, a proposal that would require congressional approval and has gained little traction among lawmakers.
Trump is not the first president to tout major economic projects with uncertain futures or turn to financial assistance in an election year.

Former Democratic president Joe Biden announced billions of dollars in student loan relief ahead of the 2024 election, while congressional Democrats backed expanded health-insurance subsidies and other benefits aimed at easing household costs.

When Trump unveiled plans for US$200 billion in South Korean investment in energy systems across the US, including the LNG pipeline, Alaska Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, who is locked in a tight reelection race, stood alongside him.
Seoul quickly pushed back, saying no investment decision had been made.
The project, led by developer Glenfarne Group, would include a 1,300km pipeline carrying natural gas for export to Asian markets.

Trump also appeared with Iowa Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson and other Republicans in competitive races in the state as he promoted a planned US$15 billion steel complex as evidence that his tariffs are reviving American manufacturing.
That project, led by Mesabi Metallics and its Indian parent company Essar Group, faces questions over financing and site selection.
A company spokesperson said it has not finalised a deal with the state, that a site for the project is still under review.
Trump also pledged US$100 million in Pentagon funding for pharmaceutical-ingredients maker Anthea to revive a shuttered drug plant in Kentucky, tying the money to Republicans winning the midterms.
But the office of Democratic Governor Andy Beshear said it knew nothing about the project.
The writers are from Reuters

54e6a756d7e5205e: The Education Ministry has flagged 691 teachers out of 82,126 scanned across primary and secondary schools as needing urgent mental health care and psychological intervention.
There are three worrying reasons for the teachers' poor mental health.
Firstly, they are overwhelmed by heavy workloads, toxic school leadership and increasing digital and administrative demands.
Secondly, they face severe debt and financial challenges, coupled with stressful work performance demands.
Thirdly, they experience harassment from parents, which spurs isolation and hesitation to seek help.

The findings come from recent screenings based on the ministry's Psychological Well-Being Inventory (IKPsi) framework. Of the teachers flagged, 636 were at a "moderate" level — their mental reserves were spent due to chronic stress, and they experienced early burnout and persistent emotional exhaustion.
They were given preventive counselling, focusing on stress management and coping mechanisms.
Meanwhile, 32 teachers were categorised as "moderately low" and faced major psychological distress while struggling to cope with high workload, anxiety, sleep disruption and isolation.

Counsellors are helping them cope with crushing debt or toxic workplaces. Finally, 23 teachers categorised as "low" experienced psychological distress, burnout and clinical depression so severe that they can't live and work healthily.
They have been placed under psychiatric evaluation, intensive therapy and medical leave.
This might be a problem: the ministry's IKPsi screening is rolled out in phases, meaning that many teachers were already in poor mental health before screening.

Teachers hide their symptoms and answer "perfectly" on official forms, fearing a bad score would ruin their performance reviews, affect promotions and grade advancements, and lead to them being labelled as problematic or "weak".
Furthermore, the relatively low number of teachers flagged suggests an underrepresentation due to how the screening was structured.
A reference to developed nations tells a more desperate situation.
In Australia, 52 per cent of teachers suffer from clinical depression, 35 per cent in the United Kingdom, 79 per cent in the United States, while the global average is 25 to 35 per cent.
These figures suggest that the Education Ministry has only identified teachers already at an acute stage, leaving the much larger group neglected.
Nevertheless, the screening is a positive step towards early detection. To tackle the problem, stigma against teachers seeking help must be removed, and their privacy and confidentiality shielded.
Teachers should not be made to feel ashamed to ask for help. Instead, this must be seen as being responsible, not a sign of professional weakness.
With the first step of early identification underway, success will depend on the ministry's sustained support for teacher recovery.

600797b39656f003: Just days after Daemonarchy, there's another new OS in the BSD family – and one that is heading determinedly in almost the opposite direction.

AlpineBSD is so new that it barely exists yet. There are no installation media available, though it's possible to manually bootstrap an installation. What AlpineBSD does already have is an AI policy, and the plan is to avoid "the output of generative AI models (e.g. LLMs)" as far as possible:
"Any software whose code, documentation, binaries, or other assets include, in any part, the output of a generative AI tool such as an LLM, is considered 'tainted' for our purposes."
The core idea is to combine the kernel of NetBSD with "a userspace inspired by Alpine Linux and the objective of making it possible to use as little AI-generated software as possible."
Back in 2024, the NetBSD project made its position on AI plain. Its commit guidelines say that "code generated by a Large Language Model […] is presumed to be tainted code."
Back in July, Linus Torvalds stated that "Linux is not one of those anti-AI projects". Since then, NetBSD has seen a spike in donations and interest.

For someone mainly used to Linux, trying to install NetBSD is a little like hopping in a time machine to 30 years ago, and we speak from personal experience of Linux in the mid-1990s. As we mentioned when Slackware turned 30 a few years ago, back in 1996, this vulture tried Slackware 3.0 on his own hardware, and we never did manage to install it.
We tried NetBSD 11 a couple of months ago, and despite considerable help from the folks on the NetBSD-users mailing list, we failed to get the CDE desktop to start.

As an example, installing software on NetBSD is not the easy, comfortable task it is on Linux. It does have a package manager for handling binary packages: it's called pkgin, but as the NetBSD FAQ mentions, it's an optional extra. You must manually tick a box in the setup program to install pkgin with the rest of the OS, and when we tried NetBSD 9.3 four years ago, we didn't know that, overlooked that checkbox, and had to find a way to add pkgin later. (It is quite tricky to install a package manager when you don't have a package manager to install it with.)

This time around, we discovered that pkgin sometimes doesn't complete the installation process for you – it just leaves a text file in a destination directory somewhere, and you're expected to know that, go there, read it, and do any further steps yourself.

The NetBSD community has been quietly going its own way since 1993. It has its own ideas about what is normal, and its users expect that. Some folks on the mailing list told us that they never use binary packages anyway – they compile what they need from source code.

AlpineBSD's ports repository and source code are hosted on Sourcehut, under the account of sircmpwn, better known as Drew DeVault. We have quoted DeVault a few times over the years: we've often found that his views align with our own in various ways… such as about the best laptops ever made, and on simplicity in Linux distro design, or even on dot-com billionaires at FOSDEM.

Alpine's tools are quite well-suited to being adapted to other systems. We have previously mentioned the use of its packaging tool, APK, in the GNU-free Chimera Linux, which uses much of the FreeBSD userland, and also in Adélie Linux.

We will follow AlpineBSD with interest. There's strong appeal in the plan of combining perhaps the best-known, longest-established AI-free Unix-like kernel with the user-facing parts of pretty much the smallest and cleanest Linux distro there is. The AI advocates often warn LLM skeptics that they risk being left behind. Well, here's an OS for those who don't want to surf the AI wave. ®

0c2aadbf932902dc: GEORGE TOWN: The government wants local content to be given greater consideration in procurement by government agencies, government-linked companies (GLCs) and multinational corporations (MNCs) to create more opportunities for local micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
Entrepreneur Development and Cooperatives Minister Steven Sim said the approach was aimed at ensuring local businesses benefited from investments and the development of domestic supply chains.

"We also want government procurements, GLC procurements and, of course, MNC procurements to have a perspective for local content. We want foreign direct investment (FDI) to come in to benefit local businesses. So, there must be a requirement for local content," he said.
He said this during a panel discussion with Grant Thornton Malaysia National Tax Practice Leader Datin Seah Siew Yun at the Grant Thornton Tax Seminar on Budget 2027 here today.
Sim said local content requirements were among the components of the Scale Action Plan, which would form the ministry's next phase of longer-term structural reforms for the MSME sector.
He said Scale covered SME redefinition, cash flow protection, artificial intelligence (AI) adoption, local content requirements and easier access to financing.
The ministry was looking at implementing the reforms through legislation, regulations or policy, he added.
On FDI, Sim said the government had also revised its investment incentive system under the new incentive framework, with tax incentives linked to key performance indicators (KPIs).

The criteria included creating high-paying jobs for Malaysians and developing local supply chains, with the approach intended to ensure foreign investments generated spillover benefits for MSMEs instead of benefiting only large companies.

Meanwhile, Sim said GLCs and government-linked investment companies (GLICs) had an important role in developing local industries and helping smaller businesses grow, while avoiding crowding them out of the market.

He said the government had instructed GLCs and GLICs to invest up to RM25 billion annually in developing local supply chains, adding that part of the funds should be invested domestically to build local industries.

Sim said strengthening MSMEs was crucial as they accounted for about 96 per cent of business establishments in Malaysia, although their contribution to gross domestic product (GDP) remained below 40 per cent.

The government was targeting MSMEs to contribute at least 40 per cent to GDP, he said, noting that while SMEs also made up the overwhelming majority of business establishments in many developed economies, their contribution to GDP was higher.
8e139f205de28e8f: KUALA LUMPUR: French President Emmanuel Macron is expected to visit Malaysia in less than three weeks, providing an opportunity to strengthen economic and business ties between the two countries.

Sim said Malaysia and France have enjoyed more than 350 years of trade ties.

He cited Airbus and Safran as key players in Malaysia's aerospace ecosystem, while STMicroelectronics has established high-volume manufacturing operations in Johor.
On trade, Sim said negotiations for a Malaysia-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) were progressing, with the latest round of discussions held in Brussels in September.

"These are very exciting times for Malaysia and the European Union, especially France. I think this is on the right track and in the right direction," he said.
An FTA with the EU could provide further opportunities to expand market access and strengthen trade and investment flows between Malaysia and European businesses.
Meanwhile, French ambassador to Malaysia Marc Abensour said Macron's upcoming visit would provide a significant opportunity to elevate bilateral relations to the level of a strategic partnership.

He said it would be the first visit by a French president to Malaysia in nearly a decade, following Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim's visit to Paris in July 2025 and French Minister for Foreign Trade Nicolas Forissier's visit to Malaysia.
Abensour said France and Malaysia were increasingly aligned in their efforts to strengthen economic security and protect critical supply chains amid growing geopolitical uncertainties.
"At the core of this relationship is a partnership for sovereignty. In an era where trade, energy and technology are increasingly weaponised, economic security is paramount.
"We must secure critical value chains to strengthen our mutual resilience," he said.
Abensour said France is now Malaysia's second-largest European investor, with its investment stock growing by 190 per cent over the past decade, he said.
Bilateral trade between the two countries exceeded RM22 billion in 2025, representing an 11 per cent increase, driven partly by a 40 per cent surge in French exports, particularly in aerospace.
He also highlighted Safran's €113 million expansion of its facility in Negri Sembilan, which is expected to double its capacity.

He said French companies had established a significant presence in Malaysia, employing more than 30,000 people and supporting the country's ambition to move up the value chain through high-technology industries and higher-skilled jobs.
Abensour said the presidential visit would also feature a business forum focusing on three strategic areas: digital sovereignty, aerospace and energy transition.
He said both countries could benefit from closer collaboration in developing diversified and resilient energy systems.

"Accelerating the transition to diversified, resilient energy systems is an urgent priority for both our nations, creating tremendous opportunities for French and Malaysian companies to jointly build the industries of tomorrow," he said.
While acknowledging Malaysia's economic resilience and projected growth of around five per cent in 2026 and 2027, he said reliance on crude-related subsidies carried significant fiscal costs.

Accelerating the transition towards diversified and resilient energy systems would therefore create opportunities for companies from both countries to develop new industries and technologies, he added.

d746f8602acb3702: NASA has posted a contract opportunity notice, also known as a request for information, from commercial space orgs who can service the Hubble Space Telescope.

Hubble was always looked after by NASA astronauts flying on the Space Shuttle, yet the last Hubble Space Telescope (HST) servicing mission was the STS-125 Space Shuttle flight, launched on May 11, 2009. At the time, scientists hoped the mission would add another five years of operational life to the venerable spacecraft. Almost 17 years on, the HST (aka Hubble) is still delivering science.

However, time is running out for the observatory. NASA reckons there is a 10 percent chance it could reenter the Earth's atmosphere by September 2032, rising to 50 percent by December 2033. As the end of the Swift mission showed, increased solar activity can cause greater-than-anticipated atmospheric drag.

Also, like Swift, Hubble has no propulsion system, and so when it reenters (as it will, without intervention), the reentry will be uncontrolled. Hubble is sufficiently massive that there is a remote chance somebody on the ground could have a very bad day when that happens.
As such, one mission option suggested by NASA is a vehicle to grapple the observatory and perform a controlled reentry and disposal.

However, there are other options. Something to boost the telescope's orbit up to at least 600 km, or another to "enhance its ongoing performance and increase its resilience and expected on-orbit lifetime."

Both are intriguing options, and important since, as NASA acknowledges, no replacement for Hubble is expected before the 2040s, when the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) could become operational. Despite the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Nancy Roman Space Telescope, Hubble remains in high demand, with NASA reporting a 7:1 oversubscription.

Before becoming NASA Administrator, Jared Isaacman advocated a SpaceX mission to boost the Hubble, but the idea was ultimately rejected. Similar plans could now be dusted off. NASA's requirement is for a mission to occur by 2032, and not harm the Hubble.

A soft-capture mechanism was fitted to Hubble during the STS-125 mission, which will mean docking with the spacecraft will be easier than the grappling planned for Swift. Then, the question is what to do with it. A controlled reentry is one option. The other options – boosting to a higher altitude or "enhance its ongoing performance and increase its resilience" are intriguing. Northrop Grumman's Mission Extension Vehicle (MEV), for example, is capable of on-orbit servicing and extending the lifetime of satellites. The Hubble is an order of magnitude more challenging, but the technological hurdles can be overcome with time and funding.

Last year, The Register spoke with Dr John Grunsfeld, one of the astronauts (now retired) who worked on Hubble during the STS-125 mission. Grunsfeld told us that the veteran spacecraft faced death by a thousand cuts as its budget was whittled away. The observatory itself recently switched from three to one gyro mode (the telescope uses gyros to control where it is pointed) to eke out a few more years of operational life.

At this point, NASA is looking for information and comment – this isn't a request for proposals. There is no indication of how much the agency expects to pay. However, the timescale is immutable. Without intervention, Hubble will make an uncontrolled reentry in the coming years. ®

a4bbda93949cff44: The University of Manchester is scrutinizing why growing adoption of AI tools has so far failed to translate into the forecast productivity gains, however, researchers are struggling to give easy answers to close the "AI ambition gap."

In a report, also called “The AI Ambition Gap,” the UK university’s Productivity Institute mulls over the advances that have been made in AI and the expanding adoption of it, and sets out what business leaders and policymakers can do to realize the potential benefits.
The report was commissioned by IT services biz Bytes Technology Group.

One reason for the lack of results is that organizations have invested heavily up front on retraining staff, reorganizing the way they work and other adjustments. Those costs show up straight away, yet the payback doesn’t come until later.

Another reason, the report suggests, is that AI tools can raise productivity at the level of individual tasks, but these gains do not automatically translate into greater productivity across a worker’s whole role or the entire organization.

It cites the example of software developers using GitHub Copilot who completed around 26 percent more tasks, and professionals using ChatGPT for routine writing and analysis that reduced task completion time by 40 percent while improving the quality of the output by 18 percent.

However, a study of AI dev tools found these have increased coding activity by approximately 240 percent, while the number of actual software releases has only grown by about 30 percent. The gap is due to humans still needing to check and test their work before release.

High task exposure to AI does not automatically make a worker more productive, the researchers say. Jobs typically combine automatable activities with tasks that require judgement, coordination, client interaction and critical thinking. As AI removes or accelerates some activities, those complementary human tasks become the constraint on time saving and the translation of task-level gains into greater productivity

Job outcomes therefore depend on task composition and complementary human expertise, the report continues. It suggests AI may in part displace labor from existing tasks, while also creating new tasks in which workers retain a comparative advantage.

This could be good news for the UK, the researchers state. Compared with five other nations (US, Brazil, Colombia, India and South Africa), Blighty has the highest share of workers in occupations with both high exposure to AI and "high complementarity," it claims. This is in part related to the country’s large financial and professional business service sectors, which are characterized by a high share of cognitive occupations.
This is just as well, as the government is pinning its hopes on using AI to drive economic recovery in a strategy outlined at the start of last year.

Britain's AI sector is relatively large by European standards, and the report cites recent OECD estimates that high-exposure economies such as the UK and the US could see annual labor productivity gains of between 0.4 and 1.3 percentage points.

Even an annual uplift of around 0.5 to 0.7 percentage points would represent a significant step change relative to the UK’s stalled productivity performance over the past decade, it says, if this effect is sustained.

The Productivity Institute lists several "mutually reinforcing enablers" to help organizations close the ambition gap it identifies. None is particularly surprising, especially if you have read other reports advising on corporate success with AI adoption.

One is management setting strategic direction for the organization, another is strengthening worker capabilities through greater knowledge and data literacy to help organizations turn individual insight into shared learning. Others include implementing AI governance and focusing on applications that can create new products, improve core processes or solve previously intractable problems.
"AI's productivity potential becomes real when faster tasks lead to better performance across the business," said Bart van Ark, professor at The Productivity Institute and lead author on the report.

"The ambition gap lies between those individual efficiencies and sustained business results. Closing it requires firms to invest in management, skills and the redesign of workflows alongside the technology."

The conclusion is that companies must have faith and keep investing in AI, and eventually the benefits will come if you are doing the right things. These include focusing on high-value use cases linked to strategy, customer value and operational bottlenecks, plus treating AI as a workplace redesign.
Policymakers could help out businesses here by assisting identifying relevant opportunities, the report says, to reduce adoption risks and uncertainty.

Other reports published this week were more defined in their message: Gartner said 75 percent of corporate board members have yet to see any productivity gains or reduce costs from AI use, and private equity biz Apollo Global Management reckons only the biggest tech vendors are enjoying some sort of AI payoff. ®

13ee6f913c1b831e: DAMASCUS, Oct 30 — Taxi driver Mohammed Kanaan drives his shiny new electric car around Damascus’s rundown streets, hoping for higher profits as spiking petrol prices made his old car too expensive to run.

He is among some in the Syrian capital who are steering towards electric cars — mostly Chinese-made — after repeated fuel shortages during the country’s civil war and petrol price hikes, most recently due to the Middle East war.
“I used to have a car that ran on petrol but lately fuel quality has been low and prices have gone up,” said Kanaan, 42, who had barely been covering his operating costs.
“In the end, I decided to buy an electric car and set up a charging point,” he told AFP.
Before the overthrow of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad nearly two years ago, it was rare to see modern cars in Damascus, particularly after civil war erupted in 2011.
The economy tanked, and imports of new vehicles screeched to a halt due to Western sanctions, which have largely been lifted since the new authorities took power.
When the new authorities came to power and reduced tariffs, some 100,000 cars were imported, before they halted imports of used cars due to concerns over quality.
Not all Syrians can afford to make the switch to electric, with the percentage remaining negligible as most still live in poverty.
Sub-par petrol
Some Syrians took to the streets in protest last month after petrol costs jumped by 26 percent following a government decision to increase prices amid global surges due to the regional conflict.
Kanaan said his old gas-guzzler needed US$26 (RM105) worth of petrol to drive around 200km, but he can now cover the same distance for around US$6 by charging his car through the state power grid.
During the civil war, Damascus experienced lengthy power cuts, but supply has improved in recent months as authorities seek to revive the economy and ailing infrastructure.
Still, some people with electric cars have set up solar charging stations to dodge the problem altogether.
Other issues persist. Drivers told AFP that a few weeks earlier, a batch of poor-quality petrol caused problems and breakdowns for hundreds of cars.
The energy ministry subsequently said the sub-par petrol had reached markets due to an “operational error”, pledging accountability and compensation for affected motorists.
Syria depends partly on imported petrol, leaving its people susceptible to shortages and long lines at stations.
Citing energy ministry figures, state news agency SANA said last month that Syria’s average daily petrol supply was around 2.32 million litres, around a third of it imported.
‘Everybody is happy’
Walking between vehicles at his family company’s showroom outside Damascus, Hamza Sukkar, 25, said electric car purchases had accelerated recently.

“For around eight months, the demand for electric cars and plug-in hybrid vehicles has increased due to the rise in petrol prices and its low quality, pushing people to turn to electric cars,” he told AFP.
The cheapest petrol-powered car in his showroom costs more than US$12,000, while the electric cars start at US$9,000, making them an increasingly attractive choice.
“We now sell three to four electric cars for every petrol-powered car,” Sukkar said.
This reflects global figures, where one in four new cars sold worldwide in 2025 was electric, according to the International Energy Agency.
Though Syria as a whole is far from that proportion, the market for electric cars is growing rapidly.
Transport companies are also noticing a shift in gear.

At the headquarters of YallaGo!, a leading ride-hailing app in Damascus, local operations manager Rami al-Hamad said “the number of electric cars registered with us has risen by around 20 per cent” in recent months.
He attributed the change to “lower operating costs compared to running petrol-powered cars”, allowing drivers a chance of higher profits.
But many Syrians lack the funds to buy the cars in the first place, while ensuring regular charging and maintenance can also be a challenge, Hamad noted.
Taxi driver Ahmed al-Lahham, who has been using an electric car for three months, was among those who appeared satisfied with the change.
“Electric cars are new and economical. Passengers are happy with a new car, and I’m happy with the lower costs... so everybody is happy,” he said. — AFP
17233aba2f705efe: LONDON, Oct 30 — A leading UK conservation charity announced today it had raised some £30 million (RM163 million) via crowdfunding to buy a huge swathe of rolling moorlands and forests to transform into a sanctuary for biodiversity.
After an intense two-year campaign, the Wildlife Trusts has purchased the whole 3,800-hectares of the Rothbury Estate in northern Northumberland, England’s largest land acquisition in three decades.

The purchase of the sprawling site, as large as central London, will be the opportunity “to create something very special for generations to come”, said renowned environmentalist David Attenborough, who backed the campaign.
The trusts’ director general Craig Bennett thanked the thousands of people who had donated to the campaign.
“Working alongside local communities, farmers and fellow land managers who know and care for this landscape so deeply, we can help this special place continue to thrive,” he added in a statement.
Some £17 million towards the cost of the land was donated by 25,000 individuals.
The estate was sold by the Percy family — the Dukes of Northumberland — who had owned it for almost eight centuries, using the land until 2022 for grouse shooting.

A red soldier beetle on the Rothbury Estate in Northumberland, north-east England. A leading UK conservation charity announced October 30, it had raised some £30 million via crowdfunding to buy a huge swathe of rolling moorlands and forests to transform into a sanctuary for biodiversity. — AFP pic

The current duke’s son, Max Percy, said it was too difficult to manage from his home in southern England, and after putting it up for sale in 2023 agreed to give the Wildlife Trusts two years to raise the funds.

The association also received £5 million from the National Lottery Heritage Fund, which finances projects to protect UK heritage, as well as a pledge of £1.94 million from the Department of Environment.

Bordered by several nature reserves and restoration project areas, the Wildlife Trusts and owners of those sites dream of one day creating a 65-kilometre-long biodiversity corridor stretching inland from the estate by the North Sea.
It would provide a much-needed sanctuary for wildlife, such as cuckoos, butterflies, pine martens and golden eagles as well as red squirrels, in the densely-populated, nature-ravaged UK.
The Wildlife Trusts also want to encourage the dozen farmers, mainly keeping sheep, to adopt more environmentally friendly practices, using fewer pesticides and chemical fertilisers.

The UK government is far from its objective to conserve and manage 30 percent of its land and seas for nature by 2030. According to the Wildlife Trusts, the acquisition of the Rothbury Estate could help it meet its goal. — AFP
6087501939d87ced: SRASHEN, Oct 30 — From a hillside above Armenia’s Shikahogh nature reserve, local official Marat Harutyunyan pointed to forests cleared for Azerbaijan’s military, construction Yerevan says threatens rare wildlife and the livelihoods of local villagers.
The battle over the fate of the forest exposes the deep, lingering tensions between the two countries as they seek to broker a lasting peace after three decades of hostility and multiple wars.
In advances in 2021-2022, Azerbaijan captured parts of the reserve that lies along the countries’ shared border.
The conflict culminated in 2023 when it retook Karabakh from Armenian separatists, prompting the entire Armenian population — some 100,000 people — to flee.
The two countries have since tried to broker a permanent peace deal and last year initialled an agreement in Washington, seen as a major step towards ratification.
But while the capitals talk of detente, in the rural southern Armenian region of Syunik, residents are still on edge.
Nearby Azerbaijani military positions and landmines cause them to fear for their safety.
“All the land is directly in the enemy’s sights,” said Harut Aghatelyan, a 35-year-old biologist who has worked at the reserve for the past 15 years.
He has repeatedly found dead animals with missing legs — blown up in landmine blasts that echo through the woods.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A view shows Azeri military sites in forests of the Shikahogh nature reserve as seen from the vicinity of the Armenian village of Srashen October 22, 2026. — AFP pic
‘Cut down everything’
After seizing part of the area, Azerbaijan’s military is now building wide forest paths to improve access and supply lines.
Above Srashen village, pale roads snake through the autumn woodland, and a police checkpoint blocks the old route towards the reserve.
Hilltop Armenian and Azerbaijani flags mark competing positions, sometimes only a few hundred metres apart.

Azerbaijan’s advances have left a nearby village, Nerkin-Hand, surrounded on three sides, as its troops “occupy more than 2,700 hectares of the reserve and several hundred hectares of agricultural land”, Harutyunyan, the Armenia official, said.
“They cut down everything, without checking whether a species is in the Red Book or not,” he added, referring to Armenia’s register of endangered species.
Armenia has highlighted the issue as it hosts the UN’s COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, where states gather to review global efforts to protect species and their habitats.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Forest expert Ayser Ghazaryan talks in the vicinity of the village of Srashen in Armenia's Shikahogh nature reserve October 22, 2026. — AFP pic
‘Large-scale ecocide’
Azerbaijan has rejected accusations of occupying Armenian territory, saying that the border in the area has not been formally demarcated.
Established in 1958, Shikahogh covers roughly 12,400 hectares of oak and beech forests, plane tree groves and yew — an endangered species.
It also shelters Caucasian leopards, brown bears and bezoar goats.
Harutyunyan fears tree felling and engineering work could trigger landslides, mudflows and rockfalls.
But the military presence and landmines have made assessing the consequences on the ground impossible, residents and specialists say.
“Nobody knows the true extent of the damage,” said forest expert Ayser Ghazaryan.
His analysis of satellite images indicates earthworks across about 90 hectares, including some 60 hectares of forest, and the felling of an estimated 14,000 to 16,000 cubic metres of timber.
It is not clear whether a full recovery from what he called “large-scale ecocide” is even possible.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Muraz Arzumanyan rides on a car in the vicinity of the village of Srashen in Armenia’s Shikahogh nature reserve October 22, 2026. — AFP pic
‘No security’
The loss of farmland and grazing is also threatening locals’ livelihoods.
Muraz Arzumanyan, 26, is unemployed and lives with his parents. Trained as a metallurgist, he previously served as a soldier with the Armenian army.
“How can I start a family and have children when there is no security?” he said.
“I cannot imagine my child growing up here, going into the yard to play and run around, constantly in someone’s sights.”
The school in Shikahogh has just one pupil.
Elderly residents say they can no longer visit relatives’ graves.
The municipality runs free buses and hopes those who left will one day return.
Aghatelyan, the biologist, meanwhile is determined to stay.
He raises rabbits and refuses to leave the village where his family has lived for generations.
“I was born and grew up surrounded by forests. I love these forests,” he said.
“My child is 18 months old, and I want him to grow up here.” — AFP
616acf3c46324517: MUNICH, Oct 30 — Bayern Munich host long-time foes Borussia Dortmund tomorrow after a rollercoaster week punctuated by coach Vincent Kompany’s hospitalisation and Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph.
Germany captain Joshua Kimmich, a mainstay in Bayern’s midfield, has missed three games on compassionate leave due to the sudden death of his father.
Luis Diaz, Manuel Neuer, Jamal Musiala and Aleksander Pavlovic have all battled injury for the defending champions.
Bayern’s issues have pushed what is usually the biggest match of the Bundesliga season into the background.
The only unbeaten teams after seven matchdays, Bayern and Dortmund sit level on points, with tomorrow’s hosts ahead on goal difference.
Dortmund coach Niko Kovac said Thursday his side, who have also battled injury issues this season, were “getting closer” to Bayern.
But Bayern’s main task will be to shut out the noise and focus on the game.
‘Highs and the lows’
After showing signs of illness in Bayern’s 6-1 thumping of RB Leipzig, Kompany returned to the dugout for last week’s 2-2 home draw with Arsenal, but collapsed on the training pitch two days later.
Later diagnosed with meningeal irritation, the Belgian was released after five days in hospital on Wednesday, but Bayern said it will likely be “weeks, not days” until he returns to work.
Charged with carrying Kompany’s clipboard, assistant Aaron Danks hoped the waves of emotion would galvanise the side.
“You’ve seen the full extremes of life in the last week. The joys and highs for Harry, and the lows of some of the things we’ve had to go through in the last seven days,” Danks said Tuesday.
“Internally we have to find a balance... In these moments, you understand the human being is the most important thing...
“These moments do bring you closer, because they’re challenging moments, but to get through these moments we’ve had to rely on our team spirit and our togetherness.”
At the other end of the emotional spectrum is Kane, who received the game’s highest individual honour on Monday.
Kane said Wednesday it had been a “crazy week” for himself and the club, adding: “I get quite embarrassed by it, but I know it’s a big deal.
“It’s been a whirlwind 48 hours, it’s nice to be back here and feel at home again.”
Kane became the first Englishman since Michael Owen in 2001 and just the fifth ever to win the Ballon d’Or, with some calling for the England captain to be knighted.
“I certainly wouldn’t say no, that’s for sure,” Kane said. “But it’ll feel a bit weird everyone calling me ‘sir’, so we’ll just keep it as Harry.
“If it happens, it’ll be incredible and something I’ll be massively proud of, but I don’t want to get too carried away.”
World Cup winner Lothar Matthaeus, who won the Ballon d’Or in 1990 with Inter Milan, said Kane would respond well to the recognition.
“When you win the Ballon d’Or, the story is not over. It has to motivate you,” Matthaeus told AFP and other media on Wednesday.
“For me, for sure it was an honour to win, but football is a team sport. This Ballon d’Or is not only for Kane, it’s also for Bayern Munich.” — AFP
e0630518d70431be: CAPE TOWN, Oct 30 — Ntombekhaya Makeleni stopped using the communal toilets in her Cape Town neighbourhood after a group of men tried to force their way in as she was inside one day before dawn.
Now the 53-year-old relies on a bucket that is emptied outside later, as do many others in the deprived township of Khayelitsha where thousands live in informal shacks with no sanitation.
The lack of a decent toilet is pushing Makeleni to the polls in South Africa’s local government elections next week. “I will be voting because after voting, things will be fixed,” she told AFP.

The November 4 poll promises a glimpse into whether frustrations with local government failures are changing political loyalties — including for the once long-dominant African National Congress (ANC) — ahead of the 2029 general election.
A lack of basic services such as water and power, crumbling infrastructure and high unemployment are high among the concerns of more than 29 million people registered to vote.
In the east coast city of Durban, 27-year-old Nikesh Nunkoo said water cuts in his neighbourhood of Shallcross could last anywhere from three days to two weeks.
Having voted in three previous elections, he was still weighing whether to cast a ballot this time. “I don’t have any hope that things would be better in the next five years,” he said.
Nkanyiso Hadebe, 24, who lives in an informal settlement in the city’s Chatsworth area, was clear. “I will not vote because voting changes nothing,” he said.

More than 500 parties are registered with the electoral commission, reflecting a political landscape that has become increasingly fragmented as support for traditional powerhouses, such as the ANC of late anti-apartheid icon Nelson Mandela, has eroded.
An Ipsos survey published in March found nearly half of South Africans felt no political party represented their views, while only 38 per cent believed their municipality was doing its job well.
‘A shame’
For the first time since democracy in 1994, the ANC slid under the symbolic 50-per cent threshold in 2021’s local elections. It lost its national parliamentary majority in 2024.

The second-largest party, the liberal Democratic Alliance (DA), governs Cape Town and has run a determined campaign for Johannesburg, playing up the failures of the ANC-led council running the economic hub.
But in Cape Town itself, the contrast between affluent suburbs and poorer townships remains stark three decades after the end of apartheid.
“Residents, especially in townships, are not asking for much. They want basic services,” political commentator Kuhle Zwakala of Stellenbosch University said.
“To be talking about electricity, water and sanitation issues 30 years into democracy is a shame.”
Not all voters will be swayed by service delivery issues, said Oscar van Heerden, a senior research fellow at the Centre for African Diplomacy and Leadership.
“There is also an identity factor,” he told AFP, noting enduring support for the ANC in historically black townships and for the DA among the white electorate.
A newcomer to local government elections is ex-president Jacob Zuma’s MK party, which secured third place in the previous national polls.
For some younger South Africans without liberation-era loyalties and most affected by the 33 per cent unemployment rate, voting seems pointless.
Ntokozo Mthethwa, a 21-year-old IT student from Durban’s Umlazi township, doubted any party could deliver on its promises. “I see no future for me here,” he said.
Coalitions
Voter turnout will be a key factor on Wednesday: only 46 per cent of registered voters cast ballots in the 2021 local elections, compared with 58.6 per cent in the 2024 polls.
The results, which are due from Sunday, are likely to reinforce the trend towards coalition governments and test whether they can produce stable local councils.
Since the last municipal elections, no party was able to hold a majority in just under a third of the 257 councils, according to research by the Mapungubwe Institute for Strategic Reflection.
By February 2026, 74 municipalities were governed by coalitions or minority administrations, it said. — AFP

9260761e03b27b17: BANGKOK, Oct 30 — Malaysian physician Dr Mary Suma Cardosa has made history as the first Asian to become president of the International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) in the organisation’s more than 50-year history.
Cardosa assumed the two-year presidency, which runs until 2028, at the closing of the 2026 World Congress on Pain in Bangkok on Friday, succeeding Andrew Rice of the United Kingdom.
In a statement issued by IASP, she said her presidency would focus on advancing pain science, strengthening healthcare education and improving access to effective pain management worldwide.

“Pain affects people in every country, but access to effective pain care remains profoundly unequal,” she said, highlighting the importance of education, stronger clinical services and multidisciplinary cooperation.

An anaesthesiologist with more than three decades of experience in pain medicine, Cardosa has played a pivotal role in developing Malaysia’s pain management services and strengthening pain education in the country and across Southeast Asia.
Her contributions include establishing the Health Ministry’s first acute pain service in 1993 and the country’s first multidisciplinary pain clinic in 2000.
She also spearheaded Malaysia’s Pain Free Hospital initiative, launched in 2011 to improve pain recognition and management in healthcare facilities.
Cardosa previously made history in 2011 as the first woman to serve as president of the Malaysian Medical Association.

Beyond Malaysia, Cardosa has contributed to regional and international initiatives to expand pain-care capacity, including training healthcare professionals and supporting the development of multidisciplinary services in resource-limited countries.

As IASP president, she will lead the association’s global efforts to advance pain research and translate scientific knowledge into better patient care, alongside the implementation of its 2026-2030 Strategic Plan.

IASP is a leading international organisation dedicated to the study of pain and the translation of scientific knowledge into improved pain relief worldwide. It brings together scientists, clinicians, healthcare professionals, and policymakers to advance pain research, education, and care. — Bernama
15a682682dd2b890: LONDON: Britain's competition watchdog opened an investigation into whether Meta was imposing "exploitative" new terms allowing it to use media content for its own products, including AI, without giving publishers adequate choice.

dabac286004ebbf1: KUALA LUMPUR: Bestinet Sdn Bhd has been ordered to pay RM10,000 in costs after the High Court threw out its attempt to serve legal papers on Bloomberg LP in the US by courier.

The court allowed Bloomberg LP’s application to set aside the service. Bestinet had in March this year sent its writ and statement of claim to Bloomberg’s offices in New York and Washington DC via courier.
The court said serving legal papers outside Malaysia involves the sovereignty of another country, as it seeks to bring a foreign party under Malaysian jurisdiction.
It said that although courier, email and the internet have made service easier, respect for another country’s sovereignty must still be observed.

Because Malaysia is not part of the Hague Convention, which sets standard rules for serving papers between countries, such service must strictly follow Order 11 of the Rules of Court 2012 and the laws of the receiving country.
The court found Bestinet had breached both.

It also rejected Bestinet’s argument that the issue no longer mattered because Bloomberg LP had already entered appearance in court, saying that appearing to challenge bad service does not make the service valid.

In April, Bloomberg (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd had applied to strike out a libel suit filed by Bestinet and its founder Aminul Islam Abdul Nor over an article linking them to a migrant worker recruitment syndicate.
In June, the High Court dismissed Bloomberg’s application to strike out the libel suit, allowing Bestinet's legal action to proceed.
e55f3be4fd89e714: KUALA LUMPUR: MAA Group Bhd's external auditors have highlighted a material uncertainty related to the group’s ability to continue as a going concern, the company reported in a filing with Bursa Malaysia.

The company reported losses of RM106.9 million for the 2026 financial year which ended on June 30, with the group's current liabilities of RM102.5 million exceeding its current assets of RM99.4 million by RM3.1 million.
It said its external auditors, KPMG PLT, have issued an unqualified audit opinion on its financial statements for the financial year.

“These conditions indicate that material uncertainties exist that may cast significant doubt on the ability of the group to continue as a going concern and to meet its financial obligations over the next 12 months from the date of the authorisation of these financial statements,” said the group.
MAA said the group's financial conditions are temporary and that it can meet its financial obligations through several mitigation measures.

These include the proposed disposal of equity interests in certain non-consolidated entities, identified properties and a hotel operation, which are expected to generate proceeds of RM139.1 million. Additionally, this involves ongoing efforts to recover credit-impaired loans from its financial services operation, with an expected gross settlement of RM38 million.

MAA said it has also secured funding through the issuance of investment notes by a subsidiary and is pursuing further issuances to raise additional funds. In addition, it has obtained continued financial support from a substantial shareholder.
“Accordingly, the directors consider it appropriate to prepare the group's and the company's financial statements for FY2026 on a going concern basis,” said MAA.

5035702997edf71b: <!--kg-card-end: html--> My ears perked up when I heard Apple’s new foldable phones were cracking. I licked my lips when the company announced it’s releasing a touch-screen laptop. This was a company that once charged $19 for a polishing cloth, asked $200 for a VESA mount, and sold $700 wheels for the Mac Pro. Now it’s borrowing tired ideas from its competitors and launching hardware its previous leaders rejected.

The once dominant company is struggling to find its feet in an AI-driven post-Tim Cook world. John Ternus is the new CEO — a 25 year veteran of the company with a track record of pushing harebrained hardware schemes like the much reviled Touch Bar and lawsuit inducing butterfly keyboard.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> With Ternus at the helm, I feel there’s a good chance Apple’s best days are behind it, that it will have to make do with less, that it’s déclassé. Apple, blindsided by AI and relying on crowdpleasing hardware gimmicks, is downwardly mobile. It’s in its slop era. The company that once asked consumers to “Think Different” is now releasing hardware that’s just like everything else on the market.

Apple is not adjusting to this new position well. AI boosters agree that Siri AI is awful. Apple HomeView is a $300 Apple Watch meant to replace the family hearth. The iPhone Duo has only been out for a few days and all people can talk about is the cracks, yet Ternus is on the cover of Time Magazine this week holding the folding iPhone Duo and staring at the camera. “The other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy,” Ternus told Time. Many people holding cracked iPhone Duos this week are learning just what (not) cheap and crappy looks like.

Flailing from crackgate, Apple announced the launch of a touch-screen laptop, an idea Steve Jobs extensively tested and said “doesn’t work,” an idea Cook once compared to combining a toaster with a refrigerator. What’s next? What if the toaster-refigerator folded? Ternus has been trying to make an 18-inch foldable iPad happen for years. Maybe Apple will solve the screen cracking issues by then. Or maybe Ternus will continue to try to put a hat on a hat.
I have been waiting for this moment for more than a decade. I am relishing Apple’s recent trajectory more than I should. I confess I harbor a secret and petty grudge.

In 2010, when Apple released the iPhone 4 I was working as a floor manager at a Banana Republic in Dallas. I was interested in smart phones, of course, but Dallas is an expensive city and the iPhone was a luxury. I made do with my Motorola Razr. But the suit-wearing middle management retail psychopaths that were my coworkers saw my lack of an iPhone as a weakness. It was not, as they say now, On Brand.

I had started at the store in the stock room, working my way up to manage the backroom before ascending to a coveted position on the sales floor. The other managers made it clear that a Razr was a “backroom” phone and someone in a prominent position on the floor needed to be seen using an iPhone.
At first, I was not told to buy an iPhone. The message came in the form of subtle and not so subtle bullying deployed over weeks.
“Still using that old phone?” they’d say.“Didn’t you get a raise?” someone would ask a week later.
“Try not to use that thing on the sales floor,” one co-worker told me, pointing at my Razr. “We’re trying to project a certain image here.”

The social pressure had the opposite of its intended effect. I resisted. Eventually one of the friendlier managers pulled me aside. He told me that my colleagues thought it was weird that I didn't have an iPhone. He said I needed to buy one to fit in and he said the store could give me an advance on my paycheck to make it happen.

Ever the contrarian and pissed I was experiencing high school style bullying as a full grown adult, I threw in with Google instead. I got an HTC Dream. My coworkers weren’t happy, but they stopped bringing up the iPhone.

I’ve been an Android user ever since and studiously avoided Apple products until I broke down a few years ago and bought a Macbook Air. Time heals all wounds and Windows laptops are garbage. I’d even been considering changing from Android to iPhone because the privacy features are more robust. I’ve never been averse to a fast food meal either and maybe I’m a little more comfortable with Apple now that the cracks are starting to show in the foldable phone.
