7ee69c9901d03744: The UK's top health quango has called on family doctors to figure out how to preserve health information and get in touch with patients after a website provider collapsed earlier this month.

NHS England has taken the unusual step of writing to GPs, warning them of the risks to patient information and continuity of service following the disruption to potentially hundreds of practices around the UK.

Silicon Practice Digital Health Solutions — owned by Schappit Ltd — has gone into administration. Reports suggest some GP websites have gone offline completely. Practice managers fear the extra workload and are struggling to stand up alternative forms of communication since the switch to digital channels.
NHS England is the government unit which runs the health service in England, but it is not directly responsible for GP practices, the vast majority of which are independent contractors.
Nonetheless, the quango’s CTO, Kevin Humphries, wrote to practices and NHS organizations this week outlining his priorities in mitigating the impact of tech service collapse.

They include finding ways of preserving any historical patient information, particularly where it has not been moved to clinical systems, managing the online consultation backlog to make sure no additional requests are added, and identifying channels for patient access until new online systems are available.

Practices should also consider whether they have a legal obligation to tell the Information Commissioner's Office if the "availability, integrity, confidentiality or recoverability of personal data" is affected, according to the communication seen by The Register.

NHS management bodies called Integrated Care Boards are responsible for GP IT service arrangements, making sure they include "clinical safety, data security, cyber security and business continuity assurance across the GP IT supply chain," Humphries said.

They need to find someone to lead their recovery plan and contact affected practices and trusts. They should also "work with practices and other impacted organizations to support them in revisiting and assessing whether to enact business continuity and disaster recovery plans," Humphries said.

Questions over how an urgent NHS-wide response is required for the collapse of a relatively small supplier may come later. Among them will be the due diligence conducted before Schappit Ltd was added to a government framework in July.

GP and open-source tech campaigner Marcus Baw has published a free, open source template for an alternative website should practices want to bring systems in-house. He said the template is based on accessible NHS web standards, and has the same look-and-feel of common NHS websites.

"Practices can deploy it for free, and take back in-house control of their own website. It's a replacement website template which practices can set up using Claude Code in the web in an afternoon," he said. ®
81328d5ce6bd7697: LONDON, Oct 30 — Researchers have warned that the social media “manosphere” should be treated as a public health issue similar to the tobacco industry, in a report published in The Lancet today.
The report looks at the so-called manosphere, which it defines as the collection of online communities united by shared beliefs about “masculinity, misogyny, and male victimisation”.
It details the health impacts of the manosphere — which blames feminism for disadvantaging men and a masculinity crisis — including on men’s mental health and violence against women.
It also says the movement “delegitimises” men and boys seeking help.

“By reframing the manosphere as a public health issue rather than just a regulatory issue, we open up a number of additional policy levers that public health approaches can provide,” author Sarah J Hawkes told BBC Radio 4.

The University College London global public health professor called for a coordinated government response to the crisis, including better access to skills and jobs as well as to mental health services.
She also pointed out that people make “a lot of money” through such messaging, including by encouraging boys and men to invest in financial schemes and buy unregulated supplements and hormones.

Co-author Kent Buse, health policy professor at Monash University Malaysia, said the manosphere thrived on online platforms deploying a similar playbook to the tobacco industry: “blame the individual, and call regulation an attack on freedom.”

“Boys and men are not the problem,” said Buse. “The problem is the conditions that leave them isolated and without a secure future, and the companies that profit from their anger and insecurity.” — AFP
e5c7d310b6b456c7: VATICAN CITY: Pope Leo XIV warned Friday against giving artificial intelligence agents legal personhood or rights, saying the responsibility for their actions should lie firmly with their human creators.

"Machines are tools, not persons," he said in a speech to leading international AI experts gathered at the Vatican for a dialogue on the technology's future and the responsibilities of the scientific community and public institutions.

"So-called artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain, do not mature through relationships and do not know from within what love, work, friendship or responsibility mean," the pope said.

"Today, some propose granting these systems rights, or even legal personhood. Such an approach risks obscuring human responsibility and leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity," he added.
The debate over the risks of the technology has intensified in recent months, fuelled by several incidents of systems taking unauthorised actions and apocalyptic warnings from industry professionals.
Leo, 71, has warned repeatedly about the need to ensure AI is used ethically. His first encyclical, published in May, called for putting the technology at the service of human dignity.
He said Friday that the future of artificial intelligence "is not predetermined", and humans have "the responsibility to guide, change and, when necessary, reject its applications."
There are some decisions that must never be delegated, the head of the Catholic Church said.

"Those affecting human life, freedom and the use of force must always remain subject to effective, informed and responsible human oversight," Leo said, repeating his call for a ban on lethal autonomous weapons.
Intelligent technologies must be directed toward the common good, he said.
There was an "urgent" need for "shared standards, independent oversight and clear mechanisms of accountability".
It was key to ensure "decisions concerning the development and use of AI can be examined, challenged when necessary, and accompanied by appropriate remedies for any harm caused," he added.
9a6416611e7f74a5: SHAH ALAM, Oct 30 — The High Court here today ruled that a joint management body (JMB) cannot impose a blanket ban on keeping pets in private residential units through its house rules.

In a statement, lawyers Rajesh Nagarajan and Sachpreetraj Singh Sohanpal, who represented former national hurdler Noraseela Mohd Khalid, said the court partially allowed her application against the JMB of Shang Villa Condominium, declaring that House Rule 9.0 could not be used to prohibit her from keeping her three cats in her residential unit.

They said the court ruled that the mere presence of pets in a residential unit did not constitute a breach of house rules and that any enforcement action must be based on By-law 14 of the Strata Management (Maintenance and Management) Regulations 2015 and supported by evidence.
“The court decided that there is no blanket prohibition. House Rule 9.0 cannot be used to prohibit or penalise Ms Noraseela merely for keeping her three cats; Enforcement must be evidence-based.
“There must be a factual basis connecting the particular animal to an alleged nuisance, danger or other prohibited circumstance,” the statement said.

The lawyers said the court also found that general complaints about animals were insufficient, as the evidence did not establish that Noraseela’s cats were responsible for the incidents cited by the JMB.
They said evidence from a neighbour supported Noraseela’s account that the cats were properly cared for, while veterinary certificates indicated that they were in good health.

The court also declared invalid and unenforceable the provisions of House Rule 9.0 that allowed animals to be removed from common property without notifying their owners and excluded liability for any resulting loss, insofar as they bypassed the requirements, notice procedures and safeguards under By-law 14.

“This judgment confirms that a JMB is not above the law. House rules cannot be used to circumvent statutory safeguards or to create powers the legislation does not confer. The law regulates irresponsible conduct. It does not authorise discrimination against responsible pet owners.

“Legitimate complaints about animals must be addressed, and this decision does not stand in the way of that. But management must act on evidence, not on a presumption that every pet is a nuisance,” the statement said.

In a document shared with the media, Noraseela, in her application contested the validity of House Rule 9.0, arguing that it contradicted the Strata Management Act 2013 (SMA 2013), which allows residents to keep pets subject to reasonable regulations to prevent nuisance, danger or annoyance.

She argued that Section 70(2) of the Act prohibited house rules that were inconsistent with its provisions, while Section 150 did not empower the Joint Management Body (JMB) to impose a blanket ban on pets but only to regulate their keeping for management purposes.
Noraseela therefore contended that House Rule 9.0 was unlawful and invalid as it went beyond the powers provided under the Act.

She also argued that the blanket ban under House Rule 9.0 was excessive and disproportionate as it applied to all residents without requiring evidence of nuisance or harm, claiming that it violated the principle of proportionality under Article 8 of the Federal Constitution and interfered with her right to enjoy and use her property under Article 13. — Bernama
819535fbaa89ec70: NEW YORK: ExxonMobil reported Friday that third-quarter profits more than doubled to US$15.4 billion, as it benefited from higher oil prices and refining margins due to the US-Iran war.
Profits in the period were slightly more than double the US$7.5 billion in the year-ago period, while revenues were about 33% higher at US$113.2 billion.

Oil prices averaged around US$85 per barrel during the period, about a third more than in the 2025 quarter. The results are the latest instance of soaring profits from petroleum companies in the wake of the US-Israel attacks on Iran launched in late February.

The most dramatic lift to the oil giant's financial performance from the Middle East upheaval was in its refining business, where the company processes crude oil into gasoline, diesel and other petroleum products.

Refining margins were US$50.3 per barrel, almost three times the level in the year-ago period, as the company cited efforts to boost output of diesel and other key products that have seen supplies tighten.
"Refining capacity in Russia and the Middle East remained curtailed, with roughly 10% of global capacity offline," the company said in prepared remarks ahead of a conference call.
"North American refineries sustained high operating rates during the quarter but were unable to fully offset reduced global refining capacity availability," according to the remarks.
The efforts to boost output translated into 100% crude unit utilisation at US Gulf Coast refineries, ExxonMobil said in its press release.
In terms of upstream output, ExxonMobil produced 4.5 million barrels per day of oil equivalent, down almost six percent from the year-ago level.
The company continues to contend with damaged petroleum sites in the Middle East, where disruptions have led to a US$2.9 billion hit so far in 2026.
Shares of ExxonMobil rose 2% in pre-market trading.
01e3da261c2e8c21: A court-ordered reassessment will set new values for every property in Allegheny County. Robert D. Strovers/Moments Collection via Getty ImagesAllegheny County will undergo a countywide reassessment of every property it taxes for the first time since 2012. A county judge ordered the reassessment in August 2026, requiring the work to begin by July 1, 2027, and finish within five years. The goal is to bring property values in line with today’s market. That could shift the tax burden among property owners across the county. State anti-windfall rules may require local governments to lower their tax rates after a reassessment to ensure they balance and equalize the tax reassessments. Individual bills may go up or down. For many homeowners, property taxes are confusing. Terms such as assessment, millage rate and school district tax come up often, but taxpayers may not know what they mean or how each one affects their annual tax bill. In Pittsburgh, property taxes pay for schools, parks, libraries, public safety and other local services. I research and teach government finance at Penn State Harrisburg, including a course on state and local taxation. Here’s a plain-language guide to how Pittsburgh’s property taxes work. What your home is worth – on paper The first concept is the property assessment. Allegheny County’s Office of Property Assessments gives every property an assessed value. That value is the basis for calculating property taxes. The Allegheny County Courthouse is also home to the county treasurer’s office, which collects county property taxes. tupungato/iStock Collection via Getty Images Plus An assessed value isn’t necessarily what a home would sell for today. Some places, such as Philadelphia, assess property at full market value. Other jurisdictions assess property at a set percentage of market value. In Cook County, Illinois, which includes Chicago, homes are assessed at 10% of their market value. That doesn’t mean Chicago-area homeowners pay less. When assessments are a smaller share of market value, tax rates are set higher to raise the same amount of money. Allegheny County assesses at full value, but it uses what properties were worth in 2012. The court-ordered reassessment is meant to close the gap between those 2012 values and today’s market. Allegheny County’s 14-year gap would be unusual almost anywhere else. Pennsylvania is the only state that doesn’t require counties to reassess on a regular schedule, while most states do so at least every six years. Within Pennsylvania, though, Allegheny is far from the worst: Butler County hasn’t reassessed since 1969. Homeowners can look up their assessment on the county’s real estate portal. What a mill means Once a property has an assessed value, each local government applies a millage rate to figure out the tax owed. One mill equals $1 of tax for every $1,000 of assessed value. A home assessed at $100,000 has 100 units of $1,000 in value. Pittsburgh property owners pay property taxes to three government entities: Allegheny County, the City of Pittsburgh and Pittsburgh Public Schools. Each one sets its own millage rate. For 2026, the city’s general rate is 9.67 mills. The city also charges 0.5 mill for parks and 0.25 mill for libraries. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, and Allegheny County charges 6.43 mills. Together, those rates add up to 27.307 mills. For a city home assessed at $100,000, that comes to about $2,731 a year before any exemptions or discounts. The county’s property tax worksheet and the county treasurer’s millage rate page list current rates. These rates are set each year, and all of them will be cut when reassessed values take effect, since the law requires rates to drop as total values rise. The biggest slice: Schools School taxes are often the largest share of a homeowner’s property tax bill. In Pennsylvania, property taxes are a major source of revenue for public schools. They help fund salaries for teachers, updates and maintainance for buildings, transportation, and technology and educational programs. School tax rates vary widely across Allegheny County. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, well below the suburban districts around it. North Allegheny, one of the lowest-taxing suburban districts, charges about 20.4 mills for the 2026-27 school year. Two of the highest are Mt. Lebanon at about 32 mills and Penn Hills at about 32.6 mills. The county treasurer publishes a full list of school district rates. Help for homeowners and seniors Some homeowners qualify for programs that lower their tax bills. The Allegheny County Homestead exemption, known as Act 50, cuts $18,000 from the assessed value of a qualified, owner-occupied, primary residence property’s county taxes. There’s no income limit: Any homeowner who lives in the property as their primary residence qualifies. A home assessed at $100,000 is taxed on just $82,000, which saves about $116 a year. Enrolling in Act 50 also automatically applies Pittsburgh’s $15,000 exemption, which covers the parks and library levies, and a larger Pittsburgh Public Schools exemption that is set each year. Applications for this exemption are due March 1 and need to be filed only once. The senior citizen tax relief program, known as Act 77, takes another 30% off county taxes for homeowners who are at least 60, have household incomes of $30,000 or less and have owned and lived in their home for at least 10 years. For a qualifying senior with that $100,000 home, the county bill would drop from about $527 to about $369. If you think your assessment’s too high Homeowners who believe their assessment is too high can appeal their assessment to the county’s Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. Filing is free; appeals can be submitted online, by email or in person. Appeals are filed the year before the tax year they affect. The appeal window for 2027 bills closed Sept. 1, 2026. The next window, for 2028 bills, is expected to run from July 1 to Sept. 1, 2027, around the time the reassessment is set to begin. At an appeal hearing, homeowners can argue their property’s value using either 2012 prices or today’s market. Recent sales of similar homes nearby can help show whether an assessment is out of line. The board can lower the assessment, leave it as is or raise it. What reassessment means for you Pittsburgh property taxes come down to two elements: the property’s assessed value and the millage rates set by the county, the city and the school district. Understanding how these elements work together can help homeowners read and comprehend their tax bills and better plan for one of the biggest ongoing costs of owning a home, next to the mortgage payment. That understanding will matter more as the reassessment gets underway. When new values take effect, some homeowners will see their share of the tax burden rise and others will see it fall. The direction depends on how their property’s value has changed compared with changes of other similar properties since 2012. Read more of our stories about Pittsburgh and Pennsylvania. 62c5ca7a60baabf4: Economic pessimism among Americans in both political parties is deepening ahead of the November midterm elections, amid factors such as high energy prices and cost-of-living pressures. AP Photo/Jeff ChiuPolling is looking grim for Republicans ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, 2026, due in large part to deep pessimism among the public about the economy. At first glance, this might seem surprising. With the exception of inflation, many economic measures remain strong, including gross domestic product growth. But consumer sentiment continues to languish. This has prompted a debate over whether mere “vibes” are in play, or whether these long-used metrics are no longer capturing something fundamental to Americans’ economic well-being. This debate matters politically because voters are placing an overwhelming priority on the economy as an issue in the midterms. A Pew Research survey in early October 2026 found that 84% of registered voters said the economy was very important to their vote, and the concern is bipartisan. Among the issues in that Pew survey, for example, “the economy” was the least polarizing, with 82% of Republicans and 88% of Democrats ranking it as very important. Meanwhile, the overall drop in voters’ economic outlook has largely been driven by growing pessimism among Republicans. While Democrats remain much gloomier about the economy than Republicans, the gap is narrowing. These trends help explain why Democrats are expected to make significant gains in Congress: This election will likely be seen as an indictment of how well the economy is working for ordinary Americans under President Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress, despite strong macroeconomic measures. So what is going on? As a scholar of financial markets and global inequality, I believe the relationship between how people see their own finances and their view of the broader economy is also changing on a more fundamental level. And this shift will affect how they judge the next class of lawmakers in power. Reality versus ‘vibes’ When scholars try to understand how people judge the economy – and how they separate their own personal circumstances from the broader economy – one of their key reference points is the University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index. It asks respondents about their personal finances, their short-term and long-term economic outlook, and whether they think it’s a good time to make major purchases. This gauge has historically tracked key economic measures of consumer spending and inflation: The state of the broader economy usually shapes the way people think about their own financial well-being. But in recent years, these have diverged. By many measures, the economy is doing well, but people feel they’re falling behind. And this has only become more pronounced ahead of the midterms. Despite strong consumer spending, robust business investment and low unemployment, consumer sentiment keeps slipping and is now 10% below where it was a year ago, according to the Michigan index. Some commentators point to ongoing inflation as the reason for gloom. It has remained stubbornly above the Federal Reserve’s annual 2% target rate due to drivers like tariffs, energy price hikes stemming from Middle East turmoil, and massive amounts of investment in the artificial intelligence build-out. But what’s really happening is that consumer sentiment data and inflation data have become untethered. Inflation has actually dropped sharply from its 21st-century peak of 9.1% in June 2022 after the pandemic to 3.7% in September 2026, but consumer sentiment is lower now than it was even then. What about wages? Here, too, the data also doesn’t fully explain this disconnect. While inflation makes consumer goods pricier, it also lifts pay. Inflation-adjusted wages actually increased between 2022 and the first half of 2026, all while consumer sentiment remained weak. What has changed in recent months is that inflation-adjusted wages are now falling – which could help explain the darkening outlook among voters. Inequality versus growth One possibility is that deeply entrenched inequality explains this divergence. Compared with other eras of moderate-to-high inflation, the U.S. economy today is much more unequal. Income inequality has increased over the past 20 years, narrowing only during the 2008 and 2020 crises before quickly widening to prior levels. This trend is important for understanding which consumers are shelling out cash. The Fed has consistently cited strong consumer spending in its economic assessments, but the richest 10% of Americans account for half of that spending today. Meanwhile, spending by the bottom 80% of earners has fallen behind inflation. In other words, the strong total consumer spending figures reported as official data are being driven by very wealthy Americans and fail to reflect the experience of typical consumers who are the bulk of the electorate. This trend of increasing inequality has been particularly acute in terms of wealth: The top 0.1% of American households together own five times as much wealth as the bottom 50%. Much of this reflects the uneven gains of the stock market boom and how wealth is taxed. In short, Americans’ economic malaise might be driven by concerns over income and wealth that conventional measures don’t fully capture. A surging stock market in 2026 helped boost Americans’ retirement accounts, but it hasn’t translated into greater consumer confidence. AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura It’s not just about me When it comes to consumer surveys like the University of Michigan index, economists generally assume that the answers reflect the personal experience of respondents. But I agree with other scholars who argue that sometimes these answers may be based less on people’s own circumstances and more on how they view the economy as a whole. This assessment could reflect, for example, concerns like equity, equality of opportunity and economic justice. When responses are driven by a concern for collective well-being rather than just personal material self-interest, social scientists refer to such perceptions as “sociotropic.” This last point isn’t just theoretical. Research suggests voters tend to weight their perceptions of the economy more heavily than their personal financial circumstances when deciding whether to vote for the incumbent party. Trade is one good example. Americans’ preferences for trade policy are driven less by how a particular measure, like tariffs, would impact them personally and more by how they think it would affect the country as a whole. If consumer sentiment follows a similar path, that could explain the divergence between generally strong economic trends and weak consumer sentiment. People are thinking not just about their own conditions but those of the U.S. as a whole, and it’s possible that their understanding of “the economy” includes its relationship to inequality. Understanding the disconnect between the economic data traditionally used to assess the economy’s health and Americans’ perceptions of that economy is important not just to the scholars trying to make sense of it – it could also help set an agenda for the incoming Congress. If economic insecurity punishes the governing party at the polls, the next Congress will be expected to do something about it once sworn in. Voters generally back the incumbent party when the economy is doing well and the out-party when it’s not. But how they judge the health of the economy is not straightforward, and the past six years suggest that improving headline measures of economic health – without regard to Americans’ lived experience and their concerns about what kind of economy is being built – may not be enough to assuage voters’ concerns. Erin Kay Lockwood does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
b028783102042288: ROME, Oct 30 — Thousands of students and workers took to the streets across Italy today, calling for more school funding and relief from the soaring cost of living, amid a high police presence to avert possible clashes.

Friday’s Italy-wide protest comes after weeks of demonstrations, led by students who have set up tent camps and occupied schools to make their demands heard, fuelled by similar movements in nearby France and Spain.

A general strike called by Italy’s USB trade union attracted thousands of workers to today’s protests, including truck drivers, taxi drivers and farmers who have rallied in recent weeks over the spike in fuel prices and to oppose rising defence spending.

Marches were held in dozens of cities up and down the country, including in Bologna, Genoa, Naples, and Turin—where a few minor skirmishes between protesters and riot police occurred at the start of the protest.
In Rome, university student Beatrice Chilelli told AFP students were “at a breaking point”.

“They can’t afford to pay exorbitant tuition fees, and rent... which weighs heavily on their parents’ shoulders,” said the 21-year-old, citing student housing in Rome that could reach 1,200 euros per month for a single room.

Thousands of people left Rome’s central Termini train station, accompanied by two tractors and a taxi, making their way past the Colosseum as they waved flags, unfurled banners and shouted into megaphones.
An AFP photographer witnessed a heavy police presence outside the Economy Ministry, which the procession passed by.
“We need more houses, not bombs!” sang one group in the crowd, as a troupe of protesters gave a brief performance imitating terrified civilians in a Gaza bombing raid.

The Milan protest also began at the central train station, but then headed outside the city—far from the centre where young vandals had looted stores, destroyed property and clashed with police two weeks ago after another sanctioned cost-of-living demonstration.
“Let’s reclaim our future” read one banner unfurled by students in Milan.
Police in riot gear blocked off streets, but no major clashes had been reported as of midday.
Besides students, the demonstrators at today’s protest included teachers, workers and retired people, with one man in Rome bearing a sign that read Pensioners - Pissed Off and Furious.
Many pro-Palestine flags were seen in the crowds in major cities.
Ahead of the demonstration, a spokesperson for the OSA student movement, 18-year-old Laura Teresi, told AFP she expected a “massive” mobilisation that would empty out schools.

“We will take to the streets to denounce the rearmament policies of (Prime Minister Giorgia) Meloni’s government and the rising cost of living, which is weighing ever more heavily on families, workers and students,” she added.
The students will also protest against the “endless budget cuts to teaching”, Teresi said.
Law and order
Following the October 17-18 weekend of clashes between youth and police in Milan, Meloni’s hard-right government toughened laws on public gatherings while easing rules on detaining minors.
The government also last week agreed on a 175.2-million-euro (US$195 million) aid package for truck drivers, farmers and fishermen hit by soaring fuel prices linked to the war in the Middle East.

Measures in favour of young people and families are also planned in the draft 2027 budget currently being discussed among the various governing parties, such as an annual bonus of 2,500 euros for workers under 30.

“I hope this can provide answers for young people in general... who feel that the state doesn’t care about them,” Meloni said at a press conference on Wednesday, stressing that these measures were “not for those who smash windows”. — AFP

114920bae2772585: Nissan has a new version of its best-selling Rogue SUV, and it’s launching the model here with the latest version of its e-Power hybrid system, which Ars tested back in February. Most of the hybrid cars you can buy today are parallel hybrids, which means that they have an internal combustion engine and an electric motor, both of which drive some or all of the wheels—everything works in parallel. But there’s another approach. Instead of connecting the engine to the wheels via a transmission, it can act as a generator and charge the traction battery, which in turn powers the electric motor. Since the engine and motor work in series, this is known as a series hybrid.

That’s mostly how the Chevrolet Volt worked. As does Honda’s hybrid CR-V. Well, mostly; engineers worked out it was more efficient for those cars' gasoline engines to directly drive the wheels at highway speeds, something that to this day makes a certain subset of hybrid car enthusiast irrationally angry. If you know anyone like that in your life, send them to wherever the nearest Nissan dealership is, because the 2027 Rogue Hybrid is exactly what they’ve been asking for.

Under the hood, with its crisp shut line and slim horizontal lights that give me something of a Range Rover vibe, there’s a 1.5 L, three-cylinder turbocharged direct-injection engine that generates 148 hp (110 kW). It only revs to 5,200 rpm because it’s optimized to charge the battery, not cope with the various loads of an engine connected to a gearbox and the wheels. That also allows the engine to operate at a rather impressive 42 percent thermal efficiency—we would need to look at Formula 1 engines to find higher.

7233c4faba05d32c: LABUAN, Oct 30 — An eatery operator here was compounded after charging an additional RM3 for a serving of soup that was not listed on the restaurant’s displayed price menu.

KPDN Labuan director Junaidah Arbain said the action followed a consumer complaint lodged through the ministry’s e-Aduan portal, with an inspection at about 10am finding that the displayed price list included additional charges for rice and noodles but did not specify the price of extra soup.

“Following the non-compliance detected, we issued a compound to the operator under the Price Control and Anti-Profiteering (Price Marking for Goods and Charges for Services) Order 2020, under the Price Control and Anti-Profiteering Act 2011,” she told Bernama today.
Junaidah said individuals convicted of an offence under the order could be fined up to RM50,000, while companies could face fines of up to RM100,000.

She reminded restaurant and food outlet operators to display their menus and all additional charges completely, clearly and prominently, with price lists and charges stated in Bahasa Melayu or accompanied by a translation if presented in another language, and prices indicated in ringgit or sen.
She said that transparent pricing was essential to protecting consumer rights, as customers were entitled to know the cost of goods and services before placing an order or making a purchase.

“KPDN Labuan would continue to intensify enforcement and monitoring activities to safeguard consumer interests, and members of the public are encouraged to report business-related non-compliance through the ministry’s official complaint channels,” she added. — Bernama
270f566cb245bf77: GEORGE TOWN, Oct 30 — The government wants local content to be given greater consideration in government, government-linked company (GLC) and multinational corporation (MNC) procurements to create more opportunities for local micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).

Entrepreneur Development and Cooperatives Minister Steven Sim Chee Keong said the approach is aimed at ensuring local businesses benefit from investments and the development of domestic supply chains.

“We also want government procurements, GLC procurements and, of course, MNC procurements to have a perspective for local content. We want foreign direct investment (FDI) to come in to benefit local businesses. So, there must be a requirement for local contents,” he said.
He said this during a panel discussion with Grant Thornton Malaysia National Tax Practice Leader Datin Seah Siew Yun at the Grant Thornton Tax Seminar on Budget 2027 here today.
Sim said local content requirement is one of the components under the SCALE Action Plan, which will form the ministry’s next phase of longer-term structural reforms for the MSME sector.

746fe27f30474833: Thousands of GCHQ storage drives containing sensitive data have been lost for years, and the British signals intelligence agency still cannot explain where they are.

According to the Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office’s (IPCO) annual report, the missing storage drives have been known to officials for years, and may contain data related to the Investigatory Powers Act (IPA).

"I remain concerned that GCHQ has not yet established a sufficiently clear understanding of the scale, location, and recoverability of lost removable media that may contain IPA-related data, notwithstanding that the underlying issues were first drawn to my attention several years ago," wrote investigatory powers commissioner Lord Brian Leveson.

"While I recognize the technical and practical challenges involved, the passage of time without a comprehensive account heightens the importance of sustained senior focus and assured remediation. Given the potential sensitivity of the material involved, I will continue to monitor progress closely.”
Described as "a very significant number," the report notes that GCHQ has scoped the maximum number of potentially lost drives, but is unaware of the exact scale of the issue.

The agency has embarked on "a program of further work" to locate as many of the lost devices as possible, which includes implementing an automated asset-tracking system by the end of the year. After this is up and running, it said it will be able to provide a more precise number of lost drives.

A GCHQ spokesperson told The Register: "As IPCO have reported, our management system for removable media was previously not sufficiently robust to effectively track the items that were registered for use. IPCO are right to note the flaws in the data the system produced, and we have taken action against all their recommendations.

"We recognize the importance of security of removable media in our systems, and have a range of measures to mitigate the risks posed by these items. The findings in the report have been addressed comprehensively, and all necessary steps to correct this issue have been taken."
Peter Sommer, digital forensics expert and visiting professor at de Montfort and Birmingham City universities, told us:

"Bearing in mind the sort of highly sensitive data collected and processed by GCHQ IPCO is right to be very concerned, the more so as the issue is already several years old. Vast quantities of data can be stored on the cheapest lowest cost hard disks and cards. At a much more modest level as an expert witness I know how important it is to keep careful track of the data entrusted to me."

Losing important devices is not an achievement that's exclusive to GCHQ. Myriad stories like this have emerged from all corners of the public sector over the years, such as the British Minidstry of Defence misplacing USB drives containing secret information in the mid-noughties, civil servants routinely losing their BlackBerry handsets, and UK police losing thousands of devices, too.
The missing storage drives comprise just one of the agency's various transgressions highlighted by IPCO in its report.
There are also "significant concerns" over the lax safeguards used to restrict the UK's overseas partners when accessing bulk-intercepted data collected by GCHQ.

IPCO was satisfied at how GCHQ ensured its own analysts remained compliant with safeguards around accessing confidential material related to journalism, journalistic sources, and privileged legal information.
However, there were concerns around how these same safeguards were applied to its international partners, which have access to its so-called bulk data interception "product."

The report notes that most partners were properly restricted from accessing such material, although an internal probe found that there were inadequate arrangements in respect to one partner and their access to journalistic material.
Both GCHQ and the overseas agency committed to rectifying the situation.
GCHQ was also questioned after a software bug in a web app "used by a relatively small section of the public" misidentified individuals thought to be participating in terrorist activities.

The agency identified and reported the flaw in the software, which it used for "target discovery work," and although it only affected a small number of individuals, the errors led to five port stops made under the Terrorism Act and caused "serious prejudice" to the victims.

A port stop, for the uninitiated, involves law enforcement detaining a suspect at a UK port, airport, train station, or within one mile of the Northern Ireland border, and can be carried out without suspicion.

Once detained, individuals have a legal responsibility to provide passwords to their electronic devices, which can be seized for up to seven days, and in some cases have their biometric markers taken.
Failure to comply can lead to a three-month prison term.
IPCO ruled, however, that there was ultimately no error made as defined by the IPA.

“This is because the activity was lawfully authorised under an interception warrant and the adoption of an unintentionally and unforeseeably imperfect target discovery methodology did not constitute such an error,” the report stated.
Despite the agency’s vast technical expertise, IPCO said that the issue affecting the software was not foreseeable.

GCHQ was not the only offender among the UK intelligence community (UKIC), with MI5's mishandling of the infamous Agent X case taking center stage in the report. Agent X was an anonymous MI5 informant whose real identity has never been publicly released.
A secret inquiry by IPCO as well as the report revealed that MI5 managed Agent X despite knowing he was a violent misogynist obsessed with extreme violence.

Lord Leveson said "the case of Agent X is as serious as anything I have dealt with as Commissioner," after MI5 gave false evidence to the High Court and Investigatory Powers Tribunal to protect a foreign neo-Nazi informant who was under police investigation for abusing his partner, referred to publicly as "Beth." ®

298d4aed9fdf5e94: My colleagues and I discovered a new species of extinct crocodile from a fossil found in the same rocks used to carve the Great Sphinx of Giza. Today, there are only two species of the long-snouted gavial crocodile, both of which are endangered: Gavialis gangeticus and Tomistoma schlegelii. They are found only in freshwater environments on the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. However, the fossil record of gavials goes back 80 million years, to the time of the dinosaurs. It shows that they were once diverse, with more than 40 species known, and lived all over the globe. So how did a group of crocodiles that today cannot tolerate saltwater once live all over the world? Our discovery may help to solve this puzzle. Although the distribution of the continents differed from today, most were already separated by oceans. My colleagues and I have been trying to understand how gavials achieved this cosmopolitan distribution, while also seeking to unlock what led to their current predicament. Studying the anatomy of the skeletons of living and fossil gavials has given us a better understanding of the group’s evolution in recent years. CT scans have enabled us to look inside their skulls, giving us a window into their brains and sensory systems. This has revealed new anatomical information that helps differentiate species, and has allowed us to infer aspects of the biology and ecology of some of the extinct species. For example, in an extinct group of crocodile relatives known to have lived entirely in the ocean, other researchers found thickening of the outer wall of their inner ear to cope with the higher pressures seen at ocean depths. My colleagues and I have found similar evidence for a marine lifestyle in some fossil gavials. This ability to live in the ocean was lost in living species, which are restricted to rivers and lakes. Several of the gavial fossils we have been studying from Africa and Europe were first reported in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and they were often described as species of Tomistoma, i.e. closely related to Tomistoma schlegelii, one of the two living species of gavials. Our previous work and that of others has shown that some of these extinct species are not closely related to Tomistoma, with new names given for some of them. However, many of these historically described species remain neglected. Led by my former PhD student, Paul Burke, now a researcher at the Swedish Museum of Natural History in Stockholm, along with colleagues from Egypt and Germany, we re-examined one of these species in a new study. In the 1920s, several fossils were collected from northeastern Egypt. These were found in a limestone rock, known as the Mokattam Formation, that had formed 45 million years ago in a shallow marine environment when sea levels were higher. This region was submerged at this time. These fossils, including a nearly complete skull, were described in 1927 as belonging to Tomistoma, because of their superficial resemblance to the living species, Tomistoma schlegelii. However, aided by the use of CT scanning, our team was able to identify several anatomical differences, including the presence of raised rims around the eye sockets, which are absent in Tomistoma. The Great Sphinx of Giza. Fernanda-Belen/Shutterstock The Mokattam Formation already has a legacy: 4,500 years ago, these rocks were used to carve the Great Sphinx of Giza. The gavial skull shares more than this origin story though. Just as the Sphinx is famously missing the tip of its nose, the fossil is also missing the tip of its snout. This coincidence led us to name the new crocodile Herugavialis cairensis after the Egyptian falcon-headed god Heru (also known as Horus), who is often thought to be the inspiration for the iconic Sphinx. Both northern Africa and southern Europe hosted a high diversity of gavials (and other crocodiles) during much of the last 80 million years, with these species thriving in the shallow, marine environments that covered much of the Mediterranean region at the time. Unlike living gavials, it is likely that some of these species could cross oceans. This diversity appears to have persisted through the devastating mass extinction that wiped out the dinosaurs, and probably fluctuated during alternating warmer and cooler intervals over the next 60 million years, tied to higher and lower sea levels, respectively. However, crocodiles disappeared from the Mediterranean region approximately 6 million years ago and never returned. Their demise coincides with an event known as the Messinian salinity crisis, when the Mediterranean essentially dried up as a result of being sealed off from the Atlantic Ocean. As the seawater became increasingly salty with the heightened evaporation of water, it would have become ever more intolerable to the animals inhabiting it, even those usually able to live in saltwater, leading to the loss of crocodiles and many other species. The signature of this event can still be observed today, with the Mediterranean Sea still much saltier than the oceans, and crocodiles entirely absent from this region. The remaining living gavials live far away from the Mediterranean, but the loss of the adaptations that would allow them to live in saltwater means that they would not be able to survive there regardless. Rapid and extreme changes in temperature, sea level, and aridification are critical components of the current climate emergency, and events such as the Messinian salinity crisis show that they can have a lasting impact on biodiversity, spanning millions of years. Philip Mannion receives funding from The Royal Society and UK Research and Innovation.

d0fbea4a4fb246d0: NEW YORK: Adidas is hoping this weekend's New York City Marathon will be its chance to run a victory lap, after runners wearing its shoes clocked up eight wins at prized World Marathon Majors this year, boosting sales and outpacing longstanding rival Nike.
Revenue in its Running sector was up 19% in the company's record-breaking third-quarter (Q3) earnings, it reported on Thursday.

The wins have come at just the right time for Adidas, with marathoning enjoying a modern golden age of record-breaking participation — from competitive athletes to casual pavement-pounders willing to shell out hundreds of dollars for shoes that they hope will give them an added boost.
The London Marathon, one of seven World Marathon Majors after Sydney was added to the original six in 2025, announced it would split its race into two days to account for the overwhelming interest.
New York Road Runners told Reuters it expects record turnout again this year at the NYC Marathon, after drawing roughly a quarter of a million applicants.
"Running as an industry is having a little bit of a heyday," Patrick Nava, general manager for Adidas Running, told Reuters.
On Sunday, Adidas will be looking to Kenyan Benson Kipruto for its latest win as he defends his NYC Marathon title.
He said he was recruited to Adidas shortly after placing second in his debut over the distance in Athens 10 years ago.
He has since won major titles including Chicago in 2022 and Tokyo in 2024, as well as taking Olympic bronze in Paris.
"We have signed very good athletes," Adidas CEO Bjorn Gulden told reporters on Thursday. "And to be honest with you, I think we have the best products," he added.
The repeated high-profile wins give Adidas legitimacy as a brand, said Drake MacFarlane, a research analyst at M Science, adding that the sector was "a core opportunity" for the German firm.
Adidas says its increasing dominance in running kit sales is thanks to a coordinated multiyear effort in a sport that has become ever more competitive.
"Everybody can talk about innovation, but there's a very simple way in which you measure innovation, which is how much you win," Nava said.
The brand has over 100 people working in service of running shoe innovation compared to a few dozen some years ago, it said.
It also relies on a network of coaches, experts and athletes to recruit signature stars as early as the youth level.
Early Nike dominance

Nike kicked off the "super shoe" footrace in 2017, with its Zoom Vaporfly Elite shoe that powered Kenyan great and twice Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge in his early effort at breaking the marathon's two-hour barrier.
By 2019, Nike was so dominant that athletes and reporters questioned whether Nike-sponsored athletes had an unfair advantage over their competitors.
That year, Nike's men and women won 10 of the 12 golds available at the six World Marathon Majors.
Adidas broke into the pack with its first carbon-infused super shoe in 2020.
However, its pivotal year came three years later, when it fundamentally reshaped how it develops shoes, prioritizing rapid deployment.
"The average development time for, I'm going to call it a normal running shoe, is anywhere between 18 and 24 months," said Nava.
"By comparison, the core work for the brand's modern elite line 'Evo' took nine months.
"When we think we have a good one that's good enough that we like, then we sort of drop it and we have the athletes use it," he said.
"Right now they're using the Evo 3. We are already working on a couple of the next iterations. It's this continuous like, 'Test, refine, redevelop', and then 'Retest, redefine, redevelop'," he added.
'A pace that nobody has seen'
Nike said innovations in shoe technology and the increasing popularity of marathoning have led to a more competitive sector.

"There's more investment in this area and, you know, just the cost of even competing in this space continues to rise," Tanya Hvizdak, vice-president and general manager for global running at Nike, told Reuters.
Earlier this month, Nike said it was deepening a restructuring, announcing a plan to cut more jobs and ​shake up its global business divisions after forecasting a steep drop in full-year revenue.
However, Nike's Running business sector has remained one of the areas where it is still seeing growth, despite its relatively lackluster marathon results.
The unit has reported six consecutive quarters of double-digit growth, and Nike says its share of the max-cushioning category nearly tripled over the past year.
Strong showings at the Chicago Marathon, where its athletes accounted for six of the top 10 men's finishes and three of the top five women's, were bright spots for the year.
"You're going to see us innovating at a pace that nobody has seen in prior years.
"And that's going to be something that's going to be unrelenting that we're pretty excited about. And our athletes are leading that for us," Hvizdak said.
Smaller brands like On, Asics and Under Armour are also competing for a spot on the podium.
However, one of the challenges for running is that — unlike sports such as soccer, where a household name is enough to move a product — selling marathon shoes requires wins, said Nava.
"You don't have necessarily the superstars like you have in football," he said.
"You know, you put something on a (Lionel) Messi or on a Lamine Yamal, that will have immediate impact, right?.

"Running is a little bit different in the sense you need that to be credible because you can say like, 'Hey, I actually objectively say that we have some of the best shoes in the industry'," he added.

b24a0e868e9de3a3: BEIJING: China's central bank said on Friday it would conduct overnight reverse repo operations every working day starting next Monday, in a step towards making the rate its main policy anchor.

The People's Bank of China will carry out the overnight operations through a fixed-rate, quantity-based tender on each business day, with the operating rate currently at 1.25%, it said in a statement.
The central bank, which flagged the shift earlier this month, said the move was aimed at further improving its management of short-term interest rates.

"What occurred today is arguably the clearest signal yet that the PBOC is moving toward an overnight-rate-based operating system similar to those employed by major central banks including the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan," said Zhou Hao, chief economist at Guotai Junan International.
PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng said earlier this month at a financial forum that the central bank was studying switching its main policy rate to the overnight reverse repo rate.

The overnight operation rate of 1.25%, disclosed by the PBOC for the first time, is broadly in line with market expectations and reported borrowing cost, and sits below the 7-day reverse repo rate CN7DRRP=PBOC of 1.4%.

In Friday's statement, the PBOC said its seven-day reverse repo operations would shift to a fixed-quantity, interest-rate tender with multiple winning bid rates, and would be conducted mainly around tax payment periods and month-ends.

Ming Ming, chief economist at Citic Securities, said the reform of the short-end mechanism laid the groundwork for diversifying the pricing benchmarks for loan rates and for the transmission of broad-based declines in interest rates.

Other tools that were previously priced at a spread above or below the seven-day reverse repo rate - including temporary repo and reverse repo operations and repo facilities for overseas central bank-type institutions - will instead be priced at a spread to the overnight reverse repo rate, with the size of the spreads left unchanged, the PBOC said.
Overnight reverse repo operations debuted in late June as the latest addition to the PBOC's toolkit.
f80187438a4d406e: MELAKA, Oct 30 — MCA has announced that it will contest one more state seat in the 16th Melaka state election, after Kota Laksamana was returned to Barisan Nasional (BN) by Perikatan Nasional (PN).

MCA president Datuk Seri Wee Ka Siong said Melvin Chua will be fielded as the candidate, following discussions between BN and PN after the latter indicated that MCA is better suited to contest the seat.

“This decision was only made and agreed upon today by the party’s top leadership, following the decision to return the seat to an MCA candidate representing BN in the Kota Laksamana state constituency, after taking into consideration his suitability based on his involvement and services in the area,” he told a press conference during a visit to the Bandar Hilir MCA operations room in Melaka Raya here today.

Wee said Melvin is a familiar figure among the local community, particularly through his involvement in community activities and his service in the Melaka Historic City Council (MBMB) administrative area.
The addition of Kota Laksamana means MCA will contest four seats, including Machap Jaya, Kelebang and Bandar Hilir.

Wee said the latest development would not affect MCA’s preparations, despite the decision being made at the last minute, as the party had long been prepared, particularly in the traditional constituencies it was contesting.
He said MCA, as BN’s component party, is ready to face any challenge and has no problem fielding candidates in seats where it is required to contest.
“We have never shied away from our responsibilities. We have no problem contesting any seat and we are ready to face any situation.
“MCA will continue striving to gain the people’s support and put up a fight in the constituencies it contests, including seats considered difficult to win in the Melaka state polls,” he said.
The Election Commission has fixed tomorrow as nomination day for the Melaka state election, with polling set for November 14 and early voting on November 10. — Bernama

436c69c242f6f0fb: Welcome to Edition 9.17 of the Rocket Report! It's been a while since an American company announced plans for a medium-lift new launch vehicle, but that's what happened this week when a startup named Cowboy Space revealed specs for its Big Iron rocket, named for the classic country-western song by Marty Robbins. I'm a huge fan of the name. Maybe Cowboy Space is striking while the iron is hot as the space industry frets over demand for launch outpacing supply. However, Cowboy Space lags far behind so many other launch providers nearing the launch pad with their medium-class rockets, and the company didn't have much hardware to show at this week's big reveal. In other words, don't mistake style for substance. But we're rocket fans at Ars, and we wish them luck.

As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don't want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.

Virgin's new rocket plane reaches home port. The first of Virgin Galactic's new Delta-class rocket planes left its Arizona factory Wednesday for a trip to Spaceport America in neighboring New Mexico, where it will undergo preparations for a test campaign culminating in suborbital flights to the edge of space, Ars reports. Virgin Galactic expects the craft's first commercial spaceflight to take place "early" in the second quarter of 2027, but like every other projected date in aerospace, this should be taken with a grain of salt. Virgin Galactic halted commercial flights of its previous vehicle, VSS Unity, in 2024.
be88fc3299defd2b: Accenture is using AI across its recruiting process, although it maintains that final hiring decisions remain in human hands.
Speaking to at its recent investor day, the global tech consultancy and outsourcing biz said it was using AI agents to sift through resumes (or CVs if you’re in the UK) and schedule interviews.
Kate Clifford, global chief leadership and HR, said it was helping clients adopt a similar application of the nascent technology.

"We call it frictionless recruiting, which is really our agentic recruiting solution. We put in an agentic recruiting solution where agents now do all the interview scheduling. Agents can screen a resume. We have assessments that deeply understand the skills of the candidates to help that process move much, much faster. Now a human always makes a hiring decision," she said.

Clifford said the agent technology was used to help recruitment staff get through their work more quickly. "Our recruiters needed to spend time with candidates. They needed to spend time sourcing, but where they were actually spending their time was scheduling interviews, where they were actually spending their time was typing information into a system," she said.
The executive claimed the agentic process reduced the time taken to hire for roles by 28 percent and improved candidate quality by 30 percent.

AI agents also help new recruits get up to speed. Whereas it once took six months for an entry-level hire to become productive, the time has been cut to six weeks using AI agents, Clifford claimed, allowing them to produce billable work more rapidly.

Accenture claims to serve around 9,000 clients — including some of the world’s largest businesses and government departments — with tech advice and services. For example, it won a contract with the US Internal Revenue Services worth $2.6 billion in 2023. Any tech pro looking for a job with the company is likely being screened by AI as part of the process.

The company also expects internal staff to get on the AI bandwagon. A memo sent to senior staff in February informed them that promotions to top roles at the corporation would necessitate "regular adoption" of AI tooling, and it is tracking usage.

But not everyone is convinced by the value of AI in recruitment. A study published in 2022 found the idea that AI-powered recruitment software creates a fairer process was unfounded. A paper published in the journal Philosophy and Technology demonstrated that the software is little more than "automated pseudoscience."
Tech job-hunters applying for a lucrative role at Accenture will be hoping the technology has moved on since then. ®

b39d1c21d5028f0d: LABUAN, Oct 30 — Malaysia will continue strengthening its military capabilities in Sabah to safeguard national security amid regional geopolitical developments, but the move is not a direct response to the Philippines’ military build-up on Balabac Island, Defence Minister Datuk Seri Mohamed Khaled Nordin said.

He said every country has the right to enhance its defence capabilities, and Malaysia was similarly committed to ensuring its armed forces remained prepared for any potential escalation of regional tensions.

“Every country has the right to strengthen its military capabilities, and Malaysia will do the same. However, our efforts are not a reaction to what the Philippines is doing in its southern region, but part of our preparations to ensure that any escalation of tensions will have minimal impact on Malaysia,” he told reporters after receiving the FA-50M aircrafts from South Korea at the Labuan Royal Malaysian Air Force (RMAF) base here.

Khaled was commenting on the Philippine government’s efforts to strengthen military facilities on Balabac Island in southern Palawan, which has been designated as a military cooperation site accessible to the United States forces.
Khaled said strengthening Malaysia’s defence capabilities, particularly in Sabah, remained a key priority of the Defence Ministry.

He said the ministry would determine the number of FA-50M light combat aircraft to be stationed at the Royal Malaysian Air Force (RMAF) base in Labuan following the planned decommissioning of Hawk fighter aircraft in 2028.
“Once the Hawk aircraft are phased out in 2028, we will determine how many FA-50M aircraft will be stationed at the Labuan air base,” he said.
He said the government had also decided to install new radar systems in Sabah, including on Layang-Layang Island, to enhance surveillance and early detection capabilities.

“The ministry would also increase military personnel in Sabah, where more than 10,000 troops are currently stationed, while new military camps have been developed to strengthen operational readiness,” he said.

Khaled reiterated that the initiatives were part of Malaysia’s continuing efforts to reinforce national defence and protect its sovereignty, rather than a response to military developments in neighbouring countries. — Bernama
5957d3479db22719: MELAKA, Oct 30 — Pakatan Harapan (PH) does not regard multi-cornered contests in the Melaka state election as a disadvantage, saying a crowded field could instead create more opportunities for the coalition to secure victories.

Melaka PH chairman Adly Zahari said a straight fight did not necessarily give a party an advantage, as three- or four-cornered contests could, in certain circumstances, offer better prospects from a strategic standpoint.

“Based on my experience in previous four-cornered contests, having more candidates is not necessarily an obstacle to winning. Instead, it can create opportunities that contesting parties can take advantage of.

“There are certainly challenges as well as advantages in terms of our strategy. Sometimes, a straight fight can be more difficult than a three-cornered contest,” he told reporters after a tea reception with Melaka media practitioners in Ayer Keroh here today.
Also present was Melaka PKR chairman Adam Adli Abd Halim.
Adly said PH’s decision to increase the number of seats it is contesting from 21 to 24 was also made after assessing the current political landscape and the coalition’s prospects of winning.
He said the coalition had initially settled on contesting 21 seats on October 24 before reviewing its position and identifying further opportunities to strengthen its chances.

The decision, he said, should not be interpreted as a failure in negotiations with any political party, as PH had made its assessment based on its own capabilities and prevailing political developments.
He said another principle taken into consideration was to ensure that no state constituency was won uncontested, allowing voters to exercise their democratic right to choose their representatives.
“For example, when we realised that Bersatu was not fielding a candidate in a particular seat, that decision had been made without consulting us.
“So we stepped in to ensure the democratic process could proceed as it should. Voters must be given the opportunity to make their choice,” he said.
Nominations will take place tomorrow, with early voting on November 10 and polling on November 14. — Bernama
536dd6d74a2ef22e: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 30 — The Finance Ministry (MOF) has never issued any directive to cancel rural road projects, but has only deferred new contracts to prevent outstanding payments to contractors from continuing to accumulate, according to the prime minister’s senior political adviser, Tengku Datuk Seri Zafrul Tengku Abdul Aziz.

He said the deferment was necessary following rural road development expenditure exceeding the original allocations approved by Parliament annually since 2022, resulting in increased contractual commitments and outstanding payments to contractors.

“The deferment of new contracts does not mean existing projects have been cancelled. MOF has never issued any directive to cancel projects. New contracts were deferred to prevent outstanding payments from continuing to increase.

“These are two different things. That is why the country’s finances must be managed prudently, not merely by approving projects but also by ensuring sufficient allocations are available to pay for them,” he said in a video shared on his social media today.

Tengku Zafrul said claims that rural road allocations, particularly in Sabah and Sarawak, had been deliberately reduced should be assessed based on the government’s actual expenditure figures for the period concerned.

He said rural road expenditure for the 2023-2027 period, including allocations for this year and next year, had increased to RM11 billion compared with RM3.7 billion for the 2018-2022 period, representing almost a threefold increase.
“In Sabah and Sarawak alone, actual rural road expenditure this year reached RM1.41 billion, the highest in the past 10 years.

“Since 2023, RM4.6 billion has been spent. Every year, approximately half of the country’s total rural road expenditure is channelled to Sabah and Sarawak. Sabah and Sarawak have not been sidelined. Sabah and Sarawak have been given priority,” he said.

Tengku Zafrul said MOF had to balance the allocation needs of all ministries, including those responsible for health, education and rural development, to ensure the government’s financial commitments could be met.
He said when a ministry made spending commitments that exceeded its approved allocation, MOF had to seek additional financial resources to meet those requirements.

In this regard, Prime Minister and Finance Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim had approved an additional RM500 million in expenditure for 2026, using savings from the development allocations of other ministries, to enable outstanding payments to contractors to be settled.
He said the government understood that many villages in Sabah and Sarawak were still waiting for better road facilities.
In this connection, Budget 2027 provides RM2.27 billion for rural road development, while RM34.9 billion has been allocated to Sabah and Sarawak, the highest amount among all states.
He also reminded all parties that development issues in the two states should not be used as political ammunition.

“As the prime minister has stressed, allocations alone are not enough without good governance. What matters is that projects are implemented, contractors are paid and the people benefit. That is our priority,” he said. — Bernama

c388429d79ce6ccc: KETAPANG, Oct 30 — Deep in a forest in Indonesian Borneo, conservationists open a cage. A female orangutan and her baby waste little time, clambering up the towering trees and disappearing into the canopy, safe at last.
The pair were among nine orangutans rescued from devastating wildfires ravaging their forest home in Ketapang, West Kalimantan province, in August and September.
Nursed back to health over several weeks, they now have a new home in Batu Nyambu, a 23,000-hectare protected area in the same province.
When they were rescued, the animals were in bad shape, YIARI wildlife rehabilitation foundation CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez told AFP journalists who went along for the release.
“Some of them had burns on their hands and feet, and some of them were skinny and malnourished,” said Sanchez.
“They had to be cared for and fed until they were in good condition again.”

The journey to get them to their new home was long and arduous, with conservation workers trekking for hours through steep, slippery terrain, carrying the orangutans in cages suspended from poles digging into their shoulders.
Conservationists clapped in joy as the apes fled the cages on Thursday and returned to the wild where they belong.
Among the nine orangutans were four pairs of mothers and their young.
Sanchez said three of the mothers were pregnant again—a fact discovered during the final health check before their release.
One of those expecting is Mama Ocha, who was rescued along with her baby, Ocha.
“The team will stay around to make sure that she is all right and that she can deliver her baby, and that will be an excellent outcome,” said Sanchez.
Once widespread across Southeast Asia, orangutans are now critically endangered.
According to conservation group WWF, only around 104,000 remain in the wild in Borneo and Sumatra, less than half the estimated population a century ago.
Extremely stressed
The rescued orangutans spent four to eight weeks recovering in a rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, regaining their strength after the trauma of the fires and smoke.
YIARI veterinarian Ishma Maula said their release could not be delayed any longer.
“While they were in quarantine and rehabilitation, they were extremely stressed and showed abnormal behaviour,” she said.
“We decided to release them as soon as possible after finding a habitat that was safe for them.”

Batu Nyambu was chosen as their new home because its forests remain largely untouched and provide abundant food and shelter, offering the best chance for the animals to rebuild their lives, Sanchez said.
The team had to travel by car, kayak and hours on foot through dense forest to reach the release site.
The rescue came as concern for Borneo’s orangutans grows, with wildfires continuing to tear through their shrinking habitat.
Indonesia’s forestry ministry says at least 51 orangutans have been rescued from burning forests in West Kalimantan between early August and mid-October.
Last month, the International Union for Conservation of Nature said fires were burning in areas that support more than half of Borneo’s orangutan population.
Deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas estimates the blazes consumed more than 1.9 million hectares of land in the first nine months of the year.
Experts say much of the destruction is linked to slash-and-burn land-clearing practices, often associated with the expansion of timber, palm oil and mining operations. — AFP
4109480da7f7c507: Two insurers are teaming up to launch what every high-tech homeowner may soon need: household insurance for robotic mishaps.
Humanoid robots are tipped by some to be the next big technology trend, with industry figures like Nvidia's Jensen Huang predicting they'll be everywhere from factories to the home.
But as with anything AI-driven, things can go horribly wrong, especially when automatons are roaming a home carrying out tasks. They have even been labelled as potential "botnets in physical form."

The timing may be apt, then, for the UK's first domestic humanoid robot insurance policy. Specialist insurer Adrian Flux is offering to cover British customers as part of its home insurance range, underwritten by Texas-based Tokio Marine HCC.

The two firms say the product is meant to get ahead of an emerging market, with domestic robots expected to appear in UK homes from 2027. Demand has already appeared in the US, where robotics and AI companies have launched humanoid robots for the home, with early models costing around $20,000.
These are less like the near-human elderly care robot in the BBC comedy series Ann Droid, and more like vaguely human-shaped machines.

The policy covers damage to, and theft of, the robot itself, plus any damage it causes to the home or belongings. It also includes personal liability if the android injures someone or damages their property, and emergency recovery or safe disablement of the humanoid after a sudden or unforeseen malfunction, such as - perhaps - attempting to chop off your fingers or put your cat on the stove.

“As robots start to arrive in people's homes, we wanted to provide clarity on who is responsible if something goes wrong," says Gerry Bucke, general manager for the insurance biz Adrian Flux. "Like the driverless car policy we launched in 2016, it will be updated as the technology and the risks evolve."

Beyond the home, investment is pouring into humanoids across a range of applications. Chinese carmaker Chery using them as showroom sales staff, while another firm has demonstrated them in automotive manufacturing.
Elon Musk famously predicted thousands of Optimus robots in Tesla factories by the end of 2025, but still believes its humanoid robot will be the company’s biggest product. ®

bd1638bb7d840be3: MADRID: Spanish inflation in October remained at 4.9%, its highest level since February 2023, official data showed Friday, one month before an election in which the cost of living will be a major issue.
However, Spain's dynamic economic growth - which Socialist prime minister Pedro Sanchez's government has regularly used to defend its record - maintained its rhythm at 0.6% in the third quarter.
The provisional October inflation of 4.9% released by the National Statistics Institute (INE) is equal to September's figure for the EU's fourth-largest economy.
The soaring costs of gas and other fuels kept inflation high despite a year-on-year drop in the price of items including food, non-alcoholic drinks and clothing, the INE said.

The Middle East war, sparked in February by US-Israeli strikes on Iran, has roiled global energy markets as the conflict disrupts key supply chains for oil and gas, notably due to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Although Spain is less dependent on fossil fuel imports than other major economies, thanks to its use of nuclear and renewable energy, the volatility in oil and gas costs has caused inflation to spike.
The left-wing government introduced a cap of 15% on the increase of natural gas prices as well as fuel discounts through to December in a bid to shield consumers.
The INE also announced that GDP growth between July and September reached 0.6%, mostly thanks to internal demand, after a 0.7% increase in the second quarter.
Earlier this month, the Bank of Spain predicted that GDP growth would hit 2.6% this year, citing resilient household spending in one of the world's most dynamic developed economies.

However, the cost of living is a key issue for voters, especially Spain's long-running housing crisis, with protests over the issue culminating in Sanchez's calling of a snap general election on Nov 29.

Although Spain continues to outperform larger EU peers such as France and Germany, "the clearest threat to growth comes from rising prices", said Pedro Aznar, a professor at the Esade business school.
"For now, the growth of employment and wages are compensating for the negative impact of the rise in the cost of living," Aznar told AFP.

However, with inflation and housing costs weighing on purchasing power, "the government is receiving relatively little electoral benefit from the country's macroeconomic outperformance", according to ING analyst Pablo Muylle.

0407bda14ae0b38b: PARIS, Oct 30 — African football’s showpiece tournament, the Africa Cup of Nations will be held every two years the continent’s ruling body announced yesterday in a reversal of a decision taken last year.

“The African Football Confederation (CAF) Executive Committee today unanimously decided that the CAF Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) will return to taking place every two years,” a statement said.

CAF said part of the reasoning for performing a U-turn on the decision was the length of time it would take for Afcon’s replacement competition, the Africa Nations League Pan-African Competition, to become financially viable.

Motsepe added that the decision was also taken in the interests “of African players employed by football clubs outside Africa”.
That may prove contentious with their clubs looking at losing key players every two years as opposed to four.
Next year’s tournament is being co-hosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda and CAF said the following three would take place in 2028, 2031 and 2033.

“The forthcoming Fifa World Cup will take place in 2030 and in accordance with the Fifa tradition, the final tournament of the Afcon and other Confederations National Teams competitions may not take place during the year of the Fifa World Cup,” said Motsepe, explaining the three-year gap between the 2028 edition and the following one.
