6f6710d68f17938f: LONDON: Tax advantages and high energy prices will drive further consolidation in Britain's North Sea oil and gas fields after a flurry of deals this year, 11 industry analysts and bankers said.

A rise in oil and gas prices to multiyear highs caused by disruption linked to the US-Israeli war with Iran has generated huge amounts of cash for the industry, which has been reporting results this week.

However, the price rises have also increased inflation for everyone, sharpening the appetite for scale to justify production in the mature North Sea Basin, which the British government views as a secure, domestic supply source.
Oil and gas M&A involving a UK target or buyer has reached US$19.6 billion year-to-date, exceeding the US$16.5 billion for all of 2025, according to LSEG data.
That makes 2026 the strongest year for activity since at least 2022, when Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine led to a previous energy crisis.

Among the analysts and bankers who spoke to Reuters, James McCormack of investment bank and research firm Cavendish said the pool of potential buyers was relatively small, but that did not preclude more deals.
He described the UK North Sea as "an increasingly concentrated market when it comes to credible buyers with the balance sheet, tax capacity and decommissioning capability to execute material deals".
As relative costs are especially high in ageing oil and gas fields, Cavendish in a report published in September said the pressure was on for mergers.

"Companies that can offer diversification, liquidity and development capital are attracting premium valuations, while sub-scale operators face growing pressure to merge, seek capital in deeper markets, or accept takeover approaches," it said.
Alexander Franke, an energy consultant at Oliver Wyman, also predicted the need to contain costs would drive more activity with the caveat the pace would depend on oil price outlook.
Any unexpected fall in energy prices could deter buyers, while sustained rises could boost cash flow and funding for acquisitions.
UK tax rate adds to case for deals
"British taxes are a further incentive to maximise efficiency," the bankers and analysts said.

An Energy Profits Levy, introduced by the previous Conservative government and increased under the current Labour government, has pushed the headline tax rate on UK upstream oil and gas activities to 78%.
"There's been a lot of tax-driven consolidation in recent years," Greig Aitken, director of corporate research at Wood Mackenzie, said.
Others also highlighted the advantage of scale in the tax context.

"There's still a rationale for two UK North Sea players to combine, so that the enlarged company can take advantage of the tax credits as well as operational synergies," Tony White of advisory firm MKI said.
Shifting strategy could make investors pause
Apart from the unpredictability of energy prices, investment decisions are complicated by the uncertainty of government policy.
The British government has said it remains committed to achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, but it approved earlier this month the development of the Jackdaw North Sea gas field.

In its autumn budget statement on Wednesday, it reiterated its long-term commitment to keeping oil and gas in the energy mix, although it did not announce any new measures for the oil and gas industry.

The decision on Jackdaw followed years of debate as environmental campaigners said there was no justification for investment in fossil fuel production, while others said the project would provide jobs and a domestic source of natural gas at less environmental cost than imported supplies.
BP's North Sea sale
The biggest oil companies for years have been withdrawing from the ageing North Sea to focus on bigger prospects elsewhere.
Shell, has opted to manage its remaining North Sea exposure through partnerships and joint ventures, including the creation of Adura with Norway's Equinor.
BP, the last major with a significant North Sea focus, this July announced plans to sell its oil and gas fields in the basin as part of a portfolio overhaul to improve profitability.
Analysts have estimated the sale could raise US$2 billion and trigger another wave of consolidation.

"Most likely the buyer is another North Sea consolidator. Value will be driven by infrastructure and tax synergies rather than by reserves alone," Cavendish's McCormack said, naming UK companies EnQuest, NEO NEXT+ and Ithaca as possible buyers.
The next round of bidding will be in December, one person with knowledge of the process said. BP had no further comment.
Amjad Bseisu, CEO of EnQuest, has said he is interested in the assets. The company had no further comment.
Ithaca declined to comment, while NEO NEXT+ did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Start of a broader consolidation cycle
UK-listed companies have drawn rival bids, including from international would-be buyers.
London-listed Genel Energy in September raised its offer to US$436 million for Britain's Capricorn Energy, outbidding Norway's DNO.
Israel's Ratio Petroleum outbid Serica Energy with a sweetened US$196 million offer for Pharos Energy in August.
Serica said it continues to evaluate acquisition opportunities in both the UK North Sea and international markets.

This month Gulf Keystone Petroleum and ShaMaran Petroleum announced a US$601 million all-share merger, while Ithaca has agreed to buy three offshore oil assets from Canada's Suncor for C$1.2 billion (US$853.49 million).
Even Pharos CEO Katherine Roe, a former investment banker, said she was surprised by the bidding war for the company.

She told Reuters rising costs and limited diversification left smaller producers more exposed to political, operational and energy price risks, but that consolidation can improve efficiency and investor returns.
"To receive a cash bid at a 30% premium with liquidity in a way that's just not achievable on a daily basis is ... the best outcome for shareholders," Roe said.

edf030352b667085: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinical psychologists, they can represent something more sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders.

A new report suggests that the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up between 1990 and 2023—by a whopping 71%. By 2023, there were an estimated 18.1 million people living with one of these two disorders.

What’s worse is that the number is likely to be much higher than that once we factor in other eating disorders. And, disturbingly, those in the field are already starting to see GLP-1 weight-loss drugs exacerbating the issue.

Cheri Levinson is a clinical psychologist at the University of Louisville in Kentucky who has specialized in eating disorders for almost 20 years. She says she’s now seeing more patients with more severe symptoms than at any other time in her career, and that many of them are misusing GLP-1s. “This is the worst I’ve seen things,” she says.

Eating disorders are mental health conditions in which people’s eating behaviors impact their health. They include anorexia nervosa (defined by a fear of weight gain), bulimia nervosa (in which people binge and purge), binge eating disorder, and others.

It’s thought that some people have a genetic predisposition to certain eating disorders, but that some external factor is what triggers their onset. That might be stress, or social pressure to be skinny. Often, simply restricting food intake can trigger an eating disorder, says Levinson.

Eating disorders—along with the pressure to look thin—were already prevalent in the 1990s (the heroin chic era springs to mind). To find out how things might have changed since then, Ruhai Bai at the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University in China and his colleagues pulled together data from studies and surveys conducted on populations around the world. The team used statistical models to fill in any data gaps.

That research allowed the researchers to estimate the annual incidence of two eating disorders—anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—for each of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023. They also estimated the impact those disorders had on global health by calculating their disability-adjusted life years (one DALY represents a year of healthy life lost).

The findings, published in JAMA Psychiatry on Wednesday, are unsettling. Between 1990 and 2023, there was a 71% increase in the incidence of those two eating disorders, the team found. Those conditions had a huge impact on global health, too. In 2023, they “cost the world the equivalent of about 3.83 million years of healthy life,” says Bai.

Bai and his colleagues expect these figures to continue to rise. In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people had either anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa; by 2050, the team predict, the two conditions could affect 21.8 million people.

It gets worse. Those two conditions represent less than half of all eating disorders, says Levinson, who was not involved in Bai’s study. The true impact of these disorders is “probably three times the rate that they’re reporting,” she says.
Bai and his colleagues didn’t explore the reasons for this rise (although Bai points out that it can’t be entirely explained by population growth). So how did we get here?

Social media may have played a role. “Social media comparisons, influencers, challenges, diet trends can all be precipitating … events for an eating disorder,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist at the University of North Carolina, who was not involved in the new study. Bulik has been studying and treating eating disorders since the early 1980s. “Between 1990 and 2023 there has clearly been an upsurge of those types of environmental exposures,” she says.

Many social media users are exposed to filtered and modified images of skinny influencers who may have undergone cosmetic surgery or extreme dieting and who are promoting “thinspiration” or “fitspiration” content. But users with eating disorders appear to be more likely to engage with this content—and to be fed more of it as a result.

When researchers at the University of Melbourne investigated this phenomenon a couple of years ago, they found that the algorithms of TikTok users with eating disorders delivered 4343% more “toxic eating disorder videos” than those of users who didn’t have the disorders. They also got more content focused on dieting or exercising. Many were fed over 1000 problematic videos per month. Bulik describes social media as “quicksand” for people with, or at risk of, eating disorders.

The covid-19 pandemic—and the social isolation that accompanied lockdowns—also appears to have contributed to the rise in eating disorders. Research conducted in 2021 found that the number of people hospitalized with eating disorders in the US doubled between 2018 and 2020.

Researchers don’t yet have good data on how trends in eating disorders might have progressed since 2023. But anecdotally, things seem to be getting even worse. “There are more eating disorders, more severe eating disorders… and we’re seeing earlier ages of onset,” says Levinson. “We’re seeing eight- and nine-year-olds with eating disorders.”
“From what I’m hearing and seeing, I am not going to be surprised if that number isn’t at least doubling again,” she adds.

Levinson particularly worries about the impact of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, which have exploded in popularity in recent years. A Gallup survey conducted earlier this year suggested that 15% of Americans had used one of these drugs for weight loss. And they’re becoming more accessible—drug companies are working on new formulations that are both easier to take and more effective, and many people can buy versions of these drugs from compound pharmacies or dubious online sources.

In a small study published earlier this year, Levinson and her colleagues found that 30% of people with eating disorders had used GLP-1 drugs. The drugs might benefit some of those people. But 10% appeared to have misused the drugs. And Levinson thinks that figure is also an underestimate.

Levinson says she and her colleagues have seen children develop eating disorders after being prescribed GLP-1s for medical reasons. They’ve seen others—even children as young as 11—buy versions of these drugs over TikTok.

“We’re very concerned that GLPs will lead to even faster and more extreme weight loss in people with anorexia nervosa, and that patients will come to us in even more advanced stages of illness that become difficult to reverse,” says Bulik.

Both Bulik and Levinson are continuing to study the impacts of these drugs in eating disorders. In the meantime, both urge medical professionals to consider the risks GLP-1s might pose to people with those disorders. Bulik contributed to a set of research and clinical guidelines, published earlier this month, that recommends doctors screen for eating disorders before prescribing the drugs, for example. The guidelines also recommend more patient education and more robust monitoring of people who take GLP-1s.
If you think you or someone you know might have an eating disorder, you can find information and support at the National Eating Disorders Association.

5baff2e67cd0deb4: ‘Let us eat what we produce; that way, we all win’
Originally published on Global Voices
REB Lokal founder Rébetha Charles stands with a jar of peanut butter (manba lokal). Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.

For several decades, due to the significant reduction of tariff barriers on foreign goods — particularly those from the United States and the Dominican Republic — Haiti has depended heavily on imported products for local consumption.

The arrangement began under various structural adjustment programmes that were initiated between 1994 and 1995, through agreements between the Haitian government and international financial institutions like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. Since then, imports have practically invaded the Haitian market, creating inequitable competition for local farmers who rely on subsistence agriculture and traditional, rudimentary equipment, and significantly weakening national production.

Complicating the economic reality is Haiti’s ongoing struggle with gang violence, political instability, and the absence of adequate infrastructure; yet, many Haitians continue to take on ambitious initiatives. Take Rébetha Charles, a 38-year-old woman entrepreneur. Originally from Jérémie, Charles studied agronomy, works in the Grand’Anse department in Haiti’s southern region, of which Jérémie is the capital, and created an agri-food enterprise called REB Lokal.
Rébetha Charles. Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.

REB is a short form of her name; Lokal speaks to the pride inherent in making local products. Her company buys products from small farmers and, in its small manufacturing plant, transforms these local harvests into healthy, sustainable, tasty products.

In a WhatsApp interview, Charles says she is proud of a few key things. First, her company adds value. Through a manufacturing process that produces authentic, nutritious, and 100 percent local products, farmers have a much better guarantee of not losing their crops, whereas before, various obstacles, including spoilage, prevented them from selling their produce at market.

Charles explains that the REB Lokal project is an enterprise that transforms local agricultural products: “We work with a supplier network of almost 2,000 people, including agricultural producers and small traders. We have more than 20 employees, so we work every day to grow the project even more.”

Second, Charles is pleased with the company’s focus on providing safe, fresh food that meets modern food processing standards — its approach places value on Haitian culinary traditions to preserve the natural taste and nutritional value of local ingredients. Finally, REB Lokal makes a point of avoiding chemical additives and artificial ingredients, as part of its commitment to providing consumers with healthy, accessible, community-friendly food.

Charles didn’t initially see herself as an entrepreneur. Before she decided to enter the agro business, she was working at an international humanitarian organisation, but resigned because of a culture — fairly common in Haiti — of sexual harassment. “In Haiti,” she stresses, “a woman’s life is not easy when it comes to work. Instead of competence, sometimes there are other things they ask from us. Sometimes, some of us stand up and say, ‘No, we do not agree,’ because we went to school just like everyone else, got experience where we needed — and after that, there are things we choose not to do.”

That professional environment left her with “such a disgust for work” that, even though she had been offered other opportunities in bigger organisations, she decided to put everything on pause. Charles finally submitted her resignation letter on August 31, 2020, and launched the REB Lokal project the very next day.
Workers packaging chocolate balls at the factory. Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.

It wasn’t easy for Charles, especially at the beginning. In an interview with Chef Cassy, she said she started the business doing papita — breadfruit and banana chips — but spent more than five months making it, every single day, without getting it right. It was only by the sixth month that the papita started coming out well, and she began selling it in supermarkets. After that, things started moving quickly; every day, customers would place more orders — not bad for a small business that began with about USD 8.50, selling papita.

The business has now evolved to the point where it offers a broad range of widely available products: “We sell [our products] in the Grand’Anse department, we sell them in the south, in the west, in several other departments in the country, and we also sell internationally in the United States and Canada.”
Everything has grown out of her core commitment to Haitian farmers by purchasing their crops, and encouraging Haitian consumers to eat local products:

Mwen panse li lè li tan pou peyizan yo kapab vann sa yap pwodui. Donk, mwen santi m toujou gen yon responsabilite depi m pase yon kote ki gen dennre, bagay nou yo kap fèt nan andeyò yo, mwen anvi fè yon bagay. Ann manje sa nou pwodui, ann manje sa nou fè. Sa ap pèmèt peyizan yo pa bezwen deplase kite lakay yo pou yo ale lòt kote; yo ka rete nan zòn yo, yap travay, n ap achte, n ap kondisyonnen, nap transfòme, ou menm wap konsome. Konsa, nou tout ap soti gayan, e nap gen yon lòt peyi, nap gen yon lòt kominite.

I think it is time for farmers to be able to sell what they produce. So, I always feel a responsibility whenever I pass by a place that has crops, or things made in the countryside; I want to do something. Let us eat what we produce, let us eat what we make. This will allow farmers to not need to leave their home to go somewhere else; they can stay in their area — they work, we buy, we process, we transform, and you consume. That way, we all win, and we will have another country; another community.

Inside REB Lokal’s processing facility feels different from what one would expect. There are production rooms, transformation rooms, and packaging rooms where employees work in white coats, hairnets, and gloves.
Customers inside the REB Lokal store looking at products. Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.

There is also a shop front full of shelves with finished products — now much more diverse than just papita — displayed for sale. There are roasted peanuts, sakalapina (cornmeal with avocados), papita in both chicken and fish flavour, konparet (spiced ginger-coconut cake), corn chanchanm (traditional Haitian sweet, made from roasted corn and peanuts), honey, sugar cane syrup, chocolate powder and balls, cocoa butter, breadfruit, corn, cassava and plantain flour, baby food (made without chemicals under the supervision of paediatricians and nutritionists), alcoholic drinks, fruit juice, and castor oil.

To Rébetha Charles, who grew up in an idyllic rural community, the work of REB Lokal is close to her heart. Yet, running a business in an insecure country comes with its challenges. Gangs’ control of the main roads can make delivery slow and limit production, as the lack of access prevents products from reaching many communities. A true entrepreneur, Charles finds ways around such obstacles as best she can. She still believes that Haiti has a future, so she perseveres, believing the impossible can become possible through vision and sheer willpower.
Written by Jude Pierre Louis

f7e09342bd11e5d6: Google is paying a higher price for its bet on AI than even Alphabet's $51.4 billion in Q3 capital expenditures suggest.

The biz appears to have traded its high-performing search advertising business for the mediocre monetization of AI Overviews and AI Mode, a misstep that contributed to investor concerns as Alphabet lost roughly $500 billion in market value despite management's attempts to reassure Wall Street.
Google's year-over-year search revenue growth slowed from 17 percent in Q2 to 12 percent in Q3. It's still headed in the right direction, but at a slower rate.

During Alphabet's conference call for investors, Douglas Anmuth from JPMorgan Chase & Co asked whether that's because Google is showing fewer ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode than it shows in its traditional search results.

Chief business officer Philipp Schindler cited several reasons for that: foreign exchange rates, Europe's elimination of its customs-duty exemption, and "the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode."
To compensate, Google said it is expanding the distribution of AI Overview ads and adding multiturn ads in the US for AI Mode queries.

But some Google Ads customers appear to be more concerned about quality than quantity. In a social media post, Max Anderson, CEO of OnlyFinder, complained that Google has responded to declining search volumes by attempting to manufacture revenue growth through "short-sighted, highly extractive, customer-hostile tactics," such as charging advertisers more for lower-quality clicks, including clicks on search terms they had not agreed to target.
Eric Seufert, an analyst with Mobile Dev Memo, dismissed the doomsayers in a blog post.

"It’s tempting to look at the successive deceleration in Search revenue growth from Q1 2026 as a response to pressure from other chatbots and to assume that Search query volume is migrating elsewhere," he wrote. "But the earnings release notes that the 'year-over-year Search query growth rate [was] the highest it has been in the last five years' in Q3, so it's clear that Search usage isn't declining."

So people are still searching, and the business is still growing, but less convincingly, thanks to the lower monetization of AI Overviews and AI Mode. And Google's answer involves more ads in AI interactions.
Nate Elliott, principal analyst for AI at Emarketer, told The Register in an email that AI represents a double-edged sword for Google's ad business.

"On the one hand, Google owns the thing that people use AI for most: search," Elliott wrote. "Our surveys say that by far the top reason people use AI is to look for facts and information. Luckily for Google, people also tell us they haven't stopped using search engines – they've simply added AI as a new behavior on top of search. That means people spend more time than ever looking for information, and most of those people don't even think twice before doing their searches on Google. If Google figures out how to effectively monetize those users, that's great news for them."
But, said Elliott, people may find tools they like better than Google Search as they become accustomed to AI-based discovery.

"If ChatGPT or Claude or Muse is better at helping them find what they're looking for, people's search habits might change for the first time in a generation," he said. "That's potentially catastrophic for Google's ad business. The same is true if they maintain their market share but simply can't figure out how to make money from this new kind of discovery.

"The problem is, Google isn't giving us very much information about what the specific impact is of AI on their business right now, so everyone's reading into the tiny scraps of information they are releasing."
Elliott said it's remarkable that Google has managed to keep the largest and most mature digital ad business growing at a double-digit rate every quarter in recent years.
"But it appears that most folks disagree, and instead are concerned that the advertising business 'only' grew by 10 percent," he said. ®

6a71b2e5d2a70e69: Welcome to another instalment of On Call, the reader-contributed column The Register publishes each Friday as a cathartic service for readers who know that dealing with tech support BS can be a cow of a job.
This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Jason" who told us he had helped an agricultural equipment dealer with his computer issues for about 20 years.

"One day this guy called me to ask if I could help at a farm in Yorkshire, where he'd arranged the supply and installation of a fairly substantial system that used a computer to do effectively everything for a few hundred cattle," he told On Call.
"That meant individually feeding them, measuring milk yields, planning pregnancies, and periodically submitting all the data to the government."
Jason said other tech support folk had tried, and failed, to fix the system.
"This had somewhat soured the relationship between the agricultural equipment dealer and the farmer," he punned in his email to On Call.
Well punned, Jason.
But we digress.

"Despite not being fond of wading around in cow shit at four in the morning, I agreed to take a look at the system," Jason told us. By this time he had learned that the farm produced many tons of milk each week, so assumed he would find serious industrial-scale tech once he reached the farm.
That assumption was wrong.

"When I arrived, the first thing that I found to worry about was that the whole thing was controlled by proprietary software on a single PC running Windows XP – just after Microsoft ended mainstream support."
The other things to worry about were all acts of omission: the farm had no backups, no spare PC, and nobody on site to maintain the PC.

Jason asked if anyone was responsible for keeping the computer up to date with the security patches and was told the farmer's 14-year-old grandson had done some computer studies at school, so he got the job.
That lad had either not discovered, or deleted, the many rather racy videos Jason found on the PC.
"When the farmer's wife learned of this, there was what can best be described as a hullabaloo," Jason told On Call.

As he dug into the mess, Jason found that the computer was sending milk production data to Her Majesty's Government. He also found that neither the government, nor the farm management software vendor, had bothered to require installation of a firewall.
Jason says he installed one, made a few other tweaks, and got the system working.
"Everyone seemed pleased, or at least they did until they got my bill," he wrote. "And to be fair, they did pay it promptly."
Jason never heard from the farm again.
"I don't know if that's because it's still working OK, or if they're just too embarrassed to see me again, or they found someone cheaper who could cope with my recommendations," he wrote.

What's the strangest or dirtiest place you've been asked to deliver tech support? Don't cheese us off by holding back! Click here to send us your story so we can milk it for all it's worth in a future instalment of On Call. ®

7ff55b5046b63b80: BRUSSELS, Oct 30 — Eleven European countries pledged today to jointly release 42.6 million barrels of oil by the end of January, in line with a G7 deal struck this month to ease global energy supply concerns.

“EU member states have reaffirmed their commitment to an accelerated release of 42.6 million barrels from strategic reserves over the next months, and around half of this will be diesel,” the EU’s energy commissioner Dan Jorgensen told reporters.
Eleven countries including France, Germany and Italy said in a statement they would release the oil from their strategic reserves by the end of January 2027, including 20.5 million barrels of diesel.
The announcement comes weeks after the G7 economies said they would release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil after US President Donald Trump threatened a diesel export ban.

The other European countries involved are Belgium, Denmark, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden. Lithuania also endorsed the initiative, though it did not sign the joint pledge.
The International Energy Agency — to which all the EU nations belong — made a call in mid-October for its members to step up the release of oil stocks ahead of winter.

Trump ramped up the pressure on Europe to release reserves after the US-Israeli war with Iran sent energy prices skyrocketing, coming back to bite him at home with high fuel costs that have become a key issue ahead of congressional elections next week.
The EU said it was taking the impact of the crisis on households seriously but was not worried about supply.
“We do not expect the security of supply issue as such. But for the citizens that are struggling to pay the bills, that might not matter,” Jorgensen said. — AFP

ca5a8f25a74be452: Amazon Web Services will become a trillion-dollar business in five to ten years, and thanks to the AI boom Amazon CEO Andy Jassy thinks it should be able to grow by 40 percent or more in 2027 or 2028.

The cloud giant is already on track to generate $184 billion annual revenue this financial year, helped by 39.3 percent year-over-year growth that propelled Q3 revenue to a whisker short of $46 billion.

“It’s important to remember that the vast majority of global IT spend, about 85 percent, is still on premises, and we’re in a 10- to 20-year cycle where that equation will flip to the cloud,” he said on Amazon's Q3 earnings call.
“Conventional wisdom has been that linchpin workloads like mainframes or storage area networks would never move to the cloud,” he observed, before triumphantly noting “these workloads are moving.”
He thinks AI will help, too.

Jassy said the cloudy concern installs a new AI accelerator “about every 14 seconds, and almost as fast as we install capacity, customers are gobbling it up.” The outfit’s Bedrock AI services is already the fastest growing multi-billion dollar service in its history, Jassy said.
Core compute and storage services are also soaring: the CEO said revenue from both “grew at their fastest rates in several years.”

Jassy thinks the performance of Bedrock and core services are intertwined, because when users select AWS for AI workloads they want their cloudy inferencing rigs to be “near the rest of their data and apps.”

The CEO said AI workloads therefore “can’t help but drive core AWS demand because AI uses core for work like reinforcement learning, post-training, and tool usage, which can’t help but drive reinvestment back into our broader AWS functionality.”
He thinks this scheme is already working because margins for AI services are already “well ahead” of the figures AWS was able to achieve for its core services at a similar time in their evolution.

The company expects to make $220 billion of capital expenditure in 2026 and already spent $75.9 billion last quarter alone, most of that on AWS. Jassy said the cloud colossus is finding ways to more quickly pay for its infrastructure investments.
The CEO said it’s not easy to do that.

“I think what we’re seeing with AI, it’s the biggest transformation in our lifetime,” he said. “Would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years and you could spread the CapEx over 25 years? Yeah, it might be more convenient, but that’s not the world that we live in, and that’s not the opportunity.”

“We can fund this plan. I think it will forever change the size of Amazon. It will forever change our revenue, it will forever change our free cash flow, and we’re going to invest, and we’re going to pursue it to continue to be the significant leader like we are today.”

Amazon needs AWS to land this plane, because the cloudy concern is growing much faster than the company’s retail and operations, which saw revenue rise six percent on far slimmer margins. Jassy could at least point to Prime Video becoming “a significant business with a revenue run rate in the tens of billions of dollars, [and is] now profitable in its own right.”
Overall revenue was $180.17 bilion for the quarter.
So if the respective growth rates of AWS and the rest of Amazon continue, in a few years we could be talking about a cloud company with a retail side hustle. ®

a8784c1fd69b20a9: NEW YORK, Oct 30 — General Motors will pay US$220 million to settle litigation over the sale of drivers’ driving data that was then used to raise insurance rates, New York’s attorney general said today.

The payments resolves a suit brought by New York and 35 other states alleging GM shared the data of drivers enrolled in its Smart Driver program despite saying it would not be given to insurers without express consent, James’s office said in a press release.

The program tracked actions such as sudden braking and whether drivers exceeded the speed limit. GM sold the data to data bankers who sold the info to insurers, who in some cases lifted premiums by significant levels, according to the press release.

“General Motors collected data on their customers’ personal driving habits without their knowledge and then sold it, potentially affecting their insurance rates,” James said. “Today, we are putting a stop to this illegal violation of drivers’ privacy.”

GM in January 2025 reached a settlement with the US Federal Trade Commission over allegations it improperly collected and sold consumer data that could be used to set insurance rates.

9ef3e3dd5040cf56: NEW YORK, Oct 30 — Cryptocurrency platform Binance said today it had fallen victim to a major hack and indicated that more than US$2.5 billion (RM10.13 billion) in funds had been frozen in an effort to prevent a massive theft.

The company — the world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes — posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages on X, insisting that “user funds are completely safe” but also saying it would “cover all losses.”
The scope of the heist was not immediately known, but blockchain analytics company Chainalysis said its “current estimate on amount stolen is approx US$5.912B at time of theft.”

That would be almost four times the amount stolen in what has been the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: US$1.5 billion taken in February 2025 from the Bybit platform — an incident attributed to hackers affiliated with North Korea.
At about 0030 GMT tomorrow, Binance said all deposits and withdrawals had been “temporarily suspended while our team conducts security checks, freezes funds, and works with law enforcement.”

“This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets,” the company said.
Neither the company nor industry observers offered any explanation as to how the cyberattack might have occurred.
“It does look like a hack on Binance,” said former Binance chief Changpeng Zhao, who no longer runs the group but remains a majority shareholder.
He estimated that the total losses could be “a bit higher” than US$1 billion.
Paolo Ardoino, the CEO of Tether — a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT — said his firm froze about US$1.6 billion “related to a potential Binance exchange hack.”
Circle boss Jeremy Allaire said his company had frozen more than US$800 million in USDC.
USDT and USDC are both “stablecoins,” or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar.
The US Department of Justice and the FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, several industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.
The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on the news, except for the stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins.
At about 0025 GMT, bitcoin had lost nearly five per cent, Ethereum fell nearly six per cent, and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 per cent.

The cyberattack on Binance comes as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols. — AFP
5f6e6b9b3ba398ca: Crypto exchange Binance has paused trading after discovering unknown parties cracked one of its workers’ laptops and used it to make massive trades.
Late on Thursday, US time, the company used its social media feeds to report “Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating.”
The exchange insisted “User funds are completely safe” and warned its customers “should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.”

The company soon froze $2.5 billion worth of assets and warned that the figure could go higher “as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.”
To prevent the matter worsening, Binance halted all trading, deposits, and withdrawals. It also promised to cover any losses.
About an hour ago at the time of writing, Binance posted an update on the incident that explains what it thinks went wrong.

“Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions,” the post states.
The company also hiked the amount it thinks is at risk to $6.3 billion and repeated its promise to cover any customer losses.
The update also says Binance found no evidence of any wallet private key leak, suggesting that customers’ holdings remain secure.
When they can use them again, as Binance is yet to resume trading.

Binance hasn’t explained how attackers gained access to the engineer’s laptop. The scant details provided make it hard to rule out a successful phishing attack, or perhaps a supply chain attack on a package the developer used.
Binance says it will spill once it knows exactly what happened.

Cryptocurrency outfits have a long and inglorious history of falling victim to cyberattacks, perhaps starting with the 2011 raid on Mt Gox, to incidents allegedly perpetrated by nation-states, and, just last week, another situation possibly involving an AI-powered attacker. ®

60c3bbde02120c7c: Intel’s share price sank by almost a quarter on Thursday after the company revealed a deep dip in sales of PC processors.

The rout began after the silicon-slinger posted Q3 results that included some nice numbers, such as a 21 percent year on year revenue jump to $16.5 billion, helped by 78 percent growth for datacenter and AI products, and gross margins of 43 percent. The revenue number was at the high end of Intel’s revenue guidance of $15.8-16.8 billion, and the gross margin beat its predictions by two points.

Outweighing those upsides was a decline in revenue for client computing and physical AI products, which saw incoming cash reach $8.1 billion but fall five percent year-over-year and nine percent decline from last quarter.

In prepared remarks [PDF] published to coincide with Intel’s earnings announcement, CEO Lip Bu Tan said “In recent weeks, our customers began signaling a PC slowdown based on memory prices and availability. Year-to-date system end-point prices have increased significantly placing additional pressure on already limited IT budgets.”

“The pace of the PC correction has accelerated over the last two months, as our OEM partners are aggressively managing inventory to match the softer sell through,” he added, before predicting that the market for PC chips will shrink by 12 percent next year and remain tough “until memory availability and prices begin to normalize.”
Which may not be for years, given Korean memory-maker SK Hynix this week predicted that memory shortages will persist until the year 2030. Intel’s biggest business is therefore in trouble.
AI and Xeons riding to a rocky rescue
Tan tried to give investors reasons to be cheerful, by saying Intel sees a “resurgence in demand for CPU” sparked by customers’ desire for computing systems that consume less energy.
“Increasingly, energy efficiency is becoming the most important metric for the AI infrastructure build-out,” he said.

That matters, Tan argued, because “While GPUs are great at ‘thinking tasks,’ deterministic CPUs are far more efficient at ‘finding’ tasks. While a GPU reasoning query can run as high as multiple watt-hours of energy, a single CPU-based query could cost only joules of energy.”
The CEO reasoned that lower energy consumption is important in the context of agentic AI – the idea that we will all soon run many autonomous agents to handle personal and professional scutwork.

“Applying even conservative estimates to the total number of digital agents, and agents serviced per CPU, it is easy to anticipate a massive dollar and unit TAM [total addressable market] for CPUs over the coming five years,” Tan said. “By our estimates, server CPU TAM, largely driven by agentic workloads, could increase as much as 5X from where it is today, from $40B to more than $200B over five years.”
But during its earnings call, Intel execs admitted it may struggle to cash in on that boom in the short and longer term as the company struggles to source key supplies like silicon wafers.

Asked if Intel can meet demand for server CPUs and if investors should therefore expect further growth in datacenter product sales early in Intel’s next financial year, chief financial officer Dave Zinsner declined to offer any guidance.

“There is going to be a strong driver of demand for CPUs,” he demurred. “We see that continuing all through next year. We are working on the supply side of the equation to make sure that we can meet what customers need. We will likely not fully meet what they require, but I think we are going to be in a more challenging situation in the first half of the year than we are in the second half.”

Intel is trying to shift production around its fleet of fabs so it can crank out as much silicon as possible and will even devote some PC chip production capacity to datacenter products. But overall, Chipzilla is clearly in a spot of bother.

CEO Lip Bu Tan said his plan to “rebuild” Intel will be “a multiyear journey” and insisted “We have made enormous strides in these 18 months, including a dramatic re-sizing of our workforce, eliminating middle management and bureaucracy, streamlining our executive ranks and establishing an almost entirely new leadership team.”

He pointed to strong progress on Intel’s manufacturing processes that will bring it closer to parity with TSMC, meaning its own products will become more potent while the company’s foundry business also becomes more attractive.
And he said that Intel has restored an “engineering-centric culture” that will help the company to improve.
But the CEO also admitted “I am disappointed that we were not able to meet strong customer demand in this quarter.”
“We face near term challenges, including manufacturing supply shortages, the unprecedented memory crunch, and the resulting softness in PC demand. But I remain confident in our path forward.”

Investors did not share that confidence. Intel’s shares started the day at $92.96 apiece. Immediately after the company announced its results, shares sank to $73. At the time of writing, after-hours trading has seen the price reach $70.87, a 23.7 percent slump. ®

95fcfb629e87abc5: At the end of Star Trek: Generations (1994), surveying the wreckage of the crashed USS Enterprise he captained for nearly a decade, Jean-Luc Picard (Patrick Stewart) muses to his first officer, William Riker (Jonathan Frakes): … time is a companion that goes with us on the journey, reminds us to cherish every moment, because it will never come again. Despite the many screen roles for which Stewart would later be known, his Shakespearean roots are indelibly intertwined with almost every performance he gave. They would also give him – and many of us – something to lighten the load of COVID lockdowns. Stewart used social media in 2020 to read the internet a Shakespearean sonnet each day, later turning his delightful orations into an audiobook. For most, Stewart will best be remembered as a kaleidoscopic titan of film and television. Beginning as a firefighter on the British soap opera Coronation Street in 1967, Stewart’s illustrious screen career spanned more than 50 years and a vast array of roles. To name only a few, he was: a flamboyant interior designer a stoic Atreides weapon master in a screen adaptation of the Dune books the irreverent king of England a foul-mouthed CIA deputy director an enigmatic cult leader, and a megalomaniacal egg-alien overlord. Two key roles From his storied body of work, two roles loom largest. He was the telepathic mutant and academic Charles Xavier of the X-Men film series – a role he played for more than 25 years, including a posthumous appearance in Avengers: Doomsday (released this December). As Professor X, Stewart embodied a beloved superhero with paternal warmth and secretive, calculating intellect. He was an empathetic leader of a team of extraordinary people who had been shunned, threatened and harmed by the world for their differences. One cannot help but think this role enabled Stewart to channel much of his real-life allyship with marginalised queer communities and his support for survivors of domestic violence (which was based on his own childhood experiences). In this role, Stewart acted alongside his long-time friend Sir Ian McKellen, who played the mutant antagonist and master of metal Magneto. Ironically, McKellen had once warned Stewart not to forsake the theatre for the screen, advising that a career in film and television would go nowhere. Stewart and McKellen’s endearing friendship and acclaimed X-Men performances became the stuff of internet legend, particularly when McKellen officiated Stewart’s wedding to US singer Sunny Ozell in 2013. Stewart’s work in Star Trek as Jean-Luc Picard – captain (later admiral) of the USS Enterprise – is equally revered. As Stewart’s first major American television role, he took the captain’s chair in Star Trek: The Next Generation in 1987. He would eventually appear in seven seasons, four theatrical films, and the recent sequel series Star Trek: Picard. Despite initial reservations – including an infamous on-set incident where he stoically told his rambunctious Next Generation colleagues that “we are not here to have fun” – Stewart later embraced the role of Picard. He will be remembered as one of Star Trek’s most acclaimed and legendary performers. As Picard, Stewart created a potent role model in a franchise focused on an inclusive, utopian future. Stewart’s Picard was a respected leader, intergalactic explorer, keen orator, Shakespeare enthusiast, thoughtful diplomat, archaeology aficionado, and prolific tea-drinker – as he and other characters famously said, “tea, Earl Grey, hot”. This captain was an inspiring beacon of hope, curiosity and discovery. He advocated Starfleet ideals of exploration and community, but encouraged his crew – and, by extension, all of us – to seek out knowledge. He urged us all to solve problems with rationality and empathy, and work toward a better future for humanity. An enduring inspiration Like many others who grew up in the 1990s with Picard on the television, I still find the character’s ethos and Stewart’s performance have a profound impact on me as a scholar and educator who strives to live and teach by those ideals. Were it not for the inspiration Picard and Stewart provided me as a child, I may not have become an academic. Stewart lived the kind of important life that Picard would admire, and leaves behind a cherished body of work, as well as a legacy of dedicated social advocacy. Now, he boldly goes where you and I have not gone before. 74a19f23c8f72af9: Whenever you scan the headlines, a heart-breaking reality stares back: several Muslim-majority nations are trapped in devastating wars and armed conflicts. These crises range from full-scale international warfare to intense civil strife and localised insurgencies.

Tragically, from Iran, Iraq and Syria to Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, Somalia, Pakistan and Afghanistan, Muslims are often locked in conflict with other Muslims. This deep friction naturally prompts a difficult, uncomfortable question: can the Muslim world ever truly achieve unity?
On paper, the global ummah is bound by the most foundational of principles: belief in one God and the guidance of the Quran.
Yet, the reality on the ground is starkly fractured. It is easy for casual observers to look at this discord and assume that Islam itself is the root problem.

But if you pull back the curtain, it becomes clear that these conflicts are rarely about theology. Instead, they are driven by the exact same catalysts that spark wars anywhere else on earth: politics, money and human greed.
The truth is, most internal conflicts in the Muslim world are old-fashioned power struggles. Factions, regimes and politicians compete for control, territory and resources, plain and simple.

Consider the Sunni-Shia split. While it dates back to a seventh-century political disagreement over who should succeed Prophet Muhammad, these communities lived side-by-side in relative peace for centuries.
The divide only becomes weaponised today because authoritarian regimes and militant groups exploit it to manufacture an "us versus them" mentality.

Leaders routinely wrap their political ambitions in religious rhetoric because it remains a highly effective tool to manipulate the masses, justify violence and safeguard their power. This has been the norm in many failed Muslim states.

This dynamic plays out on a massive scale through regional chess games. Major powers like Saudi Arabia and Iran have long been locked in a geopolitical rivalry, turning vulnerable nations like Yemen and Syria into proxy battlegrounds.

Compounding the issue is that many modern borders in the region are fragile, artificially cutting across deep ethnic and tribal lines. When a central government collapses – as seen in Iraq or Libya – it creates a power vacuum that local armed groups immediately resort to violence to fill.
Coincidentally, many of these conflict zones are endowed with rich oil and gas reserves, making them highly attractive to foreign powers.

These natural resources are a double-edged sword: while they should guarantee prosperity, mismanagement leaves many states impoverished, even as the wealth draws predatory external interests. When warring domestic factions face defeat, they readily invite foreign intervention. Superpowers then step in under the guise of aid, though their true drivers are their own economic and strategic interests in the region.
Ultimately, a shared religious identity is not enough to sustain stability when states are hollowed out from within.

You cannot talk about unity without addressing daily survival. When high poverty, a lack of economic opportunity, systemic corruption and oppressive governance collide, they create a recipe for desperation. If citizens cannot build a decent life through peaceful or democratic means, sub-state conflicts and insurgencies become inevitable.

The path forward for the Muslim world is about repairing broken systems. Unity will only shift from a theological ideal to a political reality when leaders begin prioritising stable governance, economic fairness and basic human dignity over their political survival.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

ccbf2f56503f85ee: It seems like another season, but it was early this month when Anfield was meant to be the bear pit that would maul and then spit out the bad boys of Manchester City.

It was the first game after their guilty verdict and we all know how it went. Forgotten is that Liverpool gave City as good as they got before two harsh yellow cards to Ryan Gravenberch turned it all around.The bear was declawed and Liverpool’s 10 men couldn’t live with City, who ran out comfortable 3-0 winners.

That the Reds matched them for an hour didn’t fit the narrative of City defiance. Owners fiercely maintaining their innocence, players with a siege mentality, fans with inflatable bananas… all wallowing in victimhood.
They managed to win their first seven games, but then United stole their thunder with yet another crisis of their own.
After this Mancunian monopoly of headlines, it is time to go back to Liverpool, not least because Arsenal are the next visitors.
Smarting from their loss to Fleetwood, the champions will be a good test of where Liverpool are in the pecking order right now.
For there is the unmistakable whiff of meaningful momentum about them.
The roar that greeted Wesley Fofana’s penalty miss in midweek was more like the Kop we knew.
It was only a shoot-out, only the League Cup, and there were extra decibels for Chelsea, but it resonated.
Not ‘off the Richter’ like the Kop’s deafening best, but it saluted another win, their fifth in a row since the loss to City.
Two were in the Champions League (against Villarreal and LASK) that helped them to third place in the table with a 100% record.
Two in the EPL against hard-to-beat Brentford and Brighton, and now this to reach the last eight of the Carabao Cup.
And there was the added satisfaction of beating two former employees.
Xabi Alonso, who had been warmly welcomed as Bayer Leverkusen boss, was made aware what a cardinal sin it is to join Chelsea, at least in the eyes of the Kop.
But it was former skipper Jordan Henderson, who came in for most of the stick.
“Hendo’s” sterling service in Jurgen Klopp’s greatest sides was brusquely erased from memory by the sight of him in Chelsea blue.
Besides being loftily placed in three competitions, there are many reasons for optimism around the Reds right now.
The rebuild is not yet finished, but there has been unexpected progress.
Top of the list is that the stalled £400m strike force is firing.
Even the most recent – and expensive – addition, Bradley Barcola, is showing why the Reds paid PSG £125m for him after a sluggish start.
His pace is electric and although he’s very different to Mo Salah, his versatility is giving the attack more flexibility.
But the biggest improvement has come in the form of Alexander Isak, who had such a horrendous start to his Anfield career.
The Swede is now looking more like the player they broke the club record for. Cody Gakpo is also more of a force than last season, having brought his international form to the EPL.
This leaves Florian Wirtz. To say that Iraola is getting a tune out of the £116m man may still require a hearing aid.
He’s had better moments but is still way short of the little maestro they thought they were getting.
Then there’s the waspish Munoz buzzing across the entire attack, and it’s no wonder with assets like these, the Reds are mostly on the front foot.
Coupled with the ‘coming out’ of Rio Ngumoha ahead of schedule, and the teenager’s ability to flourish on both wings, too, manager Andoni Iraola has the sort of headache he doesn’t mind.

He’s been rewarded for his faith in youth by the emergence of Trey Nyoni too, and in a position where the club offered £100m fees in vain a couple of seasons ago. Ngumoha and Nyoni, a magical pair and money-savers too.
Let’s not forget Hugo Ekitike, who hopes to return from his ruptured Achilles by the end of the year.
The good news for Liverpool is that the Frenchman, who was by far the best signing of the previous transfer window, is already back working on the ball.
With that type of injury, there’s no guarantee he’ll be as lightning-fast as he once was, but his recovery is on course.
If he does return to his old form, Liverpool could boast the best attack in the business.
If attack is Liverpool’s forte, there’s encouragement all over the park. Ronald Araujo has been a masterly piece of business and gone from stopgap to cult hero playing out of position.
Whatever Barcelona want for the Uruguayan must be paid, according to his adoring fans.
Jeremy Jacquet has also made a brilliant start and looks to be Virgil van Dijk’s successor already.
And Giorgio Mamardashvili may have finally won the sceptics over with his showing against Chelsea.
The prevailing view is that Iraola has done well to fit them into the jigsaw so quickly and return Liverpool to something more like the heavy metal style of Klopp.
A slow starter – he went 10 games at Bournemouth before claiming his first win – and with the huge step up in size of club, it was felt he might need a few months to get it right.
But to have the team where they are before the end of October suggests he could become a major managerial figure.
Having come out on top – albeit narrowly – over one of his former Basque colleagues in Alonso, he now faces another in Mikel Arteta.
It’s too soon to talk of a title challenge, but if he can find a way to beat the depth of the Gunners, it won’t mean Liverpool are back, but that they are coming back.
That’s pretty good given the upheaval the club has been through.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
9370750c9f4c323d: Multiple vulnerabilities in five popular AI developer tools could allow attackers to execute code on a host machine, read and steal files, or spoof browser address bars. Researchers say flaws in OpenAI's Codex and Microsoft's VS Code remain unpatched, potentially putting developers who use affected configurations at risk.

AI security startup Forever Security discovered vulnerabilities in Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Anthropic's Claude Desktop, VS Code, and Codex, and disclosed four of the flaws to the affected vendors. GitHub independently fixed the Copilot vulnerability without receiving a report from Forever Security. All five share a common security weakness: embedded browsers granted capabilities beyond those available to conventional browsers.

Each tool “enriched its embedded browser beyond what a normal browser allows, and those enrichments undermined the traditional threat model - as agent input, as the authority on a tab’s own address, or as reach onto the host,” Forever researcher Gal Weizman wrote in a Thursday report.

Forever dubbed this class of vulnerability “Embrace,” short for EMbedded BRowser, and said the flaws led to code execution in Cursor, data theft in Claude Desktop, Codex, and VS Code, and address bar spoofing in GitHub Copilot.
Here’s what each of these looks like, starting with Cursor.
Cursor: arbitrary code execution
Typical web pages can’t run commands on the host computer because a web page’s JavaScript cannot talk to local apps.

Cursor’s integrated browser, however, allows a page to call the agent’s composer. The agent reads this as instructions and follows them, but the instructions remain hidden from human users. This opens the coding agent up to prompt injection attacks that could allow an attacker to execute commands on the host machine.

The researchers disclosed the vulnerability to Cursor on September 10, and the vendor silently patched the flaw on October 1. According to Forever, Cursor did not publish a security advisory about the issue or respond to the researchers' disclosure.
Cursor also did not reply to The Register’s request for comment.
GitHub Copilot: address bar spoofing
Under normal browser operations, a webpage cannot change the content of the address bar.

“Copilot’s browser preview works differently,” Weizman wrote. “Some pages change their address without loading a new page, and the app cannot always see that. So Copilot let the page tell the app its own address.”

The app checked only whether the text looked like a web address, starting with http, https or file, but it didn’t check where the tab really pointed to. This can be abused to trick the embedded browser into displaying a spoofed URL - such as github.com/login - in the address bar, while loading a fraudulent website - like a phishing page - underneath.

The researchers found the address-bar spoofing flaw in GitHub Copilot 1.1.27 on September 26. GitHub independently fixed the flaw in a later Copilot build (1.1.29) on October 13 without receiving a vulnerability report from Forever.
We reached out to GitHub and did not receive a response.
Claude Desktop, Codex, and VS Code: arbitrary file read
All three of these vendors’ coding assistants allow local HTML files opened in the built-in browser to escape its boundaries and access other files.

Both Claude Desktop and VS Code allow local pages access to their respective project folders, but the researchers found that these restrictions did not apply to web workers – a browser feature that allows JavaScript to run in a background thread, separate from the page's main thread.
This means a local page can start a worker, and the worker can bypass restrictions to reach any file on the machine.
Codex, however, didn’t have this same restriction, meaning a local page could read any file directly without a worker.

Weizman said his team disclosed the issue to Anthropic on July 23, and the AI vendor declined the Claude Desktop bug report as invalid for a “workspace trust” gated security boundary. A day later, however, Noma Security reported the same flaw, according to Weizman, and Anthropic accepted the report as valid.
Anthropic did not respond to The Register’s questions about either bug report or Forever’s timeline of events.

Forever disclosed the Codex bug to OpenAI on July 27 and didn’t get a response. The flaw remains unpatched, but an OpenAI spokesperson told The Register that it's aware of the issue and working to address it.

On September 10, Forever disclosed the VS Code vulnerability to Microsoft and says the vendor also labeled it as an invalid workspace trust gated security boundary issue. The researchers claim it remains unpatched. Microsoft did not respond to our request for comment.®
ff28614e0b2a21a4: ‘No independent body regularly monitored developments in prisons and communicat’d this information to the public using data.
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot from Prison Agenda‘s Substack page, used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

In Turkey, a team of two journalists and human rights activists launched a digital publication, Prison Agenda, to report on what is happening inside the country’s prisons and prison system, information that is often hidden from the Turkish public and the world.

As the Nordic Monitor noted in 2025, Turkey’s prison population has reached an unprecedented level. Citing figures from the Directorate General of Prisons and Houses of Detention, the website states that as of September 1, 2025, Turkish prisons hold 419,194 individuals. This includes 356,710 convicted prisoners and 62,484 people in pretrial detention. The figure exceeds the official capacity of 295,000 and places immense strain on the country’s penal system.

Le Monde also wrote in 2026 that a commissioned report on prison conditions among Council of Europe member states showed that France and Turkey each had 131 inmates for every 100 places, making them the two most overcrowded prison systems.

For the relatives of people in prison, as well as for national and international human rights organizations and agencies, the information provided by the Prison Agenda publication can be vital. A similar organization — Russia Behind Bars — used to work in Russia. While it did not function exclusively as a publication, it received letters from prisoners and their relatives, published news about torture or other human rights violations, and reported how the prison population had been drafted, in the hundreds of thousands, to fight Russia’s war with Ukraine. Unfortunately, it had to shut down its work within Russia because of the regime’s prosecution, but it continues to inform from abroad.

Civil society organizations, such as the publication about Prisons and Prisoners, are vital to the country and the world; they need to continue their important work within one of the most opaque systems in the world.
Global Voices interviewed one of Prison Agenda’s founder, Ahmet Kavruk, by email.
GV: Please tell us about your organization, and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project?

Ahmet Kavruk (AK): Prison Agenda is a digital publication that covers data on Turkey’s prisons, legislative changes relating to prisons, and human rights violations within them. It is guided by an independent, rights-focused approach to journalism.

We launched in January 2026. Our aim is to make the often complicated and scattered information about prisons more accessible to the public by presenting it in a clear and understandable way, and to highlight the human stories behind the statistics.

Shortly after launching in January, we reached a crossroads. We could either continue as a passion project, publishing solely in Turkish, which would be easier to sustain, but would not fulfil our potential, or evolve into a publishing model that would require more intensive work, but enable us to reach a wider audience.

It was precisely at this decision-making stage that we came across the Digital Spark call for proposals. It was one of the few support programmes capable of creating space for initiatives working in specific and often overlooked fields, such as prisons. We, therefore, drew up a plan and, should we be accepted into Digital Sparks, began to focus on the question, ‘How can we grow the Prison Agenda?’

We were particularly impressed by Digital Spark’s approach, which focuses on amplifying the voices of marginalized groups and strengthening civic participation. The fact that the project’s core objectives aligned so closely with our own area of work was a decisive factor in our decision to join the programme.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

AK: We are currently a team of two. We are both individuals with over 10 years’ experience working and producing within the prison sector in various capacities. We were aware of the growing problems in Turkey’s prisons. Through our voluntary work, professional lives and social networks, we have been trying to raise awareness of these issues.

However, our work in this field revealed not only these problems, but also a significant shortcoming. No independent body regularly monitored developments in prisons and communicated this information to the public using data. The data was scattered, technical and often difficult to access. Meanwhile, media interest tended to intensify only when there was new legislation or a high-profile incident.

Drawing on our background in journalism and our experience in human rights monitoring, we believed we could address this gap. We, therefore, launched Prison Agenda, aiming to present existing information to the public in a clear, accessible, rights-focused manner.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

AK: The most significant change for us during this project was launching our bilingual publications. By switching to English, we were able to reach beyond our existing Turkish audience and connect with a very different group of readers. The feedback from this new audience further strengthened our belief in the project’s potential.

While we initially had just one e-newsletter, we diversified our publications over time, increasing our regular e-newsletters to three. Today, Prison Agenda has evolved from a publication that shares news into a comprehensive digital media organisation that produces investigative reports, data analyses, data visualisations, thematic content, and opinion pieces.

This transformation aligns with our initial project goals of bilingual publishing and data-driven content production. In the first six months, our Turkish and English newsletters reached a total of 435 subscribers.
AK: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

AK: While our Turkish-language publications are mainly followed by the press, legislators and civil society, we have noticed that our English-language publications are attracting the attention of diplomatic missions from various countries and international-level bureaucrats. This was a significant development for us as it created an opportunity to raise awareness of prison issues in Turkey within a wider international network.

Throughout the project, we received collaboration proposals from different organisations and groups. The number of news articles citing our data and content increased, raising Prison Agenda's profile. Additionally, we started providing advice on data, sources and content to journalists reporting on prisons.

This has ensured that the information we produce is not limited to our own readers, but is made available within a wider ecosystem. We hope the network of readers and stakeholders established by Prison Agenda will help to raise awareness of prisoners’ rights and the need for humane prison conditions. The project’s aim was, indeed, to strengthen civil oversight and accountability by making information more accessible.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

AK: Prisons are, by their very nature, a rather closed field of work, with limited overlap with many other areas of rights. For this reason, we are not always able to collaborate with other civil society organisations.

One of the most significant opportunities that Digital Sparks has created for us is the chance to share a space with different civil society organisations and learn about their work first-hand. We have met groups working on issues outside our own field, developing different methods, and those who are just starting out. These encounters have enabled us to share knowledge and view our own work from an outside perspective.

One of the most significant realisations for us during this process was that civil society is much larger and broader than we had previously realised. Because Prison Agenda works in a very specific field, we realised that we were sometimes limited to our immediate circle. However, Digital Sparks showed us that this field is much broader and that there are far more areas where different struggles can intersect.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

AK: Digital Spark was the first support we received. Although we had previously been involved in various projects as part of a team, this was the first time we had been part of a project where the full responsibility rested directly with us. For this reason, it was also a new learning experience for us.

This was actually the part that challenged us the most. We learnt that a project is not limited to simply producing content and activities; it also requires managing its budget, administrative processes, reporting and responsibilities.

One of the most tangible things we learnt during this process was financial reporting. While our previous experience in this area was limited, carrying out the reporting processes required by the project provided us with valuable practical experience.

Consequently, Digital Sparks was not merely a project through which we developed Prison Agenda’s publishing capacity; it was also a significant experience in a small team transforming into a structure capable of standing on its own two feet, managing its responsibilities, and planning for the future.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

AK: Although we’re a very new organisation, we’re just as eager and enthusiastic. We have many options before us that could take us in different directions, as well as ideas that we’re keen to develop.

For example, we’re currently refining a public prison database project, and we’re also preparing to run a training course on prison journalism in the new year. We have a wide variety of datasets at our disposal that we want to make accessible to a wider audience. In the long term, we also plan to increase the number of areas we cover and deepen the content we produce in these fields.

We believe that we have not yet reached our natural limits. The digital capacity we have developed through Digital Sparks has opened up significant scope for us to expand these limits. In the near future, we intend to use the knowledge and experience we have gained to prioritise our readers, understand their requirements, and integrate their feedback into our editorial strategy.

Our aim is to transform the Prison Agenda into a structure that produces more content and enables more people to access information on prisons, bringing together different stakeholders in the process.
Written by Daria Dergacheva

6d0c83d2b64fda06: So now “gomen” employees can’t use Waze, the popular navigation app. This is a truly funny-but-not-funny situation. Somebody must have invoked some scary natural security scenarios about the dangers this US-owned, Israeli-founded company poses to our nation.

Here’s why this isn’t trivial. A company I once worked in experienced a massive computer hack. Experts from overseas were brought in to investigate. Panic reigned at the top. What I remember most from the briefings by the experts was the experts saying that everyone in the industry has either been hacked, or has been hacked and didn’t know about it.
I felt rather naked knowing somebody somewhere has a lot of detailed info about me, even if the only juicy details were about at which street corners were the best char kuey teow stalls.

It turns out one of the easiest ways to hack a human target and steal information more critical than just the locations of char kuey teow stalls is to hack their co-workers, assistants, family, friends, or football buddies and not necessarily the targets themselves.

That’s not as exciting as what happens in a James Bond movie, but rather the more plodding and low-key style of a John le Carre novel. One way or another, though, with enough cunning and guile and resources, people can find out a lot of things that others would prefer left hidden.
Why they snoop

Digital surveillance has become a massive business as well as a national security tool – checking what, when, and where we went or bought or spoke, as well as where we browsed on the internet and what social media content we generated or consumed. Artificial Intelligence has made it all easier.

The purpose of all this snooping is often just to sell you stuff, but increasingly it’s also becoming a way to control people and societies and even conduct warfare - as in the case of Elon Musk personally throttling his Starlink and Starshield services to Ukraine, thus harming Ukraine’s war efforts. That was one of the reasons many European nations are building digital alternatives to what Musk and the US offer, a trend that’s only gaining speed.

They're not just looking for alternatives for the latest digital stuff, either. Many nations have begun cutting off links they have relied on for decades with nations they no longer deem reliable for software, data centres and cloud services, computer chips, critical scientific research etc.

The big powers, especially the US and China, have been manipulating each other and others for years. China, which is fast catching up with the West in digital capabilities, looks safer today by comparison, but certainly they’re playing this same game too.
The Malaysian way

After banning Waze, Malaysia took the obvious next step by recommending the use of a home-grown alternative called TuJu, an app apparently running off the same backbone as Waze, but hosting all the captured data in some secure local data centres.

I haven’t downloaded TuJu, or used it in any shape or form. I know the locations of the best char kuey teow stalls by heart and can get there come rain or shine or traffic jams or anything else, up to a haze API level of 200. I'm fine, thank you.

Of course, we’re going about this the typical time-honoured Malaysia-Boleh way. First the government declares a critical national objective – industrialisation, national security, safety, pandemic response, etc.—and then, lo and behold, there appears a ready-made Malaysian solution!

We’ve seen this all before. The secrecy behind such decisions is often at a high level. Don’t forget even a toll highway concession agreement between the government and private parties is considered a sensitive national secret. Malaysia Boleh often actually means Malaysia Tak Boleh for the rest of us.

What little I know about TuJu doesn’t give me much confidence. The names associated with it seems to be the usual cast of characters of door openers to lucrative government contracts and not quite young genius alumni of the world’s top research universities or tech corporations or research institutions.
The other way

When it comes to high-tech, especially digital ones, I’m sceptical of people of my age and generation. We’re often the generation that calls AI “A-One”, as a famous episode involving a US cabinet member – handling education of all things! – hilariously reveals.

I wouldn’t even trust myself, even if I’m actually AI personified! The only good thing I can design and develop would be maps on napkins about the aforementioned char kuey teow locations which are, if I’m honest, not that great, after all.

But I’ve thought about making my own digital contributions during these critical times because it seems any old fogey can do it. I plan to release TuDia, an app that points out where you need to go; TangTu and TangNi to tell you when you’ve arrived here or there, and TuPun and TuLah to argue or commiserate with you when you’re lost.

And why not? The needs are real and urgent. All I’m asking for is complete access to all Malaysians’ personal data with a promise not to sell it to Elon Musk or Israel under a 50-year exclusive agreement that’ll be classified as a national secret forever.
Ah, silly dreams. I think all that’ll happen to me is, as Penangites like to say, that I’ll Pi Mai Pi Mai Tang Tu Jugak.
Which may work out as the name of another app that describes life in Malaysia Bolehland.
