Kemudian saya rasa terpanggil juga untuk mengingatkan orang muda kita supaya jangan galak sangat pasal freedom of speech and expression sampai tak kenal saudara, keluarga dan ibu bapa.

Tergempar kita membaca pasal satu kumpulan yang dikatakan orang Malaysia di Australia telah mempamerkan kepada awam bendera Malaysia yang terbalik dan ada kata tercarik-carik. Kumpulan ini dipercayai rakyat Malaysia dari Sabah dan Sarawak yang menggelarkan diri mereka Sabah dan Sarawak Keluar Malaysia (SSKM). Perbuatan ini saya anggap ‘agak berat’ dan perlu suatu komentar terhadapnya dengan cara baik dan beradab daripada bidasan dan cemuhan media sosial yang tidak terkawal.

Pertama sekali saya ingin mengucapkan terima kasih kepada menteri di Jabatan Perdana Menteri dari Sabah, Mustapha Sakmud. Beliau memberi teguran dan nasihat yang beradab dan bernas maka saya harap oang di Australia itu dengar baik-baik. Jangan terlajak kata nanti masa depan binasa. Sekarang mungkin gagah di Australia tetapi sepandai tupai melompat silap hari bulan kena balik negara sendiri semula. Siapa tahu nasib kita kecuali tuhan. Jadi, kalau kita dah ada rumah dan keluarga di sesuatu corner of the world, jangan cepat-cepat perlekeh, nanti kita juga yang terpaksa mencarinya di akhir hayat.

Isu bendera yang lalu bagi saya cukup jelas semuanya tidak disengajakan. Dari Editor Sin Chew kepada Kementerian Pendidikan, kesilapan Umno dan PAS Terengganu dan juga ‘Apek Tua’ di Pulau Pinang semuanya not on purpose. Ada yang tersilap dan ada yang cuai terlepas pandang sebab tidak pergi semak kerja suruhan kita sendiri. Saya telah mencadangkan supaya kita semua maaf-maafkan dan let it go tetapi jangan ulang lagi. Walaupun ada juga orang Umno yang suka mendabik dada sebagai paling patriotik mencemuh, menghina dan mengugut pihak yang tersilap pasang bendera, saya selalu menasihatkan individu tersebut supaya bertenang dan jangan cuba cari modal politik seperti ini.

Namun demikian, orang itu mendapat banyak political mileage dengan sandiwaranya. Saya tidak nampak pula beliau bising pasal bendera terbalik yang disengajakan orang Sabah dan Sarawak di Australia. Mungkin sebab Sabah dan Sarawak bakal sebagai king makers dalam PRU16. Kalau Onn Hafiz Ghazi gunakan istilah selective prosecution kini kita lihat ada parti yang buat selective criticism dalam isu bendera terbalik dengan sengaja.

Kembali kita kepada orang Sabah dan Sarawak di Australia ini, bagaimana kita nak nasihatkan mereka selain daripada apa yang dikatakan menteri di Jabatan Perdana Menteri itu? Biar saya guna analogi keluarga saya sebagai nasihat dan renungan untuk hidup berkeluarga. Sabah, Sarawak dan Semenanjung adalah sebuah keluarga dari aspek politik kenegaraan. Sabah dan Sarawak telah bersama Semenanjung Tanah Melayu selama 63 tahun. Umur saya sekarang 64 tahun. Saya mempunyai seorang isteri, lima orang anak, tiga orang menantu dan empat orang cucu. Ada tiga perkara penting dalam kita hidup berkeluarga.

Pertama, jangan sekali-kali guna perkataan cerai, nyah atau get out of the family. Kalau sebolehnya jangan langsung terkeluar kata-kata itu sehingga kita menghembus nafas terakhir di dunia ini. Walau apa perit sekali pun we do not say those words. Kata pepatah Melayu air yang dicincang tidak akan putus. Wise Malays. Melayu lama memang cerdik, tetapi Melayu baharu nampak terlalu gopoh-gapah. Tuhan telah menyatukan saya dan isteri. Selepas itu tuhan kurniakan kami tiga anak perempuan dan dua anak lelaki. Akhir sekali tuhan kurniakan kami semua empat orang cucu daripada perkahwinan anak-anak perempuan kami. Anak lelaki dua orang masih eligible kalau ada yang nak apply. Memang semua perkahwinan antara dua orang manusia berbeza akan ada isu, krisis dan macam-macam cabaran. Looking back semua cabaran itu 99% adalah dari diri kita sendiri dan bukan pun pasal orang lain buat. Sungguh. Blaming others for out own shortcoming is the easiest thing in the world. Jadi, kena refleksi dalaman dulu sebelum mengata salah orang ini dan orang itu. Apabila saya sakit jantung, sakit darah perut dan melalui severe panic disorder, isteri saya was by my side every time. Ada ketika yang kita tak berduit hingga kena pinjam abang sendiri atau minta anak buat loan. Itu semua lumrah hidup. We need family. Siapa lagi yang nak tolong.

Kedua, saya membina rumah di Kajang sebagai a refuge untuk semua anak saya. Saya dah siapkan konsep lima ‘studio apartmen’ yang lengkap dengan tandas, dapur, living room dan tempat tidur selesa serta aircond setiap bilik. Saya kata kalau kamu bergaduh dengan suami atau isteri you can come back and cool off di Kajang. Saya tahu berdasarkan pengalaman saya dan isteri, you cannot avoid conflicts jadi kita kena manage ia dengan menyediakan alternative refuge dan juga tempat untuk mereka mengadu. Saya dan isteri selalu mendengar keluhan anak-anak perempuan tentang suami mereka dan selalu kami mengajukan kesabaran dan pengalaman kami sendiri. Jangan cepat kita bercerai-berai atau mengadu domba sama ada dalam keluarga manusia atau keluarga negara. We can always manage whatever conflict kalau kita tidak burn the bridge dengan sesiapa.

Ketiga adalah tempat kami sediakan untuk cucu. Cucu adalah kurniaan tuhan yang amat penting bagi kehidupan kami semua. Saya sebagai ‘atuk’ dan isteri sebagai ‘nenek’ menjadikan rumah di Kajang sebagai resort bila hujung minggu dan di hari-hari cuti sekolah panjang di mana papa dan mama dua-dua bekerja di pejabat masing-masing. Saya tidak suka cucu saya ditinggalkan bertiga tanpa penyeliaan orang dewasa. Ada juga keadaan di mana bila krisis keluarga berlaku, mereka boleh menetap secara indefinitely di Kajang sehingga krisis berlalu. Seperti juga sesebuah negara, kalau kita mempunyai krisis di tempat tinggal di luar negara maka ke Malaysia jugalah kita pulang. Maka itu jangan senang-senang menolak negara atau menyisihkannya hanya kerana satu dua isu yang boleh diselesaikan dengan masa dan hikmah.

Sebagai mesej politik, kita semua ada negara dan ada keluarga dalam negara itu. Kita semua rakyat Malaysia di Semenanjung, Sabah dan Sarawak. Ia suatu gagasan penting bagi kita semua. Memang akan sentiasa ada konflik atau isu kaum, agama, politik dan sebeban lagi tetapi jika kita teguh dalam satu famili dan ada tempat untuk berlabuh maka kedua-duanya adalah important asset bagi kita. Menterbalikkan dan mencarik bendera negara dengan sengaja adalah suatu perkara yang cukup berat bagi saya. Ia sama dengan beberapa mahasiswa yang bakar gambar perdana menteri yang saban hari bekerja kuat. Itu mungkin budaya Barat atau Australia. Mungkin kumpulan tersebut hendak bakar, carik atau menterbalikkan bendera Australia pula di bawah freedom of expression di lain hari pula? Apa makna loyalty to family dan nation kalau begitu. Apa makna perbincangan dan bertolak ansur dalam hubungan antara manusia kalau jambatan dibakar terlebih dulu? Jambatan yang runtuh tidak boleh memanfaatkan sesiapa yang mungkin ada solusi baharu di masa hadapan.
Renung-renungkanlah pepatah Melayu agar tidak membakar kelambu sebab seekor nyamuk yang dimarahkan.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.

b853919723a582d4: Microsoft is beginning the rollout of a Windows 11 preview update that finally addresses a persistent power user complaint with the operating system: the right-click menu that obliterated years of muscle memory on command locations and hid others behind an additional click. The timing is notable, as the announcement comes alongside Microsoft's quarterly financial report, which showed a continued decline in the business of selling Windows licenses for new PCs.

The preview update, KB5127936, is cumulative for Windows 11 versions 26H2 and 25H2. The update will be a gradual rollout before eventually moving on to a normal rollout for all Windows 11 devices once it reaches general availability. The highlight of the new update should calm annoyed users who have spent years with custom scripts and services in an attempt to shape Windows the way they would prefer it. Users will get a "customize menu" button that controls what commands appear when they right-click their mouse. Users can toggle built-in commands such as Send To or Create Shortcut on or off, rearrange what appears on the main menu, and control which third-party extensions show up in either the main or submenus. The gripe with the right-click menu had been that Microsoft hid familiar command locations behind a top row of icons while moving other familiar commands under the "Show more options" submenu. Now, Windows users can customize the whole thing around their habits.

The original Windows 11 right-click menu is a mess. Credit: Microsoft The new preview also highlights a new Windows feature called Cloud Rebuild, a recovery option that can reinstall Windows 11 directly from the cloud, even when an existing Windows 11 fails to boot. Cloud Rebuild will pull the Windows 11 image and needed system drivers directly from Windows Update. Users will not need a custom recovery image or external media to reinstall Windows. There is an important distinction to note, however. Microsoft classifies Cloud Rebuild as a recovery option, but it behaves more like a fresh Windows install than a repair, as existing applications and files will not be included. Those worried about data security can sanitize entire system drives prior to reinstalling. For a full list of improvements coming to Windows 11, including changes to Xbox mode and settings, you can view the official Microsoft release announcement.

b36a902471af3eef: If you want to ask AI a question and watch the conversation go up in virtual flames when you're done, there's a new Mac app for that.

Howler is an open-source app from a Chinese developer going by Aries Zhou, and it takes incognito mode AI questions to a new level by making them graphically interesting and easy to access right from the desktop of a macOS device.

Anyone familiar with the Harry Potter series is likely to know where the name comes from - Howlers are letters that scream in recipients’ faces and then burst into flames, destroying themselves, which is the exact same thing the prompts ostensibly do once a user taps the Escape key.

The Howler app displays a parchment-esque letter on the screen whenever the user presses Option+H, complete with a little wax seal that shows a letter representing their chosen model. Responses to queries are written out “at a hand’s pace,” per Howler’s website, first in glowing gold that settles to a sepia-toned print.

“Besides needing translation at any time, I often want to look up a concept or learn about an event on the fly, without wanting to switch to a browser or open a separate session in Chat,” Zhou wrote in a comment on his Hacker News post showing off the applet. “So I made Howler, dedicated to Harry Potter fans, always there when you call, burning after reading.”

The biggest catch to using Howler is that setting it up involves either using an AI service that can run commands, like Claude Code or another coding agent, or running the configuration commands manually. The recommended method involves pasting a setup prompt into the agent's input field. Once set up, Howler can connect to supported AI models using an API key, or to compatible models running locally. Howler’s website states that the API key never enters the chat and is stored in the macOS Keychain for safety.

In addition to the API key for the chosen model staying local and not being printed, Howler is described on its website as only storing messages in memory with no history, sending requests straight to the chosen AI service and never through a relay, keeping no logs, and only connecting to an outside service to check for updates - and even that feature can be disabled.

It’s a handy tool for those who want to ask AI questions without leaving a chat history on their Mac – like trying to remember the name of that damn function you’re supposed to have down by now, or whether Memorial Day or Labor Day is the one in the fall. Just don’t assume the AI provider won’t retain a record of the exchange.

“Unlike regular conversations, it doesn't take up your conversation list, and you don't have to think about cleaning it up or archiving it afterward,” Zhou explained. “It's only for handling your sudden flashes of inspiration or a moment of confusion.”

And it does it with panache - sure, it’s just an interface for an AI model one could find elsewhere, but it’s easily conjured, dismissed with a snap, and is open source, to boot. You can find Howler on GitHub, or download it from its website, both linked above. ®
1905c7a2513a10b8: Vera Platforms, a startup founded by researchers at the University of Michigan, believes there's a way to make agents trustworthy enough to handle DevOps.

DevOps, which focuses on how software gets deployed and operated, is a particularly unforgiving affair. While AI agents have some leeway to make mistakes and correct errors as they generate code and work through a prompt, it's an entirely different matter when they make changes to real infrastructure running production workloads.

"Live infrastructure is unforgiving," Ang Chen, CEO of Vera Platforms and an associate professor at the University of Michigan, told The Register. "An incorrect change can take down a service, open a security hole or erase data. Mistakes are often irreversible, and there’s no safe way to experiment: running code against production infra just to see what happens isn’t an option."
For the past few years, Chen and his colleagues have been working on a way to benchmark agentic DevOps and a gym – a simulation environment – to help AI models get better at DevOps tasks.

"From the research that we did, we've figured out various weaknesses of leading models," said Chen. "For instance, [Anthropic's] Claude, although it's very strong with Python generation, it just has some fundamental limitations that it can't get right when it comes to DevOps."
An example of that, Chen said, is that when they asked Claude or OpenAI's Codex to decommission resources in the AWS cloud, the models didn't look beyond the default region.

"The default region is us-east-1," he explained. "There are various regions in AWS, but Claude doesn't have this awareness that the cloud resources could exist in multiple regions, so it only decommissioned part of the resource."
The fundamental reason, he said, is that these models have seen a lot of public code, but a lot less operational tracing.

Vera Platforms aims to remedy the situation with three products: vera-gym, a playground environment that emulates production infrastructure; vera-bench, a test for measuring where AI agents fumble DevOps tasks; and vera-agents, AI agents that have been trained in vera-gym and are ready to be deployed for DevOps tasks.

The CloudOpsBench test being released builds upon work done in 2024 that was presented at NeurIPS. According to Chen, Claude and Codex only score about a 50 percent pass rate. "It's a very, very hard set of tasks," he said.

The test covers tasks like deleting decommissioned S3 buckets, repairing a compliance event pipeline, and restoring DynamoDB write autoscaling. "The tasks are authored by senior infra operators with many years of experience, with rigorous peer review," said Chen.
This benchmark has the advantage of not requiring an actual cloud deployment.

"We have a high fidelity simulator that mimics Amazon behavior," said Chen. "So the rollout, the performance of the agent on the real cloud and the performance of the agent in our emulator is exactly the same. So for every API, we have this comparison and the agent sees the same thing."
Vera-agents, Chen said, should be available in Q1 2027.
In their academic work, the researchers describe cloud infrastructure as "critical but tedious work." With a bit more training, maybe AI agents can take over and keep things boring. ®
eae8fbff66d64621: Popular for other uses, Rust isn't typically deployed for web development. That could change, however.

With AI here to do the heavy lifting, coders may want to consider the programming language, given its runtime performance and safety guarantees, suggested Carl Lerche, an Amazon Web Services principal engineer, speaking at ScyllaDB’s 2026 P99 virtual conference last week.
Lerche was there to demonstrate his latest project, Topcoat, a framework for running web applications written in Rust.
Lerche is perhaps best known for creating Tokio, which is the most popular asynchronous Rust runtime in that ecosystem.
“Three years ago, had [I] gone out and said that Rust could be the best language for building web apps, you probably would have called me crazy,” he told the virtual audience.
Web developers gravitate towards the languages they find most familiar. These days, that means JavaScript, or possibly Ruby.

A number of web frameworks already use Rust. Both Leptos and Dioxus compile Rust into WebAssembly, which most browsers run. This approach is great for heavy computational jobs, though the upfront loading time can be a real drag.
Topcoat compiles your Rust code into more web-friendly JavaScript. For Lerche, JavaScript remains the best way to interact with the browser's Document Object Model (DOM).

“Generally, the approach taken by any Rust framework can be traced back to another ecosystem, usually a very popular one. You can't really point to a single existing framework as [Topcoat’s] main source of inspiration,” noted frontend developer Ken Kohlman, in a summary video on his “Code to the Moon” YouTube channel.
Walk on the server side

Lerche admitted that Topcoat isn’t for building complex applications, on the scale of, say, Figma, but it can easily be used for the run-of-the-mill, browser-based, database-driven applications, which is to say 90 percent of the web today.

Unlike most present-day JavaScript frameworks, Topcoat eschews the current definition of being reactive, where the program logic is dumped onto the browser when the session begins. Instead, most of the logic executes on the server, with only the results delivered to the browser (Developers can still write client-side logic using a subset of Rust, which Topcoat automatically compiles into JavaScript for the browser).

It’s an old idea recast with better tech. Server-side rendering predates reactive programming (see Apache’s server-side includes). With server-side rendering, Lerche admitted, “It might sound like we're going back to the old days of full page refreshes for every click [but] you can actually get almost all of what you think of as reactive with server-side rendering.”

But server-side programming has been making a comeback lately, especially for those devs disgruntled with React and other frameworks. HTMX, Datastar, and Phoenix LiveView all render web pages on the server, sending them back to the browser nearly completed.

Topcoat is just tweaking their ideas to fit well with Rust, Lerche said. When a user smashes a button on a web page, the whole page isn’t refreshed. Just the HTML snippet for that component is returned and refreshed by the server.
JavaScript in the front, Rust in the back

Topcoat saves load times by rendering all the components at once, rather than one by one. Also, data loading does not block the loading of the page. The server can send back a web page with placeholders into which the data will stream.

One big dollop of secret sauce that Topcoat has is that it provides a way for the component, which is already on the server, to speak directly to the database, thanks to an earlier project from Lerche called Toasty, a Rust-based asynchronous database object-relational mapper (which he spoke about at P99 2024).
“You can do your rendering right with the data immediately, so you don't have to figure out how to serialize it, send it to the client, deserialize it,” he said.

By pushing data loading deep down into the page render, the server can send the head of the HTML template to the client immediately, allowing the browser to start preloading assets (like CSS or images) while the server renders the rest of the page.

“The simplicity is incredible, and it is something that we have been sorely missing in this space. I feel like someone who doesn't really know Rust could get off the ground pretty quickly with this thing,” Kohlman said. He did agree with Lerche that Topcoat is best for smaller web projects, given that Topcoat only uses a subset of the Rust syntax.
“There's something to be said for having the full Rust syntax at your disposal,” he said. ®

1094534d9ef62277: Suspected Chinese attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including Palo Alto Networks firewalls linked to US government-affiliated organizations, according to Dream researchers.
The snoops began exploiting these servers on October 23, targeting organizations across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. The attackers also honed in on US government-affiliated firewalls.

“Within hours of compromising a US government-affiliated firewall, they had tunneled into the internal network, compromised a third server using the same PHP2Shell exploit, and launched a full Active Directory attack campaign - all through a chain that started with a single unauthenticated HTTPS request to a management interface that should never have been exposed to the internet,” the Israeli AI cybersecurity startup said in a report.
Plus, the attackers “likely still” have persistent, remote access to compromised organizations’ networks, Dream noted.

The attackers rooted the first US government-affiliated firewall on October 23, but the device crashed shortly afterward, possibly due to around 900 MB of exploit traffic. According to Dream, it remained unresponsive despite 240 automated checks over two hours. They successfully exploited the second firewall a day later, on October 24.

The compromised firewalls ran vulnerable versions of Palo Alto Networks' PAN-OS. Dream said it had been working with the vendor to investigate the compromises, and Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 researchers independently verified the attacker's tooling and confirmed Dream's reported results.

To break into the firewalls, the attackers built a custom exploit chain that includes PHP2Shell and a Fragnesia kernel flaw, and ran about 40 custom post-exploitation scripts once they were inside the targeted organizations.
Total attack chain in under 15 minutes

PHP2Shell, comprised of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, came to light early last week, along with fears that attackers would abuse the bugs to take down most of the internet. Despite “hundreds” of PHP2Shell proof-of-concept repositories on GitHub, the first reports of successful attacks didn’t start until Saturday.
Both bugs have CVSS scores of 9.2 and can be exploited without authentication to run code on vulnerable PHP servers.

The PHP2Shell exploit recovered by Dream was not a copy of any known public exploit. It “appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for the targeted firewall platform,” the researchers wrote.

The attackers combined PHP2Shell with Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300), a high-severity local privilege-escalation vulnerability affecting the Linux kernel's XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added this Linux kernel bug to its catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities on Wednesday.
Both CISA and the FBI declined to comment.

The miscreants developed a four-stage PHP2Shell exploit that allowed them to execute commands without authentication on vulnerable Palo Alto Networks firewalls. They then used Fragnesia to escalate their privileges and gain root access. The attackers targeted PAN-OS 12.1 and 12.2, which run PHP 8.0.30 with a high memory limit that enabled the exploit's memory-corruption stages.
“The total chain - from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell - completes in under 15 minutes,” the Dream team wrote.
4 steps to root
Here’s how it works: First, they flood the servers with crafted multipart POST requests to corrupt PHP’s memory, and force a predictable memory layout.

Then a second request forges the stale session ID length from the memory corruption part of the attack, forcing an out-of-bounds read and exposing the base address of libphp.so in the running process.

The attackers then exhaust PHP's memory again to force mod_data=NULL, creating a stale reference they can forge in the final stage to execute commands as the nobody user. They use Fragnesia to escalate to root and plant a web shell in a publicly accessible directory on the firewall.

After breaking in via the compromised firewalls, the attackers snooped around in Active Directory, stealing credentials and other sensitive information. With root access, the attackers also had the master key to decrypt the LDAP service account password, which they hardcoded into every subsequent script.

They also enumerated every user and group in the domain via LDAP queries, and sprayed passwords against every user account. Attackers also tried to create backdoor AD accounts and attempted SAML signing key extraction - but Dream doesn’t know if these were successful.

“The attack results - whether the password spray found valid credentials, whether the backdoor accounts were created, whether SAML keys were extracted - stayed on the management server's local filesystem and were not among the artifacts we recovered,” the researchers noted.
AI tools in the attack
The investigation also uncovered evidence that the attackers used AI tools, but noted that this was not a fully autonomous attack.

The researchers found Anthropic's Claude Code installed, an AI-powered offensive security platform called aiscan configured with Chinese models DeepSeek and Kimi, and API keys for the FOFA reconnaissance service. FOFA is a Chinese internet asset search engine similar to Shodan. The attackers used it to identify about 19,000 internet-facing Palo Alto Networks firewalls worldwide.

“The persistent tunnel into the US government organization is likely still running,” Dream warned. “And the attacker still has 19,000 fingerprinted targets they can revisit as they develop profiles for additional PAN-OS versions.”®
cb84fc15ae03dac8: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Archive of Our Own (AO3), a massive repository for fanfiction and creative writing, might be down for as long as a month after going down for "maintenance" on Thursday.

The Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the non-profit organization that runs AO3, posted on its status page early Thursday morning that the site was down for maintenance. A few hours later, it updated the status to say that it was expected to take at least 12 hours. By Thursday afternoon, it said the site restoration will take around two weeks, but could take up to a month.

“We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner. If that does happen, there may be times when the site has to be brought down temporarily until this is fully resolved. Please stay tuned for further info,” OTW wrote.

A spokesperson for OTW told 404 Media Thursday night that there are no more updates at this time beyond what's on the status page. They did, however, say that they don't expect there to be data loss. Early Friday morning, OTW added an update to the status page: "First, no AO3 data has been deleted. All your works, bookmarks, kudos, etc., are safe," it says. "Second, while we currently don't believe that the user database was stolen, we are also unable to rule it out. The AO3 database contains account information that may include your username, email address, IP address, and a hashed version of your password." They say they use hashing techniques to protect password data, but recommend users change their passwords on any other sites where they use the same password as on AO3, as a precaution.
Fanfiction Community Rocked By Etsy Sellers Turning Their Work Into Bound Books
Several popular shops, which clearly violated Etsy's terms of use and IP laws, were deleted after 404 Media reached out for comment.

It’s difficult to overstate the importance of AO3 to fan culture, fanfiction writers and readers, and its influence on internet culture in general. As of September, the open-source fanfic repository hosted over 18.4 million works spanning over 82,900 fandoms. This status update means AO3 is expected to be down during much of hoa hoa hoa season, most of ACOTAR new book release week, and on the cusp of the month formerly known as NaNoWriMo. 028d5ff4b1d516d0: An Exile Hub fellow shares their personal experiences and reflections
Originally published on Global Voices
Image from Exile Hub. Used with permission.

Exile Hub is one of Global Voices’ partners in Southeast Asia, emerging in response to the 2021 coup in Myanmar, and focusing on empowering journalists and human rights defenders. This article by a fellow of Exile Hub was published on August 15, 2026, and an edited version is republished under a content partnership agreement.
“Can I keep doing this work?”
I have asked myself that question more times than I can count.
When I first entered journalism as a young person, I was full of energy, conviction, and dreams. I believed journalism was a way to uncover the truth and to make sure people’s voices were heard.
Four years later, I began to realize that somewhere along the way, I was slowly losing parts of myself.
When I was 19, I never imagined that the career I chose would become both my livelihood and one of the reasons the road home would feel so far away.

In the early days of the 2021 revolution in Myanmar, I took part in protests. As the security situation deteriorated, I had to leave home. Eventually, I found myself in Mae Sot, a small town along the Thai–Myanmar border. There, I was fortunate to have the opportunity to study journalism for free.

I had loved writing since I was young. I started with short news pieces, then moved on to feature stories and video reporting, and eventually became a news presenter. I was proud to call myself a journalist. I was so proud, in fact, that I never used a pen name. I reported under my real name.
One of the first lessons I learned in journalism was simple: don’t put your own emotions into the story. But over time, I learned something else. Journalists are human too.
When other people’s pain becomes part of you
Sometimes I would call a source for an interview and listen as they described what had happened to them. Their pain would stay with me.
My responsibility was to listen carefully and then find the words to make their experiences visible to others. But sometimes, carrying their stories felt like carrying the pain twice.
After some interviews, I would put down my phone, open my laptop, and stare at the screen. No words would come.
I remember once speaking with a source just before mealtime. My stomach told me I was hungry, but after hearing their story, there was a heaviness in my chest, and I could not eat.
As these experiences accumulated, something began to change.
Eventually, I stopped crying.
I could finish an interview and immediately continue with the next task. But it wasn’t because the stories no longer affected me.
I had simply become numb.

And that numbness slowly changed me without my realizing it. I became tired more easily. I became irritable. I overthought things. My mood sank, and even my relationships with other people began to suffer.
Yet there was something strange about all of this.
On the days when I picked up my camera bag, carried my tripod, and went out into the field, some of that exhaustion disappeared.
Walking along windy roads, meeting people and listening to their lives, I would suddenly remember:
I still love this work.
And that’s why I couldn’t quite let it go.
When passion is not enough
COVID-19 and Myanmar’s political upheaval interrupted my education. Journalism became my livelihood, and surviving from one day to the next left little space to think seriously about my own future.
Eventually, one question began following me almost every day: What will become of me?
I became afraid that nothing would.
At the same time, media organizations were losing funding. Programs were closing. Journalists were losing their jobs.
When one of the programs I worked for ended, I became unemployed for around seven months.
It was one of the hardest periods of my life.
I told myself that if I could not find another job in journalism within a little over a year, I would change careers completely.
Fortunately, I eventually found my way back, working again as both a reporter and news presenter.
I continue because I genuinely love this work.
But love alone does not make the realities of life in exile easier. The income is not always enough to build a stable life.
And perhaps the hardest part is this:
On the days when I desperately want to go home, I cannot.
Even if I cannot return myself, I wish I could bring my family to visit me. But financially, that is not always possible either.
I want to see the people I love. I want to eat my mother’s cooking. I miss the smell of home.
Most of all, I miss my mother.
She raised me by herself, and as she grows older, I want to be able to care for her in return. One of my deepest fears is that something will happen to her before I have the chance to see her again.
That distance makes an already exhausting life in exile even heavier.
When the mind begins to affect the body
At one point, I tried counseling.
But each session cost more than THB 800 (USD 24). I could not afford to continue for the long term, so eventually I stopped.
Over time, the emotional pressure began affecting my physical health as well. I was hospitalized twice, both times in serious conditions.
Being hospitalized in another country is difficult enough, even when you can afford it. When money is already tight, the anxiety becomes even greater.
After those experiences, I stopped trying to transform my life all at once.
Instead, I started small.
I learned to be grateful that I was alive today.
If the weather was beautiful, I appreciated it.
If I finished one task, I allowed myself to feel proud of it.
I would be lying if I said I no longer worry about where I will be in five or ten years — I still do.
But I am trying to spend less time living inside an uncertain future and more time doing the best I can with the day in front of me.
I still sometimes struggle in crowded places. There are moments when breathing becomes difficult, or my emotions change quickly.
And yet, strangely, when I am out reporting, I can become completely absorbed in the work and somehow manage.
The difference now is that I have learned to accept these parts of myself rather than constantly fight against them.
I have also learned something else:
We cannot carry everything alone.
Having someone who listens, someone who cares, someone who simply asks, “Are you okay?” can sometimes feel like medicine for the mind.
Still here, still trying
When I first entered journalism, I was simply a young person who wanted to write the truth.
Four years later, after witnessing so many painful stories, I have learned that telling other people’s stories also requires learning how to care for myself.
I still do not know what my future will look like.
I do not know when the road will take me home.
But there is one thing I have come to believe:
“As long as we are still alive, there is still something we can try.”
So I keep going with that belief.
I try to spend more time with the people who have cared for me and held me up when things became difficult. I try to appreciate them while they are still beside me.
And through all the days when I long to go home, I am still trying to survive in both of the identities I carry: as a journalist and as a human being.
Written by Exile Hub

a90320b85280d9d8: It's a few years behind schedule, but development has resumed on the desktop edition of Canonical's existing immutable IoT distro, Ubuntu Core.

Engineering veep Jon Seager announced that Canonical is Accelerating Ubuntu Core Desktop on the company's Discourse forum. Even before his announcement, there was some fresh activity on the project's GitHub.

The post gives some explanation of why the effort is running so late, envisions three potential use cases, and talks a little about the work that is already going on to enable it to finally happen. There's no solid timeline given, but Seager says that "over the coming release cycle" the team will be working out what needs to happen, which means that "over the coming weeks, we'll have the infrastructure ready for… daily image builds for Ubuntu Core Desktop."

"Accelerating" sounds good, but with the best will in the world, it could hardly slow it down. In mid-2023 it looked like Desktop Ubuntu Core would arrive in 2024, and at that year's Ubuntu Summit in Rīga, Latvia, it revealed more details. At the 2024 Summit, there was a talk about a KDE version – but no release. At the 2025 Summit, the Reg FOSS desk interviewed Seager and "Where's Core Desktop?" was our first question.

The three roles his post discusses are the "browser-centric machine", a "developer workstation," and a "gaming machine." For this vulture, these goals imply two separate things. In general, this seems to indicate that it's wary of making something too specialized early on, then finding that it's not versatile enough for more challenging roles.

Secondly, we think that the company is thinking of three specific niches that rival immutable distros have occupied successfully for years. Right now, the "browser-centric" one is filled by ChromeOS and ChromeOS Flex. We use Flex – it's pretty good, even if its days are now numbered due to the new Android-based GooglebookOS.

Secondly, Fedora's Atomic editions have been around for years now – The Register first mentioned Fedora Kinoite well over five years ago. As well as Fedoras's own versions, there are also community-led distros based on the same tech, called Universal Blue. We've tried several, and while for now they offer nothing much this vulture wants, they undeniably work and they have happy users. Fedora's marketing aims at developers, and an immutable distro with containerized environments on top is harder to accidentally break with crashy work-in-progress code.

Thirdly, the games-machine niche is owned by Valve's SteamOS. Although it is native to the Steam Deck – and if you're among the lucky few, the Steam Machine and Steam Frame – you are also free to run this on your own AMD-based kit.

All three of these product families have been well-established for between five to ten years now. Canonical is lagging behind, and this is a subtle acknowledgement that it knows who the leaders are. We didn't doubt that he knows his stuff – a year ago, Seager’s blog post about The Immutable Linux Paradox went into the differences in depth.

The delay in delivering an immutable desktop is not for lack of immutable-distro technology: Canonical's had that for years. It announced Ubuntu Core 16 a decade ago, and when we tried Ubuntu Core, that was the fourth release.

Seager's post identifies some of the problems that have delayed its Core Desktop. One is that the 2023 preview required its own, specially modified version of the base core22 snap. Obviously, the company would prefer that it was based on the existing Core distro.

He also points to some essential underlying tech that is not obvious. He mentions that the Snap Store already has over 11,000 packages, but notes that many still use weak "classic" confinement – such as VS Code. This is a problem for Core, which requires strict confinement. He also notes some less-obvious things that need to work first, including smartphone-style permissions prompting, inter-snap dependencies, content snaps and snap components.

Some of the plans are ambitious, but in good ways. He discusses the need for modularity in the desktop snap packages, so that Core Desktop won’t be restricted to only GNOME. This means isolating the display manager (that is, the login screen) from the desktop, and the desktop from the browser. Here, he gives a nod to external consultancy enioka Haute Couture for its work on KDE snaps.

It's still much too easy to break any ordinary desktop Linux distro. In this vulture's extensive personal experience, the Btrfs filesystem is especially vulnerable. In four years of daily-driving a Btrfs-based distro in the 20-teens, we saw more crashes due to corrupted Btrfs volumes than in the previous two decades. However, all the vendors of Btrfs-based OSes are resolute in their denial about its real problems, which means they never get fixed. SteamOS and KDE Linux both use dual read-only Btrfs partitions, which update one another ChromeOS-style. This may be the only way to battle-harden this problematic filesystem. Canonical, on the other hand, offers integrated OpenZFS. We've been using ZFS since before the COVID pandemic, and it has yet to lose a single byte of data for us.

There are still blockers before Canonical can deliver a versatile, modular, desktop version of its existing immutable OS, but it's having another go. It's about time, and there is some new hope that we may start to see previews in the Ubuntu 27.04 timeframe. ®

8b3ed8665efbf0d7: Stenko Vlad/Shutterstock A few years ago, the singer Billie Eilish opened up on the Howard Stern Show about how she began watching porn around age 11. “I’m so angry that porn is so loved, and I’m so angry at myself for thinking that it was ok,” she said. Eilish became addicted to porn, and it led to problems. “The first few times I had sex, I was not saying no to things that were not good,” she said. She had nightmares because the content she was watching was so violent and abusive. Online porn is a multi-million dollar business, driven by algorithms designed to keep people clicking for more. These algorithms push more and more extreme content, often for free, to people who didn’t go searching for it. This can include strangulation, exploitation or incest porn, that’s often misogynistic and racist too. “If you take incest and strangulation, we can look at content studies from the 1980s, for example, when there was hardly any of that material,” Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University in the UK, tells The Conversation Weekly podcast. “Today both incest and strangulation becomes mainstream.” In the UK, the government will ban the possession and publication of incest and strangulation porn from early November. McGlynn, who worked with civil society groups to push the regulation of extreme content, says it’s a “huge step” that sends a message about the harms of “normalising sexual violence”. McGlynn, who has written a recent book about the rise of extreme porn, says large online porn platforms are pushing people towards more and more extreme content. Their business model is to keep you engaged. They want us on the platform for as long as possible, and the way to do that is to feed you more content, not necessarily what you were looking for, but also, the more extreme, the more polarising, the more shocking content … unfortunately, that seems to be what our kind of base instincts go for and what does actually engage us to keep us searching. McGlynn says an abundance of extreme and violent porn is shaping the sex lives of young people, and it can lead to an increased risk of problematic behaviour. There’s a study that followed 16,000 young people, showing that high porn use, particularly at a young age, is a big risk factor in problematic sexual behaviour of young teenage boys. And there’s studies in Australia and the US … showing that the more porn they watch, the more strangulation they see, and then the more they identify that they act out the strangulation. Nitin Nohria: Preparing for a Career in the Age of AI
Barry Ritholtz in conversation with Nitin Nohria, former dean of Harvard Business School and author of The CEO: The Role, the Reality, and the Responsibility. Bloomberg Radio.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: In the age of artificial intelligence, how should students prepare for this job market? Let’s bring in Harvard Professor Nitin Nohria. He’s former dean of the Harvard Business School. His new book is The CEO: The Role, the Reality, and the Responsibility. He’s also executive chairman at Thrive Capital, which is the venture firm run by Joshua Kushner. So let’s start with AI. If artificial intelligence is attacking that entry rung of the career ladder, how should recent college grads build the skills and judgment that used to come from those entry-level jobs?

NITIN NOHRIA: First, students should continue to use their time during their education to be even more determined to cultivate critical thinking — the capacity to interrogate themselves. When I teach cases now, one thing I’ve started to do is to ask students, “Tell me what AI said about this case.” Actually, not just tell me — read to me what your AI agent said to you about this case. Because I want them to know you can use these tools. In fact, you’ll be required to use these tools when you get to work.

NITIN NOHRIA: And then I ask them the second question: What did you agree with? What did you disagree with? What further questions did you ask to get your thinking to be improved? I think this form of critical reasoning — where we rely upon AI to inform ourselves, but then we interrogate it deeply, and we learn how to think alongside it — this is a capability that they will be required to have, and I think the best students will prepare themselves this way.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So your preference is, rather than just become a very inch-wide, mile-deep domain expert, really have the broad meta-skills — critical reading, critical thinking, and a more intelligent form of learning and working with AI. Is that the takeaway?

NITIN NOHRIA: I think so. My view increasingly is that you should think of AI very much like in the Marvel comics. Each person can develop their own superpower. You don’t need a Marvel suit; AI becomes the equivalent of your Marvel suit. But you have to tune it to yourself, right? It’s not like all Marvel heroes have the same superpowers. You will develop your own superpowers, and that’ll be your distinctive edge. How you use this extraordinary capacity to distinguish yourself, to make yourself special — that will be the new edge that people will have to find.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So, undergraduate: does the major a student takes really matter? We saw such a push towards STEM, but now it seems a lot of those technical skills are getting commoditized. How should a student be thinking about what they should be studying, how they develop judgment and communication skills? How important is the major?

NITIN NOHRIA: In the same metaphor that I used — you have to find what your unique Marvel superpower is — expertise could be one of them. It is not the case that expertise disappears. If you end up being the person who has dug deep into computer science, and you can therefore answer questions about the right way to program using AI, about the right way to create safety — all of the questions that are now being worked on by the leading researchers at the top labs — that’s not something that I, who doesn’t have that same level of intuition, experience, and expertise, will be able to do.

NITIN NOHRIA: For others, it may be writing. For others, it may be history. So I do think that a major will continue to be important. But then there will be people who take interdisciplinary majors — like Social Studies at Harvard — who say, “I’m not going to differentiate myself on expertise, because that will be for some people. I’m going to be the generalist.” And I think that being a generalist is going to be deeply important in this world too.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Yeah, no doubt. So let’s talk about that first job, which, when I was coming up, was described as the all-important first job. Is that still the case? Should people think about that first gig out of college as something that’s a little bit of an experiment, to figure out what they like and what they’re good at? Or should it be a commitment to the company, to the industry, to their bosses — just jump in with both feet? Or somewhere in between?

NITIN NOHRIA: In my experience, having taught for now almost 40 years — I teach mostly business school students, who are graduate students, but I’ve also had interaction with lots of undergraduate students — I find that students are of two types. There are people who, somewhere very early in their life, know exactly what their life’s mission is. I’ve always said to those people: get on with it. Find a place, commit, dig deep, because you already know what you want to do. Don’t waste time flitting around running experiments. The experiment of your life is already known. Now you have to find a way to deliver on it.

NITIN NOHRIA: And there are other people — and I will put myself in that category — who didn’t have a clue about what I wanted to do when I joined an undergraduate institution. Didn’t even have a clue when I went to graduate school, and had to discover through experimentation what it was that I was going to be good at. For those people, I say: don’t be afraid of experimentation. Don’t get anxious that you don’t know exactly what you want to do. But when you get the signal that this is what you want to do, listen hard. Your body, mind, and heart will tell you that this is what you were meant to do. And when that happens, lock in and pursue it with all your heart. But don’t get impatient if you don’t know very early on what it is that you want to do, and cut yourself some grace.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Really interesting advice. So, you’re executive chairman of a venture capital firm. I’ve played around in that space over the years, and one of the things I’m kind of fascinated by is how often startups — really very new companies — pivot from the initial idea to a variation, to a derivative of the original technology, and sometimes to something entirely different. How should students and new grads think about those career pivots? How should they think about, “Hey, is this just tough and I have to fight my way through? Or am I really more interested in this adjacent area of practice?”

NITIN NOHRIA: For entrepreneurs, there’s a level of persistence and a willingness to pivot as needed, because there’s such a determination to come up with the right solution for a problem that may initially have presented as A, but over time looks like it’s its adjacency. A colleague of mine, Amar Bhidé, did research at Harvard Business School on hundreds of entrepreneurs, and he found that in 80% of the cases, as you said, where they ended up was a distant cousin at best of what they started with — even when they were successful. And I think that’s not very different from people who pursue careers.

NITIN NOHRIA: Even if you’re not an entrepreneur, where you start may not be where you end up in your career. You may start as a consultant because that feels like the right way to gain some experience. You may start as a journalist, and you could end up in very different places. So I think people should remain permanently open to exploring adjacencies that they’re drawn to — and certainly to recognizing when what they’re doing is a dead end and it’s not going to actually yield anything. It’s the hardest thing for people to do sometimes, to recognize a dead end. But I also say to people: don’t be too quick to allow irritations or frictions to be seen as a dead end.

NITIN NOHRIA: So I say to people, if you’re unhappy, allow yourself to be unhappy for at least three to six months before you decide that this is a dead end. Because if you switch every time you experience unhappiness, you’re just never going to have the persistence to work through the things that you have to work through in almost any job or any career.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: That persistence reminds me of a quote I’ve heard about so many different areas, and I want to see how much it applies to a career: it should be treated as a marathon, not a sprint. True?
NITIN NOHRIA: One hundred percent. And yet, as you know, a marathon is not run at the same pace.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: Sure.

NITIN NOHRIA: If you see the great runners in a marathon, they try and set the pace early. So sometimes you want to actually set the pace early. In the middle of the race you might slow down, but you’re always trying to set a pace. At times you want to run with the group; at times you want to run alone. So yes, a marathon is a long race, but it’s not run at the same cadence throughout. I think that’s what a good career looks like as well.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Tell us about experiential learning. How should universities and students design higher education so that students really get the most out of their four years or so in college, and are best prepared for a career?

NITIN NOHRIA: I’m a huge proponent of experiential learning — but, full disclosure, I’m very biased in this regard. I think the case method that we taught by at Harvard Business School was an opportunity for students to confront experience in the classroom. In many ways, I used to think of it as the best flight simulation that you could have in business. We can’t possibly put you into a hundred business situations in the real world, but we can give you 90 minutes of simulation of different business problems. And in each case, you have to act as the protagonist. You have to think about the problem with no solution given.

NITIN NOHRIA: So that’s one form of experiential learning. But then, in my time as dean, we asked every one of our students to travel abroad, to get involved in real company situations. I think the only way to test whether the ideas that you’re learning play out in practice — how you apply your judgment — is through experiential learning. And I believe that in an age of AI, where the knowledge you have available will be at your fingertips, learning how to apply it in practical, experiential contexts will be the one profoundly powerful way of cultivating the kind of critical thinking and judgment I started our conversation with.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: You know, I was speaking with Bob Michele — he’s the head of fixed income at J.P. Morgan — and he has this quote that he tells his interns: the way to differentiate yourself is mastering AI tools the way my generation had to master the spreadsheet. Good advice?
NITIN NOHRIA: Very good advice.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Alright, our last two questions — and because you were dean at the Harvard Business School, these are going to be a little tailored to that. What is the prestige trap? What is the issue with chasing brand-name employers? Is that a sound strategy?

NITIN NOHRIA: Brands are brands because they reflect something real. I don’t think brands can sustain themselves if they don’t reflect real opportunities. So if you go to Goldman Sachs, there is something that you will learn at Goldman Sachs that’s important. Or if you go to JPMorgan Chase in banking. If you go to consulting firms like BCG, Bain & Company, McKinsey — these are brands that carry cachet because they’re important. If you are interested in media, you go to Bloomberg or Disney. These are good places to go because the brands carry something.

NITIN NOHRIA: But I think increasingly, I find at Harvard Business School that many of our students have learned that there’s a lot to be learned in places that are not brands. So the courage that people now have to start in places that aren’t already established brands has dramatically increased. And the reason that increases, I think, is that these people have come of age where great companies have been built in front of their eyes. Who knew what Facebook was going to be? Who knew what Google was going to be? In the span of 10, 15 years, extraordinary brands have been built. And so I think our students have become much more comfortable saying that while a brand provides some assurance of a good learning experience, I can also get a great learning experience if I put myself in a setting where there’s a lot more risk — but if it succeeds, it can succeed in an extraordinary way.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: And the question I’m very curious about: you’ve not only taught decades of students at Harvard, at the business school and elsewhere as well. I’m curious — what career paths of alumni from the Harvard Business School really surprised you?

NITIN NOHRIA: I think the thing that has constantly surprised me is when our students decide to stake out their own entrepreneurial journey. Fifty percent of our business school students, by the end of their careers, will have chosen an entrepreneurial path. And it can be anything from opening their own small consulting firm, to at some point deciding to start their own investment shop, to buying a small company, or even sometimes returning to their family company and deciding, “I want to run this company.”

NITIN NOHRIA: So it’s interesting. In the end, people want to have the opportunity to feel like, “I am reporting to no boss. I have ownership over what I’m building.” And yet some people will do it as soon as they graduate from the school; some people will do it 25 years later. What has constantly surprised me is: what’s the trigger that finally causes someone to say, “Okay, I now need to have the opportunity to be an entrepreneur”? And it’s amazing the different ways in which people arrive at that decision.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Really fascinating stuff. Thank you for being so generous with your time, Professor Nohria. We have been speaking with Nitin Nohria, author of the new book The CEO: The Role, the Reality, and the Responsibility, and former dean of the Harvard Business School. You’ve been listening to Bloomberg’s At The Money.
