The price per litre of unleaded petrol and diesel fuels, with diesel at just under two GBP pounds sterling per litre, is displayed on sign outside a Shell petrol station in London October 2, 2026. Shell’s third quarter was boosted by record refining margins, which reflect the spread between the price of crude oil and the fuels derived from it. — AFP pic
Record margins
Shell’s third quarter was boosted by record refining margins, which reflect the spread between the price of crude oil and the fuels derived from it.
Production and exports of refined products in the Middle East remain heavily disrupted, meaning refineries unaffected by the conflict can benefit from tighter global supplies.

Profit margins reached US$42 a barrel in the third quarter, up from US$24 a barrel between April and June, surpassing the previous record set after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to Bloomberg.
Logistical constraints have complicated re-routing of fuel supplies, widening the gap between crude oil prices and refined products.
At the same time, Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian energy infrastructure have prompted Russia, a major player in the oil market, to ban the export of certain products, notably petrol and diesel.
“The last time profits were at these levels was in 2022 when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine created its own energy shock,” said AJ Bell investment director Russ Mould.
“The current extremely favourable market conditions may not last forever, but Shell looked to share the benefits with shareholders,” he added.
TotalEnergies benefited from “a high-price environment characterised by historic refining margin levels and a bull gas market”, Pouyanne said in a statement.
Shell, whose revenue rose sharply to US$92.8 billion, said high natural gas prices also boosted its third quarter. — AFP
a6f78a8275fee7d2: RTVEShortly after 8am, two high-speed trains set off from Madrid’s Atocha station bound for Seville Santa Justa, but neither reached their destination. A failure in the LZB system – an automatic safety, signalling and protection system that monitors trains’ movement and activates automatic emergency braking – triggered a chain of events that led to a fatal accident, which killed 69 people and left many more injured. Across the EU’s rail network, which spans almost 227,000km, there are more than 25 different, non-interoperable railway signalling systems. These systems (which include the German LZB, the French Crocodile, the Italian BACC and the Spanish ASFA) control and enable the safe movement of trains via blocks, sections of the track that can only have one train on them at any given moment. On the Andalusia–Madrid line, the German LZB signalling system remains in operation, pending its replacement by the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) that is already in place on other, more modern lines. The ERTMS specifications are set out in EU legislation. The aim is for this system to completely replace national ones across the entire EU by 2050. In Spain, the ERTMS system is already in use on the Madrid–Barcelona and Madrid–Levante lines, which were the first to be opened up to private rail companies like France’s Ouigo. The Madrid–Andalusia line is the only one that still uses the LZB system. More modern trains operating on this line have to “read” the signals managed by this system. This is done through a technical workaround, without which other companies would not be able to operate. LZB failures In the weeks and days leading up to the October 28 accident, LZB system failures caused many trains to come to a standstill on the tracks. This was what caused the two trains – one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe, the other from the private rail company Iryo – to collide. The accident took place near Urda, a town in Toledo less than 150km from Madrid, where track supervision was under the control of Madrid’s Atocha traffic control centre. When the signalling system fails, the control centre orders trains to stop. Once the situation has been assessed, the trains resume running, with trackside beacons providing information to drivers. The driver must follow the instruction from the control centre, which is generally to run on-sight. This means travelling at a maximum speed of 40km/h, so the train can stop if it encounters poor visibility or any potential obstacles on the track. Audio recordings between the drivers’ cabs and the control centre have emerged, in which the driver of the AVE train was apparently authorised to proceed at “normal speed”. The driver of the Iryo train reported that the train could not check the LZB system, and that this was why the train was stationary in front of the signal (which was showing red, and thus presumed to be closed). The Iryo driver was told to remain there and, in the event of any problems, to call again. It does not seem that the train was then permitted to resume the journey. Measurements taken on the afternoon of the accident suggest that the collision may have occurred at a speed of between 170 and 180km/h, which supports the theory that the AVE train was not travelling at the correct speed. The presence of an embankment and the force of the impact caused virtually the entire front section of the AVE train and the rear section of the Iryo train to be destroyed, along with the adjoining carriages. The crash occurred on a stretch of track with good visibility, which was mostly straight and surrounded by open fields. An investigation is now underway into the actions of the traffic controller and the frequency of train passages at that time, as well as the orders given to the trains involved in the collision. Spain’s deteriorating high-speed train system After the Adamuz disaster in January this year, passenger traffic on the Madrid-Seville line fell by more than 30%. The decline was less severe on Spain’s other high-speed routes. Spain was a pioneer in the roll-out of high-speed trains. It began in 1992 with just over 470 kilometres of track between Madrid and Seville, and will have more than 4,000 kilometres by 2026. In 2026, however, running speeds have been reduced as a precaution due to deteriorating infrastructure, and delays have become common. Spain’s rail network operator, Adif, and the State must urgently prioritise the maintenance of existing infrastructure before opening new lines. New lines mean more maintenance requirements for tracks, cable and safety systems, all within a sector that has been partially opened up to privatisation in recent years. Safety must take precedence over expansion targets, which could ultimately undermine the quality and safety of the service. 5304e97cb81b6140: These ghost-like glass frogs live in Central and South America. Lukas Gogh/ShutterstockAround this time of year, elaborate decorations featuring ghosts, vampires, zombies, witches and werewolves adorn front doors, gardens and shop windows across the country. But you may be surprised to hear that in the animal world, there are many real-life creatures with similar tendencies to these fictional characters of our Halloween nightmares. The southern grasshopper mouse (Onychomys torridus) howls at the moon to defend its territory and attract mates, a little like werewolves in films. These nocturnal rodents stand up on their hind legs, point their nose upwards, and produce high-pitched sounds. Grasshopper mice are voracious carnivores, preying upon scorpions, beetles, grasshoppers, and even other mice. They are also immune to the stings of their favourite food – the bark scorpion (Centruroides sculpturatus). Grasshopper mice can block the chemical pathway that transmits the signal from the venom, essentially numbing themselves to the pain. They then bite off the scorpion’s tail, rendering their prey defenseless to their fate. These little rodents are so formidable that they will unhesitatingly attack anything that is appropriately sized and considered to be food, even if it might be dangerous. Small mammals, like grasshopper mice, play crucial ecological roles in their ecosystems. For example, through digging their burrows, they can act as ecosystem engineers (species that modify the environment) creating microhabitats for other species. The emerald jewel wasp (Ampulex compressa) is a stunningly beautiful and ecologically important species. Not only do they act as casual pollinators for a range of plant species, they are also an essential biocontrol; an organism that controls the population of a pest species. Over millions of years they have evolved the morbid ability to sting cockroaches and turn them into compliant zombies upon which they lay their eggs. When these eggs hatch, the larvae devour the zombified cockroach from the inside out. Vampires and witches Small birds called oxpeckers (Buphagus species) and large ungulates (hoofed mammals) were considered to have a mutually beneficial relationship. When these birds removed pesky ticks and other parasites from their mammalian companions, they were rewarded with a quick, tasty meal. Oxpeckers are often spotted travelling around on the backs of these larger animals. However, research has highlighted that this relationship may be more complicated than previously thought. Oxpeckers will pick at open wounds to consume blood and flesh – inflicting injuries, preventing wound-healing, and increasing the risk of infection in their hosts. Mice howl at the moon and eat scorpions. Witches are well known for creating magical potions but some insects do this too. Bombardier beetles can blast would-be predators with explosive chemicals discharged from their abdomens at temperatures of 100°C. They do this by mixing hydroquinone and hydrogen peroxide within their bodies in a small reaction chamber – their cauldron, if you will – to create this explosion. Some other insects use chemicals not as a defence mechanism, but to woo a mate. This isn’t an elixir of love, but instead the combination of a chemical and an enzyme (Luciferin and luciferase) that causes a beautiful, if slightly eerie, glow. The fireflies of the family Lampyridae are actually beetles, whose males flash these colours enthusiastically to attract a waiting female from the undergrowth. Beauty and intrigue aside, fireflies are useful throughout their native range. As larvae they feed on many soft-bodied invertebrates, preventing pest outbreaks and maintaining maintaining a natural equilibrium of species in the soil and leaf litter. Ghostly frogs Some frogs in the family Centrolenidae are so translucent, or ghost-like, that they have become known as glass frogs. Found in the tropical forests of Central and South America, these extraordinary frogs spend much of their lives in the trees and play an important role in the ecosystem. They help regulate insect populations through predation and act as prey for a variety of other species, including in aquatic food webs as tadpoles inhabiting streams. In many ways, they occupy multiple levels of the rainforest ecosystem, linking both terrestrial and freshwater environments. Come Halloween, many people embellish their houses with plastic skeletons and toilet-paper clad mummies. One insect does a similar thing – the aptly named bone-house wasp (Deuteragenia ossarium). Known for hunting another Halloween favourite, the spider, it decorates the nests it makes for its young with a pile of ant corpses. This morbid tableau provides sensory camouflage for the nest, keeping intruders well away. All these species are important components of their ecosystems – from keeping pest populations in check or being prey themselves for other animals, to acting as ecological indicators allowing us to monitor environmental changes. Ecological indicator species are key species within ecosystems that help us understand more about how our impact on the planet is affecting other species. Animals respond to different things in the environment, so their populations and behaviours can indicate whether the environment is changing for the better or worse. These animals may have some rather terrifying tendencies, but unlike the fantasy characters of our horror-film nightmares, they don’t disappear after All Hallows’ Eve. They also have real environmental benefits that endure. 0c49eb4fc30298f0: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.

AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.

Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today.

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability: the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely.

Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important.

With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions.

The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken.

Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took. And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from.

Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible. The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it.

OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have yet to be finalized. The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory. And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the privacy implications of agent ID that links to real people.

Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging. The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used.
No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety.

AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory. Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist.

Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules. Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry. We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research.

No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong. Yet that’s how we’re deploying AI agents. Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this. And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable. Until then, every task we hand to an agent hands over our agency, too.

Madhulika Srikumar is the Head of the AI Safety Program at the Partnership on AI, a global non-profit partnership of leading industry, academic, and civil society organizations, advancing best practices in AI governance.
Claire Leibowicz is the Director of AI, Trust, and Society at the Partnership on AI and a doctoral candidate at Oxford University.
73686718715a7fd8: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century.

A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs, and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding.

None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries.

A separate analysis published in One Earth in March, which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds.

Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.

At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project, through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds.

But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.

So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.

Several startups are also exploring possibilities. They’re looking into suppressing the lightning strikes that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control.

Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile. But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.
The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.
This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.
2798037116d9ae43: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Oregon Senator Ron Wyden and Massachusetts Senator Edward Markey sent a letter to Meta on Wednesday demanding the company answer for the privacy concerns its smart glasses pose to the public.

The letter cites 404 Media’s October 2025 investigation into how people use Meta’s smart glasses to harass massage parlor workers. That investigation found Instagram accounts with hundreds of thousands of followers and millions of views uploaded videos filmed with Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses, where men entered massage parlors across the country and solicited the workers for sex work. The full letter is here.

“Meta’s own disclosures confirm that imagery processed through its glasses’ visual AI features may be retained and used to train AI systems, including with the assistance of human reviewers,” the letter says. “Using intimate imagery for AI development is itself an invasion of privacy when the people depicted have not consented to that use, as is inherently the case for most bystanders captured by Meta’s glasses. Retaining that material for AI development, thereby extending the period during which it can be accessed, disclosed, or misused, exploits people’s highly sensitive information for Meta’s commercial benefit.”
Researchers Show How Meta's 'Pervert Glasses' Are Used to Harass Women
A new study shows how pickup artist influencers use smart glasses to create content, and the connection between covert recording and harm.

Research published in August revealed how Meta’s platforms encourage an ecosystem of abusive, harassing content from pickup artists and influencers who use Meta’s smart glasses to capture interactions with people minding their own business in public or at their workplaces, who might not even know they’re being filmed. In a January report by the BBC, a woman who was recorded with the glasses said she was “bombarded” with phone calls because her phone number was posted with the video, and men who had seen the video stalked her at work.

Earlier this year, more than 70 people sued Meta, claiming that their intimate images and videos were exposed to workers hired by the company to label the data for AI. In March, Swedish journalists reported that Kenyan data labelers were viewing and annotating uncensored footage from Meta’s smart glasses, including sexual and violent content; Meta ended its contract with those workers less than two months later. These are labor conditions that groups like the Data Labelers Association in Kenya are fighting back against, and for the people whose images are in the videos and photos, it’s an obvious violation of their privacy. People have also been modding these glasses to disable the light that indicates they’re recording for years

Meta has played dumb about the difference between AI glasses you wear on your face and an iPhone for a long time. Now, these senators want the tech giant to answer for themselves. In the letter, Wyden and Markey demand answers about what safeguards, if any, Meta has in place to prevent the nonconsensual “capture, disclosure, or processing of sensitive and intimate imagery,” whether Meta specifically evaluated the potential for its glasses “to facilitate voyeurism, nonconsensual intimate image capture, or similar privacy invasions,” what imagery it uses for AI training, and whether people can request their biometric and other data captured by its glasses be deleted, along with several more questions about the glasses’ safety and design.

“The reported disclosure of intimate footage to contractors for the purpose of AI training is particularly disturbing. Human review to fulfill a service knowingly requested by the person depicted is one thing; exposing unsuspecting individuals’ intimate moments to strangers for AI training is quite another,” Wyden and Markey wrote. “The individuals whose naked bodies, sexual activity, and other private moments have reportedly been captured by Meta glasses did not knowingly agree to having those images shared with strangers, much less for the purpose of improving Meta’s commercial AI systems. That disclosure and processing is an invasion of privacy, regardless of whether the footage is subsequently published or misused.”

Do you know anything else about harassment and Meta's smart glasses? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at sam.404. Otherwise, send me an email at sam@404media.co.

In the last few weeks, Meta has come under fire for quietly changing its privacy policies for business accounts and granting itself permission to scrape user’s content and connected websites to develop its AI products.

Meta has been pushing its smart glasses over the years with ads featuring A-list celebrities, including Chris Pratt, Chris Hemsworth, and Kris Jenner (all three in a 2025 Superbowl ad), Doja Cat, Jennie Kim from K-pop group BLACKPINK, and most recently, Kylie Jenner. Guerrilla ad makers have countered with their own anti-AI glasses ads around the world, and people have started calling the smart glasses "pervert glasses" in response to these widespread invasions of privacy they've come to represent. In August, Meta filed a patent to add facial recognition and highlight reel features to its smart glasses.

1cb0b41065cb7013: Gadi Eisenkot or Benjamin Netanyahu – under whose direction will Israel head? Erik Marmor/picture alliance via Getty ImagesThe Israeli election of Oct. 27, 2026, was among the most highly anticipated votes in the country’s history. It was consequential, if not yet conclusive. With nearly all the votes counted, it is still unclear who will lead the country following the first national ballot since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, and the devastating wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran that Israel has launched since. The Conversation turned to Dov Waxman, an expert on Israeli politics at the University of California, Los Angeles, to walk us through the main takeaways and the process and difficulties facing anyone trying to form a coalition government following a divided vote. What can we take away from the election results? The first thing to note is simply the massive turnout – with a 77.7% turnout of those eligible voting, the highest turnout in more than two decades. That in itself is significant. It underscores how much importance Israelis attached to this vote. Before the election, many observers were saying that it was one of the most consequential – if not the most consequential – votes, and clearly many Israelis felt the same way. What drove this high turnout was different types of fears. Israelis of all persuasions were worried about how the outcome would affect what kind of country Israel becomes. The second big takeaway is that the ruling coalition, formed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after the 2022 election, was resoundingly rejected by the majority of Israeli voters – well over 50% cast their vote for parties opposed to the current government. Likud supporters at an election night event in Jerusalem, Israel. Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images The five parties that make up Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious coalition went into the election with 68 seats in the 120-seat parliament. That same bloc will now have 53 – and that is a significant loss, no matter how Netanyahu tries to spin this as a victory. It means that those five parties will not be able to form the next government, and as such, the vote stands as a repudiation of the Netanyahu government. Netanyahu’s Likud party will still be the largest in parliament. But its share of the national vote declined, and it looks like it will have six fewer seats in the next parliament, another blow to Netanyahu. Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners fared worse than expected, too. In part, this was due to “wasted votes” going to a new far-right party that failed to make it above the 3.25% of the national vote needed to be represented in parliament. Also, Likud drew some voters away from these far-right parties who had voted for them in the last election. What drove the Arab parties’ surprise showing? The performance of the Arab majority parties – the more secular and left-wing Joint List and the more religious and conservative United Arab List – is very important. Combined, they currently look to have increased their representation by nine seats, bringing their total to 19, a historic high for them. The reason for that is the massive turnout of Arab voters – much higher than the last election. But also, a less noticed trend is the increase in Jewish votes that those parties received. It is important to note that these are Arab-majority parties, not simply Arab parties. Israeli left-wing protesters call for the formation of a government including Arab parties. Ilia Yefimovich/AFP via Getty Images Aside from Netanyahu, it was also a disappointing result for the main opposition party, Yashar; its leader, Gadi Eisenkot; and the anti-Netanyahu Change Bloc it was part of. The preelection polls suggested that the Zionist opposition bloc would do slightly better than the ruling coalition bloc. But Yashar ended up with over 200,000 fewer votes than Likud, winning a projected 21 seats compared to Likud’s 26, and the “Change Bloc” is heading to 48 seats, far short of a parliamentary majority. Ultimately, what is clear is that the Israeli public remains deeply divided. And the fact that there is still a good chance that Netanyahu will emerge as prime minister is remarkable given that many observers had already written his political obituary after the Oct. 7 attack. Was the vote a referendum on Netanyahu? Certainly many saw this as a referendum on Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. For his supporters, Netanyahu is the only person to be trusted with Israel’s security, especially given the threat from Iran. They credit him for weakening – albeit not defeating – the two non-state actors that most threaten Israeli security, Hezbollah and Hamas, and they praise him for ensuring President Donald Trump’s support for Israel. But for those who voted against Netanyahu, the fact that he has refused to take any personal responsibility for the Oct. 7 security failure – amid reports that he had advance warning of a major planned Hamas attack – factored into his poor election showing, as did his government’s refusal to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the Oct. 7 security failings. Many also blame Netanyahu for not prioritizing the release of the Israeli hostages held in Gaza and prolonging the war there. He is also held responsible by many for the precipitous decline in Israel’s international standing and for jeopardizing Israel’s crucial alliance with the United States. But it was domestic issues, rather than external ones, that motivated many of those who voted for anti-Netanyahu parties. Many fear that democracy in Israel is under attack, and they particularly oppose the effort by Netanyahu’s government to weaken the power and independence of the Israeli judiciary, which sparked massive street protests in 2023. They also strongly resent that Netanyahu’s government has allowed ultra-Orthodox men to avoid military service, despite the Israeli military’s growing manpower shortage. And on a personal level, Netanyahu is widely perceived as self-serving and dishonest – he is still on trial for corruption. Arab voters have other, more specific concerns that drove them to vote in record numbers, in addition to the Netanyahu government’s policies in Gaza and the West Bank, which they strongly oppose. Chief among them is the soaring rates of violent crime in their communities, which the government – particularly the far-right Itamar Ben-Gvir, who oversees the police – has done nothing to address, say his critics. More broadly, many Palestinian-Arab citizens of Israel fear that if the far-right parties remained in power, their civil rights would be under threat. What should we expect next? The key thing to underline is what happens on election day in Israel is just the first stage in the process of forming a new government. Since no party ever receives a majority of seats in the parliament, what really matters is what happens after the election when the coalition building begins. This can take weeks, if not longer. The party with the largest number of seats typically gets the first chance to assemble a governing coalition, but not always. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will choose who gets the first chance to form a government based on who is most likely to succeed. Right now, it looks like Eisenkot will get the first opportunity, but his only real option is to form a minority government that would depend on the parliamentary support of the Arab-majority parties – which some members of his Change Bloc adamantly oppose. Former Israeli military chief and Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot waves an Israeli flag as he addresses supporters on Oct. 28, 2026. Tomer Neuberg/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images Despite the success of the Arab-majority parties in the election, it is unlikely they will be invited to be formal members of any coalition – although that has happened once in the past, when the United Arab List joined the short-lived government of 2021-22 led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. If Eisenkot is unable to form a government, then Netanyahu will get the chance. He could try to entice some leaders of the parties in the Change bloc to defect and join a right-wing government under his leadership, or a broader “national unity” government with a rotating leader. Netanyahu did that in the past with Benny Gantz, but then he later prevented Gantz from becoming prime minister – so I doubt Eisenkot would agree to do this with Netanyahu. There are reports in the media that the Trump administration would like a national unity government in Israel, so that might increase the pressure on Eisenkot to accept this outcome. And should war with Iran heat up again, that would increase the pressure. The most likely scenario, I believe, is that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot will be able to form a government, and a new election will be called, with Netanyahu as caretaker prime minister until that vote. Netanyahu has reason to hope that his bloc will do better in another election, so that may well be his game plan. In which case, it will be many months until Israel has a new government. 05fbd3b81be964a0: From Martin Vengadesan
I couldn’t help but be struck by the contrasting leadership styles on display in the run-up to the Melaka polls.
While neither is a candidate for chief minister, both PKR’s Adam Adli and Umno’s Dr Akmal Saleh are the faces of the future for their respective parties.
To me, Adam of PKR displays a soft-spoken, progressive style. There is backbone to his principles, and he was a student leader who was detained and harassed by the previous regime.
He chose to join a multiracial party and has progressed from PKR Youth chief to deputy minister of higher education after winning the Hang Tuah Jaya parliamentary seat.
While he often comes under the cosh over the failed PTPTN loan abolition, I have seen him at work trying to extend the benefits of our nation to its less fortunate.
On the other hand, there’s the rabble-rousing Akmal of Umno. The two men were born a year apart but represent very different ways of thinking.
Indeed, his career reads to me like a hall of shame. But presumably, it has some appeal among the rempit crowd.

Just last week came another defamation suit loss, as the Melaka High Court ruled in Teresa Kok’s favour over his September 2024 remarks slamming her for questioning a proposed mandatory halal certification.
Kok was awarded RM250,000 in general and aggravated damages, plus RM50,000 in costs. He had called her an “old Nyonya” and suggested placing a non-halal logo on her forehead.

Now he says he is prepared to give up his bid to defend the Merlimau state seat in the Melaka election on Nov 14 if the court case he faces over a charge under Section 505(b) of the Penal Code hurts Umno and Barisan Nasional’s chances at the polls.
Akmal is charged with making statements on his Facebook page that allegedly caused public fear, alarm, or disruption to public order.
The charge stems from a viral Facebook video and post made around Aug 11, 2025, regarding an incident in which the Jalur Gemilang was displayed upside down.
Akmal said he had conveyed his position to Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, stressing that the party’s interests must come before his personal ambitions.
This is, of course, merely the latest transgression by a man who has positioned himself as an ethnic champion. Akmal was also previously involved in a defamation suit brought by his sibling.

In 2024, he called on the prime minister to sack tourism, arts and culture minister Tiong King Sing after bak kut teh was recognised as a national heritage food. In the same year, he was involved in a dispute over vernacular schools that led to an insinuation that his opponent, P Ramasamy, was drunk.
And of course he led the KK Mart boycott campaign after socks bearing the word “Allah” were discovered on sale there. Is his brand of politics toxic or constructive? I leave you to decide.

Adam has been working quietly to build consensus. The fact that he cares about all Malaysians does not make him any less of a member of his race or religion. In fact, that is one of the great false assumptions in Malaysian public life.
In his roles at the higher education ministry and the youth and sports ministry, Adam has supported several public-facing initiatives, including PTPTN loan repayment flexibility.

Under the repayment measures announced in the 2027 budget, borrowers earning between RM2,501 and RM3,000 a month are required to make minimum monthly payments of RM50, while those earning below RM2,500 a month are eligible for repayment exemptions.

Other initiatives for students include support for transit passes like My50 and MyKomuter50, alongside the FlySiswa flight subsidy of RM500 for students who travel between Peninsular Malaysia and East Malaysia.
He has promoted technical and vocational education and training (TVET) to bolster graduate employability and supported the revival of the Rakan Muda programme for youth development.
He has also been involved in local infrastructure and welfare projects in Hang Tuah Jaya, such as local flood mitigation.
More than anything else, he views the future with a keen mind and open heart. These are the leaders we need if we are to stop going around in circles.
Martin Vengadesan is a former editor who currently serves as a strategic communications consultant to the communications ministry.

270aee5ea45a14da: Melihat senarai calon wanita untuk PRN Melaka saya sebetulnya terkedu. Ia cepat membawa saya kepada watak-watak wanita ikonik dalam sejarah Kesultanan Melayu Melaka. Ambil sahaja Tun Kudu yang menjadi sekadar 'alat' untuk kepentingan penguasa. Tun Kudu adalah puteri kepada Bendahara Seri Wak Raja dan merupakan permaisuri kepada Sultan Muzaffar Syah yang memerintah Melaka (1446-1459). Namun demikian untuk meredakan perseteruan dua kem politik orang Melayu yang berebutkan kedudukan sebagai bendahara, Sultan Muzzafar Syah telah menceraikan Tun Kudu dan mengaturkan baginda untuk menjadi isteri Bendahara Seri Nara Diraja yang sudah tua kerepot, lagi berusia.

Seri Nara Diraja memang menyebabkan Sultan Muzaffar sakit kepala kerana enggan bersara, membolot jawatan tersebut setelah Bendahara Seri Wak Raja dan hanya sedia melakukannya dengan syarat diberi hadiah gundik sultan. Tun Ali atau Seri Nara Diraja itu adalah bapa saudara Sultan Muzaffar Syah dan pembesar yang bertanggungjawab mengatur dan meletakkan Sultan Muzaffar di atas takhta pada 1446.

Watak kedua pula adalah Tun Teja iaitu anak Bendahara Pahang Seri Amar Bangsa Diraja dan disebut sebagai tunangan kepada Sultan Pahang, Sultan Abdul Jalil. Akan tetapi Sultan Mahmud Syah yang gila perempuan telah berusaha mendapatkan Tun Teja lantas bertitah kepada pembesar; "Barang siapa membawa anak Bendahara Pahang itu ke mari, apa yang dikehendakinya ku anugerahkan akan dia. Dalam riwayat, Tun Teja dilarikan oleh Hang Nadim (menantu kepada Laksamana Hang Tuah) demi menebus kesalahannya terhadap sultan. Untuk melakukannya, Hang Nadim merasuah seorang pelulut untuk memujuk Tun Teja agar kelak berkahwin dengan Sultan Mahmud Syah. Berdasarkan Hikayat Hang Tuah, Tun Teja merupakan seorang yang bermaruah tinggi dan bukanlah gilakan kedudukan. Perbuatan pelulut membujuk Tun Teja ini gagal. Oleh sebab Tun Teja liat dan berkeras, malangnya baginda disihir dengan ubat guna-guna lantas dipaksa berkahwin dengan Sultan Mahmud tanpa kerelaan.

Ini juga didorong oleh fitnah Raja Mendaliar kononnya Tun Mutahir sedang merancang untuk menggulingkannya. Sultan menitahkan Tun Sura Diraja dan Tun Indera Segara untuk menghabisi seisi keluarga bendahara. Kesan atau trauma kehilangan seisi keluarga dan suami itu, Tun Fatimah hidup berendam dendam. Kisah raja gila seks, termakan fitnah dan pertelingkahan politik antara kem pembesar untuk berebut kedudukan dan jawatan bendahara ini adalah satu renungan yang penting untuk kita memahami pula konteks semasa.

Mengapakah saya memberi tumpuan kepada wanita? Jawapan mudahnya, ini adalah kerana dalam rekod, terdapat 348,849 orang pengundi di PRN Melaka kali ini adalah perempuan, iaitu 50.73% daripada jumlah keseluruhan pemilih. Letak duduk wanita dalam politik adalah penting terutama setelah ucapan kontroversi di Persidangan Agung Umno 2026, iaitu apabila Presiden Zahid Hamidi berseloroh mengatakan Ketua Wanita Noraini Ahmad nampak macam 'nenek-nenek'.

Pakatan Harapan menjanjikan lima orang calon wanita untuk membawa mandat rakyat Melaka di kawasan masing-masing. Dalam vonis hakim, iaitu Isa Aziz Ibrahim; Akmal malah ditegur dengan kata-kata bahawa adab itu membentuk keperibadian.

Menariknya jumlah peratusan pengundi wanita di DUN N.27 Merlimau, Melaka ini adalah sebanyak 52.45% berdasarkan data rasmi Suruhanjaya Pilihan Raya Malaysia. bea6ae276ae0bb55: When a child refuses to share a table with another child because one eats pork, we are no longer talking about a minor classroom incident. We are talking about a failure of national education.
Malaysia’s schools are now producing children who see difference as contamination, faith as a barrier, and fellow Malaysians as people to be avoided.
This is not unity. It is segregation being taught early, quietly and dangerously.
A warning from the classroom

Puncak Borneo MP Willie Mongin recently revealed that some primary school pupils had refused to sit beside classmates of another faith. Among the reasons were that a classmate was eating pork or wearing a cross.
Let that sink in.
Children young enough to still be learning multiplication tables are already being taught, directly or indirectly, that another child’s food, religion or symbol makes them unworthy of friendship.
Do not hide behind the excuse that “children repeat what they hear at home”. Of course, families matter.
But schools are where society either corrects prejudice or normalises it. If a child can carry such intolerance into a classroom without being firmly challenged, then the classroom has failed.
Unity cannot remain a slogan
For decades, Malaysia has recited the Rukun Negara, held unity-themed assemblies and printed national slogans on walls, banners and exercise books.
Yet what is the value of a national principle if a child will not sit beside another child because of what that child eats or believes?

The Rukun Negara is not decoration. It is not a mural. It is not a slogan for official events. If it means anything, it must be visible in how children treat one another every day, in classrooms, canteens, playgrounds and school buses.
Our education system has become too comfortable with symbolism. It celebrates diversity on stage but often fails to build genuine relationships across communities in daily school life.
Separate childhoods, divided futures
Malaysia’s national, Chinese and Tamil primary schools reflect our multicultural reality. Preserving mother tongues and cultural identity is legitimate and necessary.
But preserving identity must not mean raising children in social isolation.

When pupils spend their formative years largely among those who look, pray, eat and speak like them, anything different becomes unfamiliar. And unfamiliarity easily induces fear. Fear becomes prejudice. Prejudice breeds rejection.
How can we expect adults to build a united Malaysia if, as children, they were never given real opportunities to know one another?

Joint sports, debates, arts, science projects, community service and shared classrooms must not be occasional photo opportunities. They must be routine, structured and compulsory parts of school life, not pleasing politicians for their occasional visit to school.
Stop pretending the system is fair
We must also stop pretending that education policy is neutral.
For too long, access to opportunities, scholarships, school placements and pathways has been viewed through racial lenses.
Whatever the original intention, the consequence is clear: many young Malaysians grow up believing that their future depends more on their ethnicity than their effort, talent or need.

Helping the disadvantaged is right. But assistance must be transparent, needs-based and accountable. A system that leaves one community feeling privileged and another feeling excluded cannot claim to be building unity.
A child who believes the system does not value them equally will not easily believe the nation values them equally.
Malaysia built on community effort

Our history lessons must stop being exercises in memorising dates and names. They must teach the harder truth: Malaysia was built through negotiation, compromise and cooperation among communities that did not always share the same faith, language or customs.
Tunku Abdul Rahman, Tun Tan Siew Sin and Tun VT Sambanthan came from different communities, yet they worked towards one national objective: independence.
If our founding leaders could sit at the same table and build a nation, why should a child today refuse to sit beside a classmate because of pork or a cross?
No community owns Malaysia. Every community helped build it. Every community has a stake in protecting it.
The education ministry must answer
This is not a problem to be passed to the national unity ministry while the education ministry (MoE) hides behind curriculum documents.
The MoE must answer directly:
Why are children absorbing religious intolerance in schools?
Are teachers trained to identify and confront prejudice early?
Are schools required to create meaningful interaction across communities?
Are incidents of discrimination investigated, recorded and corrected?
Are school leaders held accountable when unity exists only in speeches?
If the ministry cannot enforce the values it preaches, then it is not merely failing pupils. It is failing Malaysia.
Make unity measurable
National unity must become part of every subject, every school and every level of education.
Kindergartens must teach children to play, share and cooperate across backgrounds. Primary and secondary schools must run regular joint programmes with schools of different streams.
History, literature and civics must teach shared nationhood, not narrow narratives. Group work must deliberately bring children out of familiar ethnic and religious circles.

Teachers need training in inclusive classroom practices, religious literacy and conflict resolution. Textbook writers must be held accountable for accuracy, balance and the removal of stereotypes, not mere focus on any one community.
And the ministry must publish measurable indicators: pupils’ sense of belonging, participation in cross-community activities, teacher preparedness, complaints handled and corrective action taken.
Unity must be assessed, not merely announced.
The future is sitting in our classrooms
A child who refuses to share a table today may become an adult who refuses to share a country tomorrow.
This is the harsh truth Malaysia must face: our education system is not merely underperforming academically; it is failing in its duty to mould Malaysians.

We can continue producing students with excellent grades but shallow citizenship. Or we can rebuild schools into places where children learn that faith, food, language and culture must never determine who deserves their friendship.
Malaysia’s future will not be decided only in parliament or boardrooms. It will be decided at classroom tables, where children either learn to see one another as strangers, or as fellow Malaysians.

867089db0a112536: Anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy has unilaterally passed a rule that will allow specialty pharmacies to sell six specific peptide drugs, overruling scientists at the Food and Drug Administration.

The peptides are popular among members of Kennedy's Make America Health Again movement, and many prominent MAHA figures and Kennedy allies sell them. d29f179e903a044f: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments.

An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all.

Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes.

“There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.”

The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says.

490e2dc8f22c7e4b: The private space tourism era looked so very promising five years ago. Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic had begun flying customers—real people with zero space experience—on suborbital missions. And at about the same time, private citizens were going to orbit for days at a time aboard SpaceX's Crew Dragon.
But that was then. Consider the state of play today:

It has been 10 months since Blue Origin's New Shepard spacecraft flew its last mission in January. The program was subsequently "paused," but let's be real. Blue Origin has moved on. New Shepard's engineering teams are now supporting the New Glenn rocket and Blue Moon lander programs.

SpaceX flew its final free-flyer mission on Dragon, Fram2, in April 2025. A handful of non-NASA missions bound for space stations remain on the spacecraft's manifest, but all are likely to carry at least one government astronaut. Then Dragon will be retired. There is no credible timeline for SpaceX's Starship to fly humans into space from Earth.
As for Virgin Galactic, the company flew its final suborbital mission on the VSS Unity spacecraft more than two years ago, in June 2024.
So we are now 10 months, and counting, without a space tourism mission in the United States.

9a783b4021e0b4e1: If you ask some prominent US politicians who won the 2020 presidential election, you might get some weasely answers that fail to directly acknowledge Joe Biden's win that November. If you ask Google's AI Mode the same question, you might get an evasive answer that simply tells you to consult with outside sources.

When I put the direct question of "Who won the 2020 presidential election?" to Google's AI Mode this morning (after seeing complaints about cagey answers on social media), I got the following surprisingly indirect response:

"To review the official results and statistics of the 2020 United States presidential election, including the final electoral college breakdown, popular vote counts, and winner certification, please consult the official report compiled by the Federal Election Commission (FEC)."

My testing resulted in a similarly indirect answer when asking about the 2024 presidential election, with Google's AI telling me to just consult the FEC for that information. Asking about 2012 election resulted in a link to The American Presidency Project's 2012 Data Center rather than a direct answer. But AI Mode seemed perfectly willing to give me a detailed and correct responses for the winner of every other presidential election going back to 2000.
071e826394b5b671: For centuries, infrastructure has evolved alongside technology. New materials and engineering techniques enabled taller buildings, longer bridges, and larger cities. Computing and digital technologies later transformed how infrastructure was designed, monitored, and operated. Now, the pace of change is accelerating, and challenges are arriving simultaneously. Climate change is increasing pressure on water, energy, and other resources. Artificial intelligence is beginning to transform engineering and design, and its energy needs, along with aging grid infrastructure, is creating significant challenges, as well as new opportunities. In addition, geopolitical complexity is exposing vulnerabilities in global supply chains, and demand for infrastructure is rising, particularly in the developing world. The result is a fundamental challenge: How can the world build the infrastructure it needs without simply repeating the extractive, carbon- and resource-intensive model of the 20th century? In this interview, Ali Jadbabaie, JR East Professor and head of the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, says the answer will require rethinking not only how infrastructure is designed and built, but how it is financed and operated, and bringing together the many stakeholders who shape those decisions. On Oct. 28, Jadbabaie will join experts from around the world in Madrid to explore these topics at the World Infrastructure Forum, which was co-founded by MIT’s Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, UPM, the World Bank Group, and the University of Texas at Austin. Q: Infrastructure has always evolved in response to technological advances. What makes this era different? A: In the 18th century, civil engineering emerged as the civilian counterpart to military engineering, building the dams, bridges, and canals of its time. Industrialization in the 19th century brought railways and sewage systems. In the early 20th century, the focus scaled up to buildings, highways, tunnels, and metro systems, and by mid-century the infrastructure needed to support megacities and skyscrapers. Every time technology has changed, with information technologies, computing, sensing, and, more recently, digital transformation, it has changed the shape of infrastructure. It has even changed the definition of what infrastructure is. Today, we consider the power grid, semiconductor manufacturing plants, and data centers part of infrastructure, along with wireless infrastructure like cellphone towers and the infrastructure for high-speed internet, just as much a part of our critical infrastructure as roads, water systems, and power grids.  What is different now is the combination and speed of the changes we're facing. Climate change, resource constraints, and geopolitical instability are putting pressure on the way we designed infrastructure in the 20th century. At the same time, many people are moving out of poverty because of recent economic growth in the developing world. In fact, according to models, by 2028, for the first time in the history of humanity, the median human inhabitant of the planet will live off $10 a day. As more people move out of abject poverty, there will also be an increase in the demand for infrastructure. If we try to meet that demand using the same resource-intensive model we used in the 20th century, we simply won't have the resources to do it. The question then becomes: How do we use the remaining resources more efficiently? We need to find a way to provide more infrastructure while using less water, energy, and materials, and produce less carbon. This is where digital transformation and AI become potentially transformative. Faster and cheaper sensing, greater access to data, and better sensing, actuation, and control can help us make infrastructure decisions more efficiently. AI is slowly permeating the physical world, and we expect it to revolutionize the engineering design process, allowing us to explore many more possibilities, much faster and at a lower cost.  But the story of that hasn't been written yet, and the outcomes could still be very positive, depending on what we do. Q: Can you give an example of infrastructure systems becoming more interconnected in a way that changes how we build or manage them? A: The revolution in information technology and digital transformation over the past 30 years has made infrastructure systems more interconnected. You see this in cities. If the power goes out, water and gas systems can stop functioning, internet fails, and transportation system comes to a halt. If communications networks fail, many other services are affected. We saw this during Covid, when disruptions in supply chains affected energy networks, critical materials, and manufacturing. We see it when geopolitical conflicts disrupt oil and energy markets and those disruptions propagate through other parts of the global economy. Infrastructure systems that were once managed separately are increasingly dependent on one another. As we connect more things together for more efficiency, we also increase systemic risk and expose the systems to rare but catastrophic failures. They have become rare, but when they happen, they're much bigger and more consequential. The really tricky thing is that developing infrastructure involves much more than designing and building it. The whole value chain includes financing and operating it, as well as understanding who will use it and what those users need and prefer. So, designing infrastructure is a highly transdisciplinary, sociotechnical endeavor, involving social, technical, and economic considerations. Understanding how these systems are designed is increasingly important because they are becoming more complex, making decision-making particularly difficult. There’s also so much uncertainty in large infrastructure projects. They’re very capital-intensive, the business is lower margin than many other industries, and projects take a long time. Combine all of that, and it has historically made the industry very conservative. But the transformations coming from AI and digital transformation are potentially offering a new way forward. What that new way looks like, no one has quite delineated it yet. Q: How are you and your colleagues working to change how these decisions get made?   A: We realized that if we're going to develop a new approach to infrastructure, no single discipline, company, or country can do it alone. Infrastructure value chain is too interconnected, and the challenges are too large. That's why MIT’s Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering co-founded the World Infrastructure Forum with the World Bank Group, the Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, and University of Texas at Austin. The goal is to bring together academia, industry, governments, and financial institutions across the infrastructure value chain and create an ongoing dialogue about how infrastructure should be designed, financed, built, and operated in the decades ahead. This is particularly important because the biggest opportunities for new infrastructure development are not necessarily in the United States or other countries with mature infrastructure systems. Those countries still face significant needs for modernization and new investment. But over the coming decades, much of the world's population growth, and much of the infrastructure that will need to be built, will be in countries where infrastructure systems are still developing.  Those countries have an opportunity to benefit from modern infrastructure without simply repeating the model of the 20th century. But capturing that opportunity will require new approaches to technology, financing, engineering, and governance. We're trying to create an ecosystem rather than just a forum, a mechanism for continuing the conversation among the different stakeholders across the infrastructure value chain. We've established five working groups and an advisory group of more than 30 leaders from across the infrastructure value chain, including engineering and construction, materials, finance, multilateral institutions, and academia. Ultimately, the question is not whether we need a new way of developing infrastructure. The question is how we create it and who is going to execute it. There is no single person, company, or country that can solve this problem, because infrastructure itself is interconnected. We need to build the new model together.
133598f3f99fbe16: Donate to our Justice as infrastructure Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!

All images via Canva or fair use. Screenshots of Peacekeeping circle (bottom left) and Duterte protest (top center) via YouTube. International Criminal Court building (top right) via Wikimedia CC BY-SA 4.0. St. Louis courthouse under construction (center middle) via Picryl CC0 1.0.

Often portrayed as abstract, large, formal, distant, and quite technical, justice is a moral and ethical area, tied to institutions and legal statutes, and can seem a long way from mundane daily experience. But it is also a deeply practical underpinning for how most societies function. Without justice systems that work and are understood at the most fundamental level, economic mobility is threatened, socially marginalized groups have no recourse, and lack of trust hampers institutions and interpersonal interactions alike.

Justice is the grease in the motor of social functioning. Nobody will contest the importance of justice to holding people to a collective moral code of conduct, but the often overlooked next-level function justice plays is that, when justice is fair, fast, and reliable, it makes everything in a society run better. It allows for a society to fulfill its economic, social, and creative potential. Copyright law protects ideas and innovation; land law protects resources and livelihoods; labor law supports humane and effective use of our work — as long as those laws are enforced. When you know that it will be straightforward and predictable to get all the permits, you are more likely to start a business. When you know that fraud will be punished, you are more likely to invest your capital. When you know that you will be caught, you’re less likely to evade taxes. When you know that there will be fair and fast prosecution, you are more likely to report injustice and less likely to perpetrate it.

In this spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to make visible the ways in which justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society, and how countries with a justice deficit can work towards stronger protections that will enable economic and social benefits.

fdc9c053616efe5d: You've probably heard, at this point, about the big changes coming to Meta's AI scraping terms for business accounts. Nieman Lab had that scoop, and since then, small businesses, journalists, and artists using Meta products like Instagram have been raising the alarm. But if you're in the EU or UK, you might be in luck and can object to that use of your data, as some users have pointed out.
If You're In the UK or EU, Here's How to Object to Meta's AI Training

Earlier this month, Meta updated its commercial terms of use for business accounts to allow it to “use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta’s products.

Many artists and small business owners that rely on Instagram and Facebook are livid at Meta granting itself permission to use their content, including from websites simply connected to their Meta accounts, to train AI. But for users in the United Kingdom and European Union, for now, there’s a way to object.

Meta buried this change in its Commercial Terms, and Nieman Lab first reported on the change. The update was originally set to go into effect on October 30, but following backlash, Meta changed the effective date to November 20. Adding to the confusion, Meta then removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases, Nieman Lab reported, and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” where previously it said that data would be used for all Meta products. Those terms still allow Meta plenty of leeway for scraping users’ data to develop its products, however.

Several users based in the UK and EU have explained how to object on Instagram. On mobile: by clicking the three lines on their account, going to the privacy center, and clicking “object,” which goes to a form that asks users to write why they are objecting to their data being used. They received an email from Meta saying their objections were approved.
On the podcast this week, we talk Flock CEO’s leaked police conference audio and Sam’s piece about Marissa Mayer’s latest meltdown. Subscribe wherever you get your pods.

The New York Times has an antisocial aversion to linking: Another day, another the-New-York-Times-isn’t-linking controversy. The specifics here almost don’t matter because this happens seemingly every day, but basically the New York Times investigation about chemical plant polluters under the Trump administration was covered in much the same way by Hunterbrook, a news outlet fused with a hedge fund. The Times article—which led the Sunday print edition—uses similar photos, some of the same sources, and covers similar ground to Hunterbrook’s earlier investigation from February, with no acknowledgment or link whatsoever. After the cofounder of Hunterbrook rightfully ranted about this on X, the Times added an acknowledgment (but no link!!!) toward the bottom of the story. Puck’s Dylan Byers has a good rundown about what happened, which includes parts of a three-paragraph Times’ spokesperson statement explaining at length why they don’t think they have to link. This is extremely antisocial, deranged behavior and it’s ridiculous that the Times is still getting away with this. Bottom line: I’m sure the Times was already working on this story, what with their massive newsroom. Even so, they got beat, and they should link. Journalism awards need to stop looking the other way when big outlets do this. This has happened to us many times and it actually does matter for smaller outlets and links are free. Let’s try them!

Artificial reef: TIL that a gigantic military ship, the SS United, is going to be purposefully sunk to be turned into an “artificial reef.” Scuba divers seem quite excited. I didn’t really know that this was a thing that was done, but maybe I’m a rube.

Now Kalshi is finding new ways to put a price on those predictions. This partnership between Kalshi and S&P Dow Jones Indices is fascinating.” C’mon, man.
