Today in yikes: A Roblox scraper has been grabbing more than a hundred gigabytes of data from a 3D modeling community, including more than 60 GB of adult content from a section of the site called “SmutBase.” “We don't think Roblox set out to collect adult content, and we have no evidence that any of it reached a model or a product. The scrapes were likely automated. But that is exactly the problem: as far as our logs show, nobody checked. A crawler working for a company whose platform tens of millions of children use was pointed at an adult site, and it took explicit models without telling them apart from anything else,” Open3DLabs wrote in a blog post about the scraping. “For a company being sued by several US states over child safety, ‘our AI team bulk-downloaded an adult site without looking’ is not a good position to be in.”
b65bd78dcb9b0242: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Earlier this month, Meta updated its commercial terms of use for business accounts to allow it to “use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta’s products.

Many artists and small business owners that rely on Instagram and Facebook are livid at Meta granting itself permission to use their content, including from websites simply connected to their Meta accounts, to train AI. But for users in the United Kingdom and European Union, for now, there’s a way to object.

Meta buried this change in its Commercial Terms, and Nieman Lab first reported on the change. The update was originally set to go into effect on October 30, but following backlash, Meta changed the effective date to November 20. Adding to the confusion, Meta then removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases, Nieman Lab reported, and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” where previously it said that data would be used for all Meta products. Those terms still allow Meta plenty of leeway for scraping users’ data to develop its products, however.

EU users’ personal data rights are governed by the General Data Protection Regulation and the AI Act. GDPR, which became enforceable in 2018, requires explicit consent to use personal data. This includes the right to object to one’s data being used. The AI Act, which went into effect in 2024, dictates how AI companies can use personal data, and how people can opt in or out, stating that they can withdraw consent at any time. The UK has its own version of the GDPR. The European Commission states: “The GDPR rules only apply to personal data about individuals; they do not govern data about companies or any other legal entities. However, information in relation to companies may constitute personal data where it allows the identification of a natural person.”

Several users based in the UK and EU have explained how to object on Instagram. Instagram user bookish.sil posted a walkthrough of how they did it on mobile: by clicking the three lines on their account, going to the privacy center, and clicking “object,” which goes to a form that asks users to write why they are objecting to their data being used. They received an email from Meta saying their objection was approved. Instagram user jenniqueart posted a similar walkthrough with the same results.

My Meta accounts are based in the US, but using a VPN to locate my IP address in London, I could see options in my Meta privacy settings that would let me object to the use of my information by Meta AI. To get there on desktop with a VPN on, I went to my account privacy center, clicked “Submit a privacy rights request” at the bottom, selected Instagram, clicked “How can I object to the processing of my information?” and got to a page where I could choose to object to the use of my information for Meta AI or third parties, which were two separate options.
When my location is based in the US, these options don't appear.

When I clicked through the option to “object to the use of my information for Meta AI,” however, it returned an error page that said “This form is only available to people in certain regions.” GDPR is meant to apply to wherever someone is located at the time, but since this objection applies to the preferences of one account, it might be based on where the account was created. I tried again located in Belgium and got the same results. I’ve asked Meta to clarify.

As many have already pointed out in the comments on UK and EU users who’ve posted walkthroughs, these objection steps aren’t available to people outside of those countries, and as Meta continuously changes its platform, these steps might not work for everyone always. Unless something changes before November 20, the rest of us are screwed.
ad8a7bfc37201941: Patients who think they're getting an annual checkup often end up with an unexpected bill. The Good Brigade/DigitalVision Collection via Getty ImagesI was teaching health economics when a student raised his hand. We were discussing the Affordable Care Act, or ACA, which requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services at no additional cost to patients. I explained that preventive care could cost nothing. The student had expected that, too. Instead, he said, he received a bill for more than US$500 after his checkup. He was so frustrated that he said he would never go back for another annual checkup. I suggested he contact his insurer to find out why he had been charged and whether his visit had been billed as preventive care. Then another student spoke up. Her husband had paid several hundred dollars for what he thought would be a free checkup too. The very next day, I received a $78 bill for my own Pap smear. I expected my insurance to cover this cervical cancer screening without cost-sharing because it is among the preventive services recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force and generally covered under the ACA. When I called my insurer, I learned that the visit had been billed as a regular outpatient office visit, with no mention of the Pap smear. I then called my primary care provider’s office. The clinic acknowledged a coding error and corrected it. My bill dropped to zero. As an assistant professor of health policy and addiction studies at Penn State Harrisburg, I know whom to call and what questions to ask when I receive an unexpected medical bill. Many of my graduate students worked full time and took evening classes. Would they know how to dispute a bill, or have time? Those experiences led me to investigate how often patients pay out of pocket for annual checkups. I teamed up with fellow researchers Erin Duffy and Max Crowley to examine this question. In our analysis of a Pennsylvania survey, nearly 1 in 4 insured respondents reported paying for their most recent checkup. Why a preventive visit may come with a bill Many health care services covered by insurance are subject to copayments or deductibles. A copayment is a fixed amount patients pay for a covered service, while a deductible is the amount they generally must pay for covered care before insurance starts paying. The ACA, however, requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services, including screenings for high blood pressure and certain cancers, vaccinations and counseling to help people quit smoking. These should come at no cost to patients. Generally, this applies when patients see providers who are in their insurance plan’s network. But that doesn’t mean every annual checkup is free. If a patient discusses a new symptom or asks the clinician to manage an existing condition during their annual checkup, it can result in a separate office-visit charge. A test may be billed as diagnostic rather than preventive, and coverage varies by plan and provider. Sometimes, as in my case, a coding error is responsible. Not every charge is inappropriate. The challenge is that patients often cannot tell which services should be covered, why they were billed, or whether a mistake occurred. What our survey found Previous studies have found, using insurance claims, that patients sometimes face out-of-pocket costs during preventive visits. But these records show how visits were billed, not necessarily what patients believed they were receiving. We wanted to know whether people who thought they were getting annual checkups also reported paying out of pocket. Our study, published in August 2026 in the peer-reviewed journal Prevention Science, used the 2024 Penn State Lion Poll, an online survey of Pennsylvania adults. We analyzed responses from 912 insured adults who reported an annual checkup within the preceding 10 years. Most had one in the past year. Of those respondents, 23.5% reported paying out of pocket for their most recent checkup. Among those who paid, the average reported out-of-pocket amount was $68.50. After accounting for other characteristics such as age, gender, insurance type, income and education, we found that respondents who were not familiar with ACA preventive-care protections were about 12 percentage points more likely to report paying than those who were familiar with the protections. That difference is equivalent to roughly 12 more people paying out of every 100. Those who considered healthcare unaffordable were about 13 percentage points more likely to pay than those who found it affordable. Because our survey relied on patients’ reports rather than billing records, we could not determine why individual charges occurred, or whether they were appropriate. The findings show associations, not causation, and our nonrandom sample cannot provide a precise statewide estimate. How doctor visits are billed doesn’t always match what service patients think they are receiving. adamkaz/E+ Collection via Getty Images Why these bills matter I kept thinking about the student who said he would never return for another checkup. Research has shown that even modest out-of-pocket costs can discourage people from getting recommended screenings. Delaying preventive care could mean missing opportunities to detect health problems early, when treatment may be more effective. Our survey did not find a statistically significant association between paying for a previous checkup and planning another one. However, respondents who were unfamiliar with ACA protections or considered healthcare unaffordable were less likely to plan a checkup. These findings suggest that uncertainty about costs may discourage people from seeking preventive care. What patients can do Before a visit, ask your insurer which preventive services are covered without cost-sharing and confirm that your provider is in-network. Ask the clinic whether discussing other health concerns or receiving additional tests could trigger a charge. If a bill arrives, compare it with your insurer’s explanation of benefits, which you can typically find in your online insurance account or receive by mail. Ask the provider’s billing office which services and codes were submitted and request a correction if something appears wrong. You can also contact your insurer to question or appeal a coverage decision. A colleague told me she challenged a $20 or $30 copayment requested at check-in for an annual visit after remembering our conversations. The charge was removed. Patients should not have to become experts in insurance billing to receive preventive care. Clearer coverage information and more transparent billing could help people seek care without fearing unexpected costs. 1084f4473e021767: Paying for childcare remains one of the biggest costs for households, often costing as much as housing. AP Photo/Craig MitchelldyerWhile affordability pressures are hitting Americans in many facets of their lives, from groceries to gas prices to housing costs, one important expense often gets less attention – childcare. After a huge infusion of federal funds into childcare dried up at the end of the Biden administration, experts warned that this sharp cutoff, sometimes dubbed the “childcare cliff,” would force parents to either scale back work to handle the extra caretaking or pay steep costs out of pocket. The potential effects of the federal cuts are hard to estimate, in part because states took different approaches in the aftermath. In some cases, they offset the sharp cuts in part by redirecting other funds to childcare. But several states, including Vermont, New Mexico and Kentucky, have gone further and innovated on their own to shore up support for working parents and their young children. Meanwhile, New York City is expanding free toddler slots for lower-income families, following Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s announcement to build a universal early childcare system. Taken together, these experiments point to bipartisan ways to support working parents, especially if the results of the November 2026 midterms signal a new willingness to tackle one of the biggest cost burdens for families. As researchers of sociology and childcare policy with six children from 1 to 16 years old between us, we have also gained insights from our own data gathered over 75 interviews with parents in St. Louis, Missouri, over the past few years. We see them struggling with a fragmented childcare system that’s in need of a deep strategic investment. These families face limited choices and soaring costs for an essential good that allows a parent to go to work. Out-of-pocket expenses for parents using center-based care in childcare centers and private preschool programs have more than doubled since 2019. In 2024, the national average price of childcare was US$13,128 annually, which rivals housing as the most expensive item in family budgets. States go their own way The disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic laid bare the critical role that reliable, high-quality childcare plays for working families. But we believe it also presented an opportunity for innovative investments in the nation’s fractured childcare landscape. Pandemic relief legislation in 2021 directed nearly $40 billion to shore up the supply and quality of childcare. This funding increase, which was a fourfold jump over previous levels, supported childcare staff with higher wages and allowed for other investments to improve the quality of care. The reach was vast, with stabilization funds flowing to 220,000 providers serving 9.6 million children. Many states also provided grants to create new slots and improve how providers got paid. As those funds began drying up in September 2023, some states started to address these shortfalls on their own. In some cases, they took significant steps at a policy level to channel more support to working parents. We believe these investments could serve as examples for the rest of the country. One is Vermont, which in 2023 became the first state to pass a law establishing a childcare entitlement. Following more than a decade of advocacy and bipartisan support, the law established a near-universal public childcare system, funded partially through a payroll tax of 0.44% split between employers and employees. Through an expansion of subsidies along income tiers, the number of families covered rose by 55% from July 2022 to May 2025, while flexible grants increased the number of providers and focused on improving the quality of care. About 12,000 children are now covered under this program. New Mexico went even further. In November 2025, the state became the first in the nation to offer universal childcare. Based on an older program that provided free childcare to low-income families, the initiative expanded support to all working parents regardless of income. Children draw at a daycare center in Albuquerque, N.M., which has gone further than any other state in expanding subsidies for working parents. AP Photo/Susan Montoya Bryan Before the expansion, 32,000 children were covered, a number the state aims to double by 2028. On average, the state estimates that the program will save families $12,000 a year. Meanwhile, the Kentucky legislature in April 2026 passed a measure with strong bipartisan support to make major investments in the state’s childcare infrastructure. Key provisions include free childcare for the children of childcare center employees, increased state-subsidized reimbursement rates, and required training to support very young special needs children. The Kentucky measure also loosened regulations that had made it tough for employers to share costs for care, such as renting facilities, while pitching a pilot program to open one-room “microcenters” in communities that lacked sufficient childcare options. In addition, Gov. Andy Beshear launched a complementary Pre-K for All pilot program in several counties. Another example is New York City, where Mamdani has announced an expansion for toddlers as young as 2 years old in all five of the city’s boroughs, building on the city’s programs for free childcare for 3-K and pre-K. To date, this effort has increased some slots, although the rollout in September hit bumps. The childcare crunch by the numbers Given the skyrocketing costs, over 70% of families who sought care say it’s difficult to find childcare – and that doesn’t count the 11% who fail to find any at all, according to a 2023 government survey. That report found that families with Black or Hispanic children or infants, and those living in the South and West, are more likely to run into cost as a barrier. On the supply side, three-quarters of providers say they have to turn many families away or put them on waiting lists. Center-based care for an infant costs more than in-state college tuition at a public university in 32 states, yet childcare workers, who are overwhelmingly women of color, earn the same as parking lot attendants and dog walkers. That makes them some of the lowest-paid workers in the entire economy. Amid soaring costs and scarce supply, roughly half of all U.S. families live in so-called childcare deserts – areas where there are three children under 5 for every licensed-care slot. The answer for many families in these cases is to rely on ad hoc and irregular informal care. Some parents told us they’re turning to relatives and neighbors for help. Others resorted to using unlicensed, and potentially unsafe, childcare providers because they found no other viable options. And for some remote workers, the daunting solution is to care for their kids themselves while working. The problem with such makeshift arrangements is that they tend, on average, to offer fewer of the learning opportunities linked to children’s long-term development and social mobility. And even these arrangements can be tough to afford: One single mother we interviewed told us she paid for a week’s childcare in kind with her own breast milk, which went to feed the care provider’s grandchildren. We also spoke to parents who reported choosing between childcare bills and heat, electricity or rent. Another mom told us about a more unconventional solution. She and her husband work full time but can’t afford the childcare options in their community, so she decided to join a gym that provides free childcare while its members exercise. She brings her laptop and works, rather than working out, while her toddler plays. These parents are scraping by in the absence of the affordable, subsidized childcare options commonplace in other countries. But this crunch is also a lose-lose proposition for the economy. The U.S. could lose as much as $290 billion per year by 2030 in forgone economic activity due to women not working or not working as much due to childcare pressures, according to the consultancy BCG. A path forward The Trump administration has laid out its own vision. Vice President JD Vance announced in September 2026 a preliminary proposal to repurpose existing funds for childcare subsidies as a cash transfer to married parents, provided that one spouse stays home. We believe, however, this approach fails to reflect the real needs of the millions of U.S. parents who can’t pay their bills if they only get one paycheck. In fact, under the subsidy program that Vance cited, only 16% of eligible children are reached today anyway. We believe, based on our research, that any comprehensive overhaul has four important components. First is a robust national policy for paid family leave, which would let families make the best care decisions for newborns, infants and parents themselves rather than sprinting back to work. Paid family leave would also ease demand for scarce infant care in the market. Second is an expansion of early childhood care and education programs. By publicly subsidizing childcare, particularly for low-income families and special needs kids, policymakers can help close the affordability gap for high-quality care. Third is a greater investment in childcare workers. Qualified caregivers are the cornerstone of high-quality childcare. If their wages and working conditions improve, it means fewer will have to take side hustles or quit for better jobs. Finally, providers will need more incentives to open in underserved areas. Childcare is expensive to provide and runs on thin margins. In low-income and rural areas, many families can’t pay prices that cover the true cost of care, and subsidy payments are often set below that cost. So opening a center there doesn’t make much financial sense. Startup grants, higher subsidy rates and operating support help close that gap, which makes it possible to open and stay open where need is greatest. 04f101fb6f68cf59: If you're going with a lower-cost health insurance plan, make sure to read the fine print. Pla2na/iStock via Getty Images PlusHealthcare costs are a major concern for Americans, and health insurance premiums are a primary fuel for that anxiety. Shrinking federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans led to large premium increases for millions of Americans in 2025, causing many people to drop coverage. With premiums expected to rise further and Medicaid work requirements set to begin in January 2027, many Americans are left scrambling for affordable options. We are health economists who study public policies aimed at expanding health insurance coverage. When it comes to our own health insurance, we are fortunate: We are among the roughly 160 million Americans who receive coverage through their employers. But if you don’t work for a large employer that provides health benefits, finding coverage for your family can be confusing and, increasingly, expensive. People looking for low-cost alternatives have no doubt encountered several options. They may look appealing and, in some cases, may be appropriate, but they can also carry real risks. Navigating trade-offs Historically, people who didn’t have access to employer-sponsored coverage had limited health insurance options. Before the Affordable Care Act went into effect in 2014, insurers could charge you a higher premium based on your health status, exclude coverage for preexisting medical conditions, or deny you coverage altogether. The ACA eliminated this kind of discrimination, established a minimum standard of 10 essential benefits that health insurance plans had to cover, and required plans to fully cover the cost of preventive care. It also introduced income-based subsidies that could be used to purchase coverage in newly established online marketplaces. Americans who are not insured through an employer-sponsored plan must find coverage through sources like the ACA marketplaces. mixetto/E+ via Getty Images Low-cost plans that aren’t available through ACA marketplaces are essentially vestiges of the pre-ACA health insurance landscape. Regardless of where you get coverage, choosing health insurance involves trade-offs. The more you pay in premiums, the more comprehensive your coverage will be in terms of how much you must pay when you need care and the breadth of the network of covered providers. Some trade-offs are clear when you choose a plan, but some lower-cost options may have limitations that are not immediately obvious. Less costly short-term plans As their name suggests, short-term, limited-duration plans are designed for people with temporary gaps in coverage, such as those who are between jobs or months away from qualifying for Medicare. These plans, which can be purchased for periods of up to six months, tend to be cheaper than marketplace coverage for two reasons. First, because they are not subject to ACA rules, they may not provide the full range of essential health benefits. Short-term, limited-duration plans often do not cover maternity care and commonly don’t have an annual limit on out-of-pocket costs. In fact, these plans may cap how much they will pay in a year, leaving policyholders stuck with large, unexpected expenses. Second, unlike plans offered through the ACA marketplaces, short-term, limited-duration plans are allowed to deny coverage based on your health status. Screening out higher-cost consumers reduces premiums, but if you are not in perfect health, you may not be able to find an insurer that will sell you one of these more limited plans. Because of a concern that they destabilize the market by siphoning off healthy consumers, short-term, limited-duration plans are banned in five states. Alternatives that look like insurance Another seemingly affordable option is healthcare sharing ministries, arrangements through which consumers with common religious beliefs agree to share medical expenses. Their websites resemble those of health insurance companies – for example, they often present different plan options offering different levels of benefits – but they avoid using standard insurance terms like “premium” or “deductible” because these offerings are not insurance. Because they are not regulated as insurance companies, healthcare sharing ministries are not subject to consumer protections or other state or federal requirements. There is also no guarantee that the ministry will cover your medical expenses when you submit a claim. Like short-term, limited-duration plans, healthcare sharing ministries may deny coverage based on your health history, exclude coverage for preexisting conditions and put a limit on the dollar amount they will pay in benefits. Another lower-cost option available in 14 states is health coverage offered by a farm bureau. These plans are similar to healthcare sharing ministries in that they are limited to a certain group of people – to enroll, you must be a member of the state’s farm bureau, though that does not mean you necessarily have to work in agriculture. These plans are also not subject to federal or state insurance regulations. This means that, like short-term, limited-duration plans, they can offer lower prices by not offering certain benefits required by the ACA and by screening out high-cost consumers. Unlike short-term, limited-duration plans, there is no limit on how long you can hold farm bureau coverage. Choosing a health insurance plan often requires fighting through a thicket of jargon. What should you do? Although the cost of marketplace coverage has increased dramatically since 2025, for many consumers who need coverage for more than six months, it remains the best option. If you are single with an annual income below US$64,000, a couple with an annual income below $87,000, or a family of four with an annual income less than $132,000, you should still be eligible for a premium subsidy. And you will know that the plan you are purchasing is real insurance that covers a standard set of benefits and is subject to robust consumer protections. If you are considering an alternative to marketplace coverage, there are a few things you should do to protect yourself: Make sure you ask for a summary of benefits and coverage. This is a plain language summary of a health plan’s benefits and coverage with examples of how much the plan would cover for two specific conditions – diabetes and childbirth. Insurers and employers who offer coverage are required to provide this document to anyone applying for coverage. If they cannot provide one, what they are selling may not actually be insurance. If they do provide a summary of benefits and coverage, read it carefully. As we noted earlier, one reason some options might be less expensive than a marketplace plan is that they provide much less coverage. Don’t assume that they cover all the benefits you would expect from a health insurance plan, or that they will cover the full cost of the care you receive. Finally, never enter your phone number into a “do you need insurance” website. This area is rife with fraud, including multiple cases in which telemarketers misled consumers into paying hundreds of dollars per month to purchase sham health insurance. Health insurance is expensive because healthcare is expensive – which means that consumers have to make difficult trade-offs. There is no easy answer, but beware of options that look too good to be true. They very well might be. Thomas Buchmueller is a Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. 119cf39f6711bef0: Many of the stores where people use SNAP benefits are small. O2O Creative/E+ via Getty ImagesAfter 10 states began to add new restrictions to what people could buy with Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits in early 2026, the number of convenience stores authorized to accept those benefits was 1.4% lower than would be expected based on trends in states without the policy change. That’s what we found in our study, published in October 2026 in Health Affairs Scholar – a peer-reviewed journal. SNAP, a federally funded program administered by the states, helps about 36 million low-income Americans afford groceries with government benefits that can be used at more than 250,000 stores to buy fresh fruit, ground beef, canned beans and other groceries. Using the benefits for many items, including hot food, alcohol, toiletries and pet food, has long been prohibited. States can now obtain federal waivers to prohibit SNAP benefits from being used to buy other products. The 10 states with waivers that we studied had a mix of rules. Some only barred the sale of soda and other sugary drinks. Other prohibitions applied to energy drinks, candy, cake and other prepared desserts. In states like Oklahoma and Florida that have adopted these new SNAP restrictions to discourage unhealthy diets, the number of convenience stores participating in the program has fallen relative to other states that haven’t made these changes. That was especially notable in areas with high numbers of low-income people where a large share of the population gets SNAP benefits. We analyzed the number of stores participating in SNAP from January 2025 through June 2026 for the 10 states. We compared changes to that number before and after the waivers took effect with what happened in the rest of the country. We found no clear evidence that the number of supermarkets or superstores was declining in waiver states. Although it’s slightly lower than otherwise expected, this effect is not statistically significant. Because the restrictions vary, we also investigated whether the type mattered: sugary drinks only, or sugary drinks plus other products that state officials wanted to discourage. We found the largest declines in the number of SNAP-authorized convenience stores in states restricting both drinks and candy: an average of 2.2%. Why it matters Stores in waiver states may need to update their checkout systems and train employees to prevent purchases that are no longer allowed with SNAP benefits – potentially a time-consuming burden for some retailers. That may help explain why the number of SNAP-authorized convenience stores is declining. Although most people use SNAP benefits to buy food at big stores, they also purchase some groceries at convenience stores, especially in neighborhoods where there are few supermarkets. Other federal policies are also changing how SNAP works due to provisions in the big tax and policy legislation that Congress passed in July 2025. It changed some eligibility rules and how much states pay to administer the program. Even before all those changes take effect, many people who are likely eligible for SNAP benefits are having a harder time getting them, due to the steps states are taking to prepare for the new rules. The number of Americans enrolled in the program is falling fast despite no sign that their needs are shrinking. What still isn’t known We focused on changes to the number of stores authorized to accept SNAP in states with waivers. We didn’t study whether stores closed, or exactly why stores left the program. We also don’t know what role court rulings will play. On June 22, near the end of our study, a federal court invalidated SNAP food restrictions in five states: Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee and West Virginia. Waiver programs in other states – Indiana, Utah, Idaho, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Texas and Florida – were allowed to continue. Four states had similar restrictions in the works: South Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio and Virginia. Those plans are on hold. Beginning in November 2026, most U.S. stores will also have to meet new requirements of a different kind to participate in SNAP. They’ll need to stock a wider variety of staple foods, such as grains, dairy products and produce. These requirements could pose additional challenges for convenience stores. Further research is needed to see if the effects we found change over time, including in states that introduce these restrictions after the period we studied. b6cda9ccbb3e6f68: State surveillance and policing of online expression have a long history in the country
Originally published on Global Voices
Photo by cottonbro studio. Used under a Pexels License.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Bangladesh is revising its cyber law to tackle AI-generated images, and the draft has triggered a furious debate over how much the state should police speech online. The ICT Division published the draft Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act for public comment in mid-September. It is now with a five-member cabinet committee led by Posts, Telecommunications and ICT Minister Faqir Mahbub Anam. In a discussion reported on October 19, media figures, legal analysts, and civil society representatives called for the most contested clauses to be removed.

The push follows a campaign season crowded with synthetic media. Global Voices previously reported on a study that identified 72 AI-manipulated items that gained traction between December 2025 and the February 12, 2026 election. Synthetic images of political figures were the most common tactic, alongside doctored news-channel graphics. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), which went on to win, was the most frequent target, with 47 cases.

State surveillance and policing of online expression have a long history. Section 57 of the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Act of 2006 punished online content seen as defamatory, hurtful to religious sentiment, or damaging to the state’s image. A 2013 amendment toughened it, with sentences of up to 14 years. Journalists and ordinary social media users were among those charged under it. After years of protest, the government promised to scrap Section 57. Yet when the Digital Security Act (DSA) was signed into law in October 2018, the same offenses reappeared in sections 25, 28, 29 and 31. By 2023, the law minister had told parliament that 7,001 cases had been filed under it. The writer Mushtaq Ahmed died in custody in 2021 after ten months in jail under the DSA, which led to protests at home and abroad.

The Awami League government replaced the DSA with the Cyber Security Act in 2023, but Amnesty International said it repackaged almost all of the DSA’s repressive features. After the July 2024 uprising, the interim government scrapped nine sections through a new Cyber Security Ordinance in 2025. Rights groups say hundreds of cases from earlier years are still pending.
Fakes in the election and beyond

Women in politics faced a particular kind of attack. A Daily Star analysis of AI content before the vote found that pro-Awami League pages targeted female leaders of the National Citizen Party (NCP) with fabricated images that hinted at moral and sexual impropriety. After the election, a Prothom Alo fact-check found AI-generated images and invented statements aimed at nominees for reserved women's seats. Tanvir Mahatab Abir of Rumor Scanner told the paper that visible women, especially in politics, are frequent targets of disinformation.

Not all of it is political. Data from the Daily Star shows that Facebook pages used deepfake videos of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and his family, including his daughter Zaima Rahman, to promote fake “Family Card” offers in exchange for likes and follows. Among 52 posts analyzed, 13 featured Zaima. One page administrator told the fact-checking outlet Dismislab that the aim was to gain followers quickly and sell the pages. In such cases, for many creators of synthetic content, monetization metrics on social platforms often serve as a primary driver alongside political motives.
A case that left no remedy

For ordinary women, the damage can last much longer. Farzana Sithi, a student activist known for her role in the historic student-led uprising in 2024, was targeted by a fake Facebook profile that Dismislab investigated in March 2025. Of 166 videos and reels posted between December 13, 2024, and March 17, 2025, 133 were AI-generated deepfakes. They placed her face on videos of two Indian content creators. The five most-viewed clips drew more than 4.1 million views, and the account was monetized through Facebook's Stars feature.

“These videos are an attempt to tarnish my character,” Sithi told Dismislab, adding that she was bullied and shamed as a result. She reported the profile to Facebook several times. IT experts she approached privately asked for USD 100 to USD 150 to remove the fake accounts and videos, which she said she could not afford. At the time of Dismislab’s report, the profile was still active. Comments under the reels included rape threats.
What the law covers, and what the draft would change

Legal experts point out that the existing legislative framework has struggled to keep pace with rapid advancements in synthetic media. The Cyber Protection Act was enacted on 10 April 2026 and amended on 30 June. Its Section 25 already covers blackmail, sexual harassment, revenge porn, child sexual abuse material, sextortion and the distribution of AI-generated or manipulated content.

According to the minister, these offenses carry up to two years in prison, or up to five if the victim is a woman or under 18. The law targets AI mainly when it is used to commit existing crimes. It does not set out a dedicated framework for synthetic media or political deepfakes.

The draft would change that. It adds defamation, humiliation and bullying to Section 25 and names AI-generated content explicitly. A prior investigation by Prothom Alo revealed that the maximum penalty would rise to five years in prison and a BDT 2 million fine (roughly USD 16,131), and to ten years and Tk 4 million if the target is a woman or a person under 18. A new Section 26A would punish publishing or spreading a “rumor” or “disinformation” with up to ten years in prison, a fine of BDT 4 million (roughly USD 32,262), or both. The draft defines a rumor as unverified information that causes or risks causing confusion, panic or social instability.

The government presents the changes as a response to harm already being done. Introducing an earlier amendment in June, the ICT minister said it would require platforms such as Meta to remove disputed content within a set time. Officials told Prothom Alo that the tougher penalties are meant to curb fake videos, audio and images made with AI.
Free speech concerns

Critics say the draft goes well beyond that aim. Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) warned that terms such as “rumor” and “demeaning” are defined loosely enough to allow selective enforcement. A joint statement by rights groups said the draft mirrors the repealed Digital Security Act. The Committee to Protect Journalists has objected to the prospect of journalists facing criminal liability for reporting officials consider unverified. An Asia Times analysis noted that because defamation sits inside Section 25, the heavier penalty for offenses against women would apply to it as well, and not only to sexual abuse.
Numbers, gaps and local responses

What the law would address is substantial. A report by Dhaka Tribune said police's Cyber Support for Women unit had been approached by 60,808 women by September 2024, and cited a 2024 Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics–UNFPA survey in which nearly 89 percent of women social media users reported online violence at least once. Officials say the real number is likely higher because of underreporting. The published figures do not separate cases involving AI.

Researchers describe a similar pattern across the region. A study in the Journal of Online Trust and Safety drew on three workshops with 49 journalists, lawyers, fact-checkers and advocates in Sri Lanka, India and Bangladesh. It found that women are disproportionately targeted, that platform moderation often fails in South Asian languages, and that victims struggle to reach institutional help. Sithi's (a student activist known for her role in the historic student-led uprising in 2024) experience, where the cost of private help was out of reach, fits that last finding.

Digital skills are an added concern. The Asian Development Bank reports that functional digital literacy in Bangladesh stands at 49 percent and that rural users are 29 percent less likely than urban users to use mobile internet. Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics data released in April show that 56.6 percent of men use the internet, against 50.2 percent of women. Advocates argue that people with fewer digital skills may find it harder to spot manipulated media or seek redress. These surveys, however, do not measure exposure to deepfakes directly.

Outside the government, fact-checkers are trying to keep pace. FactFest 2026, held on 27–28 September, brought together around 100 fact-checkers, journalists and researchers, according to an organizer. Its 13 sessions covered AI and gendered disinformation, among other topics. In the closing roundtable, speakers said Bangladeshi fact-checkers face shrinking funding and weak coordination with mainstream newsrooms.

The cabinet committee has yet to finalize the draft, which would then go to Parliament. Constitution Watchdog, a civil society group, has urged the government to withdraw the draft in its present form and reopen public consultation for at least 30 days. It also acknowledged the government's stated aim of protecting women and children from online abuse and responding to deepfakes. Whether a narrower law can do that without the speech provisions now under attack is the question facing lawmakers.

9e57b3c7cb0d7eb2: The crack of a bat accompanied by a roar from the crowd can capture a baseball fan’s attention, even if they miss seeing the home run. Humans may be visual creatures, but we also perceive the world around us by listening to it.  To improve artificial perception, MIT Professor Paris Smaragdis SM ’97, PhD ’01 seeks to make machines that can hear and understand sound even better than humans. A machine with super-human hearing could rapidly pinpoint the location of a traffic accident by listening for squealing tires and crunching metal, or identify when an industrial drill might break while it is boring through dense bedrock to dig a geothermal well. “I like to say that I do the same thing the computer vision folks do, but instead I do it for hearing,” says Smaragdis, a professor in the Music and Theatre Arts program of the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. His research group explores areas like machine learning for sound source separation, smart devices that can augment the audio surroundings of humans, and better tools to help people understand, manipulate, analyze, and create music. “Having had a musical background, I’ve been interested in examining these ideas. What does it take to make machines understand sound? There is a huge domain of applications for machines that can listen,” says Smaragdis, who joined MIT in 2025 and is also part of the Music Technology program and a member of the Research Laboratory of Electronics. A musical prelude Smaragdis, who grew up in Greece, began playing classical guitar at a young age. He enjoyed playing traditional pieces but reached a turning point in his musical journey when his father brought home a small synthesizer. “That little synthesizer had a function that allowed you to make your own sounds, and I became completely captivated by the possibilities,” he says. Synthesizers were taking a more prominent place in pop music during the 1980s, adding to his fascination with the technology. As he advanced through school, Smaragdis wanted to study music made with synthesizers. But this was not an educational path offered by the more traditional European conservatories at the time. Instead, he enrolled at Berklee College of Music in Boston, into a program where he could explore the use of computers and synthesizers to shape and manipulate sound. “With computers and synthesizers, I could make new sounds that have never been heard before,” he says. At the same time, Smaragdis became immersed in jazz fusion. He declared bass as his major at Berklee since it would allow him more opportunities to play with jazz ensembles. “I found the bass to be sonically more interesting than the guitar. It was a more unexplored domain, and I’ve always gravitated toward unexplored domains,” he says. That interest in the unexplored carried over into his coursework. He and mentor Richard Boulanger, a professor of electronic production and design, created new tools to help people use computers to write, produce, and enhance music.  Through his studies at Berklee, Smaragdis embarked on a collaborative project with Professor Barry Vercoe (who passed away in 2025) at the MIT Media Lab to create software synthesizers for music creation. Building on that project, Smaragdis pursued graduate studies in Vercoe’s group, where he completed his master’s degree and PhD, followed by a postdoc. “In the Media Lab, I got exposed more to the computer part of computer music. That’s where my attention shifted a bit. Now I really wanted to make computers that could understand sound,” he says. Tuning in to unexplored domains At that time, many students in the Media Lab were using signal processing techniques to help machines handle sound. Smaragdis chose a less explored approach — machine learning — to separate himself from the pack. He found that training machine-learning models to understand sound offered advantages that couldn’t be attained with traditional signal processing techniques. “Over time, it became really clear to me that we need to teach computers how to listen. We can’t just tell them how to listen. If anything, we don’t even know how we humans listen,” he says. “We don’t have a vocabulary to explain what it means to listen, or how to tell the difference between a cat’s meow and the sound of a violin.” After finishing his postdoc, Smaragdis began a career at Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs, where he worked on artificial intelligence systems that could scan video soundtracks and understand what is happening on screen.  “What if you record an entire soccer game, but you only want to watch the highlights? In computer vision, it is very difficult to identify what a highlight is. But on the other hand, if you only listen to the sounds, then when the crowd goes crazy you would know that something interesting is happening,” he says. That system was eventually incorporated into electronic devices, including a personal video recording system Mitsubishi was developing at the time, and into traffic monitoring systems and cell phones. Smaragdis later joined Adobe, where he created the audio research team that built user-friendly tools to help artists, musicians, and producers manipulate sound without needing a lot of expertise. “As we did that work, I kept coming up with deeper technical problems that needed to be resolved. I jumped into academia to address that itch,” he says. Smaragdis joined the faculty at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where he and his group incorporated the latest machine-learning techniques into audio-processing systems. One of the technologies they developed utilized neural networks for separating individual sounds from audio mixtures. That project caught the attention of the team working on the 2021 documentary mini-series “The Beatles: Get Back.” The production team enlisted Smaragdis to help clean up some archival Beatles recordings. “That was a very different way of audio processing than what I was doing in academia. Now, I had to do something that sounded good but didn’t necessarily have to look good on paper. We didn’t have a formula we could optimize,” he says. Every recording involved different challenges. For instance, in one clip John Lennon was playing music while Paul McCartney was horsing around, reading headlines from newspapers and making fun of George Harrison. “We were trying to come up with a technological solution that could help us do everything, as opposed to addressing each problem on its own,” he says. His contributions helped the team win an Emmy Award for sound editing for a nonfiction or reality program, in 2022. A concerted effort After 15 years at the University of Illinois, Smaragdis decided to join the faculty at MIT to tackle the thorny, interdisciplinary problems that were emerging in the field.  His group now focuses on two main areas. For one, they develop systems that make computers more useful tools for musicians.  One project in this area is enabling machines to understand how to listen to music, so they can provide constructive feedback to musicians. “We want to enhance the toolbox a musician has. We don’t want to use computers to replace musicians,” he says. On the other side, his group focuses on the fundamental tools scientists and artists alike can use to process, analyze, and manipulate audio. For instance, his team has recently been exploring algorithms that allow sophisticated signal processing where traditional frames of reference, such as sampling rates, frame sizes, or context-windows, are not fixed — or even defined.  That implies different computational structures that are yet unexplored, despite their potential for more efficient processing, Smaragdis says. “That requires rethinking a lot of the basics, but once you have that ability, you can start getting much more flexible and more powerful systems,” he adds. They also explore ways to incorporate the latest techniques, like large language models, into speech recognition and audio enhancement. “AI is an immensely powerful tool, but I don’t think we have found the ideal way to use it for sound and music yet,” he says. He also enjoys mentoring students and helping them materialize their visions for research projects. Since few of his students have experience using computation in sound, he emphasizes hands-on lessons so they see and hear how to transform equations into something tangible. Smaragdis still feels a thrill from making music, whether with a computer or a more traditional instrument. Off campus, he tries to play jazz bass whenever he can find the time, and enjoys exploring the rich musical community of Boston with his wife and 15-year-old son. Outside the musical realm, he plays and coaches underwater hockey — a sport where players wear diving masks and use sticks to push a heavy puck across the bottom of a pool toward their opponent’s goal. He coached the underwater hockey team at the University of Illinois, and is hoping to revive the MIT underwater hockey club soon and start hosting tournaments on campus. While underwater hockey may be a lesser-known sport, it fits with Smaragdis’ lifelong interest in pursuing the underexplored. “I’ve always like doing things that were different from what everyone else was doing. If you can create a new sound that no one has heard before, what does that mean about your ability to create new things? I still find these questions completely fascinating,” he says.
6f20fa3677e84710: From Cheli Tamilselvam Nadarajah
A school should be a place where children feel safe, friendships flourish, differences are respected, and every child knows that someone cares.
It should be a place where teachers inspire, parents trust, and children grow not only in knowledge but also in character.
Yet we read about tragic incidents of violence, bullying and the loss of young lives in our schools.
Could these tragedies have been prevented? Were there red flags? Did these children have someone to turn to?
Time to act
As an educator, I believe that a school’s greatest achievement is not simply excellent examination results, but the kind of human beings it nurtures.
What does academic excellence mean if a child is afraid to attend school, humiliated by classmates, or feels invisible within its walls?

I have had parents standing before me with tears in their eyes, asking for just one thing: that their children grow up to be good people. Their plea has stayed with me. Every child deserves an excellent education in a safe, caring and supportive environment.
Bullying is not merely a disciplinary issue that children will eventually outgrow. It can damage confidence, emotional wellbeing and a child’s sense of belonging.
While those who bully others must be held accountable, punishment alone may not change the attitudes and beliefs behind their behaviour.
We cannot condemn our children for displaying behaviours that we, as adults, have modelled, tolerated or failed to challenge.
We must protect victims, support affected children, address harmful behaviour and help every child learn responsibility, empathy and respect.
This requires more than occasional motivational talks or campaigns launched after a tragedy. It requires a sustained transformation of our school culture.
A lesson from SMK Bandar Kuching No 1

In 2006, while serving at SMK Bandar Kuching No 1 in Sarawak, I introduced the Attitude Breakthrough Challenge (ABC) to demonstrate that positive attitudes can be developed, and character strengthened through consistent practice and shared responsibility.
The initiative went beyond punishing misconduct.
It sought to empower teachers, engage parents and encourage students to take ownership of their behaviour. Students were encouraged to support one another in making better choices.
The aim was not to shame children or make them police their peers, but to build a community where positive behaviour was valued and everyone had a part to play.

Its key elements included peer accountability, teacher empowerment and parental engagement, supported by a structured system of merit and demerit codes, focusing more on the recognition of positive behaviour, and graduated responses to misconduct.

Student suspension cases recorded by the education ministry (MoE) fell from 136 in 2005 to fewer than 40 in 2006, followed by 16 in 2007, fewer than 10 in 2008, eight in 2009, six in 2010 and three in 2011.
For me, the greatest lesson was this: Negative behaviour need not be accepted as inevitable.
When teachers are empowered, parents are involved, students are accountable and positive behaviour is recognised, meaningful change becomes possible.
Making positive attitudes a way of life
The ABC, now rebranded as Positive Attitude Builds Character (PABC), must be more than a short-term programme or a slogan on a school wall; it must become a way of life.
Children need opportunities to practise positive values, supported by adults who model them and systems that reinforce them consistently.

While PABC is not a magic solution to every school safety challenge, its principles and practical experiences offer valuable lessons for a comprehensive approach to prevention, accountability, character development and student wellbeing.

We must distinguish between holding children accountable and labelling them as failures. Children who make mistakes need appropriate consequences, guidance and opportunities to change, while victims must be protected and serious misconduct addressed promptly.

A positive school culture does not happen by accident. It requires committed leadership, empowered teachers, engaged parents, responsible students and effective systems to identify problems early, monitor concerns and ensure timely follow-up.
A safe school is not one where no complaints are made. It is one where children feel safe enough to speak up and trust that adults will act.
I appeal to the MoE, school heads, parents and communities to make safe, happy and inclusive schools a national priority.
When a child feels safe, valued and happy at school, learning becomes more meaningful, relationships flourish, and every child has a greater opportunity to thrive.

Let us make the main thing the main thing: the wellbeing, character and future of our children. Amid the many demands, distractions and competing priorities that bombard us daily, we must never lose sight of what matters most.
Every child must know that someone cares
After more than four decades in education, I remain passionate about the potential of every child.

I believe in the teacher who encourages a struggling student, the school head who refuses to ignore a problem, the parent who sacrifices for a child’s future, and the child who can grow into a responsible and caring person when given the right guidance and support.

Children should not have to remember school as a place where they were afraid. They must remember it as a place where they discovered their abilities, built friendships, learnt to respect others and found adults who believed in them.
Teachers should not feel that they must fight these battles alone. They deserve to feel empowered, supported and valued.
We may not be able to prevent every difficulty a child faces in life, but we can do far more to ensure that school is never a place where a child has to live in fear.
Our children deserve better. They deserve schools that are safe, happy, caring and inclusive. The time to act is now.
Cheli Tamilselvam Nadarajah is a fomer school principal and an FMT reader.

a3c1ecdc3562be0b: Sultan Selangor yang menyambut jubli perak pemerintahannya tahun ini ada mesej tajam kepada golongan pembakar sentimen perkauman yang melihat diri sendiri sebagai wira sesuatu bangsa .
Sultan Sharafuddin Idris Shah dengan lantang menegur golongan itu - hentikan eksploitasi bangsa dan agama untuk mendapat keuntungan politik dan jangan mengheret istana ke dalam pertikaian mereka.

Titah baginda datang ketika arena politik Malaysia dicengkam permainan sentimen ras dan agama dimana hak Melayu, identiti Islam dan kedudukan masyarakat bukan Melayu berulang kali diketengahkan, secara negatif.

Lihat sahaja PRN Johor dan Negeri Sembilan yang diadakan tahun ini. Sentimen perkauman ditiup dan dibakar. Ferociously – to a level never seen before. Selain dua PRN itu, hampir semua perkara dijadikan isu bangsa dan agama di merata tempat. Politik perkauman (atau kata sesetengah orang politik identiti) dimainkan sewenang-wenangnya.

Daripada kempen pilihan raya, dibawa ke perdebatan di Parlimen, menembusi platform media sosial naratif politik berkisar tentang siapa yang konon akan kerugian, kehilangan hak, diancam dan terancam serta siapa yang benar-benar wira mempertahankan bangsa dan agama tertentu.
Retorik politikus mencetuskan naratif perkauman melampau dalam kalangan warganet yang merupakan ‘rakyat biasa’ dan pastinya golongan yang digelar atau mahu dianggap ‘laskar siber’.
Kata kolumnis politik, Lim Hong Siang, negara berada dalam situasi kebangkitan kumpulan sayap kanan ekstrem yang mengancam realiti kepelbagaian dan kebebasan.

Pada 15 Okt lalu, Ahli Parlimen Puncak Borneo Willie Mongin berkongsi maklumat di Dewan Rakyat seorang guru baru-baru ini memberitahunya, ada dalam kalangan anak sekolah yang tidak mahu duduk sebelah rakan sekelas bukan sebangsa dan seagama dengan mereka.

Daripada mana atau daripada siapa anak-anak ‘belajar’ tabiat tidak baik begitu? Kemungkinan besar daripada ibu bapa yang termakan kata-kata berbaur perkauman sang politikus dan dakyah negatif dimainkan di media sosial.

Mongin tidak beritahu di mana sekolah perkara itu berlaku. Bagi saya jika ia berlaku di Borneo yang terkenal dengan muhibah dan toleransi antara kaumnya, saya tidak terkejut jika itu juga ada berlaku di Semenanjung.
Semua ini mengancam perpaduan rakyat – merenggang hubungan antara kaum. Ramai pandai menyakiti dan ramai pula yang disakiti.
Dengan PRN Melaka pula akan diadakan tidak lama lagi pasti atau hampir pasti taktik eksploitasi ras dan agama akan diulangi politikus sebagai jalan pintas untuk mendapat kemenangan di peti undi.
Sememangnya memperalatkan isu bangsa dan agama mudah menarik perhatian dan sekali gus mendapat sokongan.

Lantas teguran Sultan Sharafuddin tepat pada masanya. Baginda tidak menamakan sesiapa. Namun, kita tahu siapa yang dimaksudkan. Kita tahu siapa penggemar permainan politik perkauman. No prizes for guessing.
The Sultan’s patience is wearing thin. “Seperti rakyat, beta juga bosan,” titah Sultan Sharafuddin yang dilapor Malaysiakini, Isnin lalu.

Baginda menyeru semua ahli politik Selangor memberi fokus terhadap serving the people, perkhidmatan baik untuk rakyat, menjana pertumbuhan ekonomi dan memastikan perpaduan yang terjalin dalam kalangan rakyat terus dipupuk dan dijaga .

Demi memastikan Selangor maintains it’s leading position in the country. Titah baginda kekuatan Selangor ialah pada rakyatnya. “Kita dianugerah masyarakat berbilang bangsa, kebudayaan dan agama yang generasi ke generasi telah hidup dan bekerja bersama dalam harmoni mencapai kemakmuran.”

Titah baginda, sememangnya boleh dirujuk atau diguna pakai untuk seluruh Malaysia bukan sahaja Selangor. Dan saranan Sultan Sharafuddin kepada ahli politik memang boleh dituju kepada semua ahli politik di semua negeri. Politikus pemain politik perkauman are everywhere in the country.

Sebenarnya, memang raja Melayu lain juga seperti Sultan Sharufuddin mahu permainan politik perkauman dinyahkan. Kita pernah dengar saranan, teguran serta nasihat mereka. Cuma politikus degil tetap degil. Yang gemar main sentimen ras untuk kemenangan pilihan raya meneruskan kegemaran mereka. Tanpa hirau nasihat raja tanpa menghiraukan kesejahteraan rakyat dan negeri masing-masing dan juga negara.

Sehingga kini, seperti Sultan Selangor, raja-raja tidak atau belum namakan sesiapa. Namun, mungkin akan tiba masa Sultan Selangor dan raja-raja lain akan menamakan politikus yang terus-menerus jadikan bangsa dan agama isu untuk dapat manfaat peti undi konon atas nama bangsa dan agama.
Mungkin akan tiba masa raja-raja mendedahkan identiti mereka kepada rakyat meskipun rakyat tahu siapa mereka .

Ini tidak mustahil berlaku, kerana bak titah Sultan Sharafuddin yang dinyatakan tadi baginda sudah bosan dengan gelagat politikus meniup sentimen perkauman. Saya yakin the other rulers are equally fed up. Their patience are also wearing thin.

394a6f85314f6ac9: From Boo Jia Cher
Recently, a friend shared a photo on social media celebrating the return of blue skies and air quality readings returning to "good" after weeks of haze.
At first glance, the photo felt uplifting. The sky was clear and cloudless.
But what caught my attention was what sat directly beneath it: a vast expanse of low-density suburbia sliced apart by a ten-lane highway packed with traffic.
In a single frame, it captured a contradiction that has become so normalised. We see the blue sky and conclude the air is clean. We see the “good” rating and assume the danger has passed.

While seasonal forest fires trigger nationwide concern and frustration, our most persistent source of harmful air pollution is not drifting in from afar. It is idling outside school gates, flowing along suburban roads, and passing us every day on highways just like the one in that photograph.

Vehicle emissions account for up to 70% of urban air pollution. Yet because we cannot easily see them, we rarely treat them with the same urgency. One of the most significant threats to public health remains hidden in plain sight.
Pollution we fear, pollution we accept

When haze hits, we pull children indoors, stock up on N95 masks, and worry about long-term health damage. Yet year-round, invisible tailpipe pollution exposes us to microscopic particulates, nitrogen dioxide, and ground-level ozone.
These pollutants penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream. They are linked to asthma, impaired lung development, cardiovascular disease, stroke and dementia.
Because these harms accumulate slowly rather than announcing themselves with burning eyes or irritated throats, we often treat them as an unavoidable part of modern life.
Children at the front line
Consider the daily routine outside almost every school. Children weave through rows of idling cars and motorcycles while parents wait with engines running and air conditioning switched on.

We would think twice about making a child stand beside an exhaust pipe. We panic when toxic haze blankets the country. Yet we have normalised school pickup arrangements that expose children to traffic pollution every single day.
The contradiction extends inside our vehicles.

Many people imagine the car interior as a protected space, but in heavy traffic ventilation systems draw in exhaust from surrounding vehicles. Pollutant concentrations inside cars can often exceed the ambient levels reported by regional monitoring stations.
We seal ourselves inside glass-and-steel boxes, convinced we are sheltered from the very pollution we are helping to create.
Unequal exposure
The burden is not distributed equally.

Millions of people live near major roads and expressways. Think of the apartments lining the Ampang-Kuala Lumpur Elevated Highway (Akleh) or landed homes built alongside the Lebuhraya Damansara–Puchong (LDP). Even with windows closed, fine particles can infiltrate indoor spaces.
For commuters waiting at bus stops along busy arterial roads, a “good” air quality reading can be almost meaningless. Exposure at street level often bears little resemblance to citywide averages.
Air pollution is not experienced as a statistic. It is experienced where people live, walk, wait, and breathe.
The other pollution
Traffic generates more than dirty air. It also produces noise.

Chronic exposure to traffic noise has been linked to hypertension, heart disease, stroke, hearing damage, stress, anxiety, sleep disruption, and impaired childhood development. Yet heavily modified cars and motorcycles continue to rumble, rev and backfire through our streets every day.
The health and peace of the wider public are routinely sacrificed so that a small minority can satisfy the need to draw attention to themselves.
Why EVs are not enough
Electric vehicles offer important benefits, but they do not solve the problem entirely.
EVs eliminate tailpipe emissions and reduce vehicle noise, yet they still generate pollution through tyre wear, brake dust and road-surface abrasion.
Because many EVs are heavier than their petrol-powered counterparts, some of these non-exhaust emissions can be substantial.

Replacing every petrol vehicle with an electric one would reduce exhaust fumes, but it would not eliminate the airborne rubber particles and roadway dust that already make up a significant share of urban particulate pollution.
The real solution
Cleaner fuels and electric vehicles are improvements, but they are ultimately technological band-aids.

Truly addressing urban air pollution requires reducing our dependence on private motor vehicles altogether. It means designing cities where walking, cycling and public transport are the default choices rather than desperate alternatives.

It means prioritising human lungs over vehicular throughput: building wide, shaded pedestrian corridors separated from traffic, reallocating road space to efficient bus networks, and creating dense, walkable neighbourhoods where daily necessities do not require a car trip.
Seeing beyond the blue sky
Clear skies can be deceiving.

Much of the harm caused by air pollution cannot be seen, but it is no less real because of that fact. We do not dismiss the germs that cause food poisoning simply because they are invisible. It is equally absurd to ignore the pollutants produced by our addiction to cars simply because they cannot be photographed.

The challenge ahead is not merely cleaner air. It is recognising that our car-dependent way of life carries hidden costs that are paid with our health, our peace, and our quality of life. Only when we acknowledge those costs can we begin the work of eliminating them.

acd9154ed738c734: From Moaz Nair
According to an opposition lawmaker, the government providing subsidies is like “giving fish to the people”. Eventually, they say, the people will become lazy.

Critics frequently echo this sentiment, arguing that giving cash aid and relief to lower- and middle-income groups acts as a drag on national output. They view it as a pure consumption cost that fails to enhance economic productivity.
However, empirical macroeconomic data suggests this perspective is deeply flawed.
Far from being simple welfare relief, targeted cash transfers — such as Malaysia’s Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) — serve as vital mechanisms for strategic economic investment.
When structured effectively, cash assistance significantly amplifies both immediate aggregate demand and long-term labour productivity.

To make the full transition into a high-income nation, our fiscal discourse must evaluate how cash assistance behaves when scaled to the middle 40% (M40) income group. We need to shift the paradigm from merely maintaining a socio-economic floor to actively constructing an upward economic ladder.
The B40 multiplier effect
To understand the productivity debate, one must first isolate the short-term stimulus created by lower-income households, which is driven by a high marginal propensity to consume (MPC).
Because B40 families operate near subsistence levels, they immediately re-inject almost every additional ringgit received into the economy for basic necessities.
This capital flows directly into local micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) whose owners, in turn, pay suppliers and workers.
Studies reviewed by the World Bank demonstrate that cash transfers consistently yield a high economic multiplier, where every RM1 distributed generates upwards of RM2 to RM2.50 in local GDP growth.
Beyond immediate retail velocity, mitigating extreme financial stress unlocks long-term labour output by alleviating cognitive load and physical deprivation.
Cash aid provides the financial breathing room necessary for individuals to undergo technical and vocational education and training (TVET) or make the transition towards higher-value employment.
Furthermore, when paired with healthcare initiatives like PeKa B40 (ProtectHealth B40), cash transfers improve nutritional status and preventive care, fostering a healthier, more alert workforce.

This intervention yields its greatest dividends in future human capital, as targeted aid is reinvested into children’s education, mitigating school dropout rates and systematically elevating the skills ceiling of the next generation.
Not a policy panacea
Nevertheless, economists caution that cash handouts alone do not constitute a policy panacea.
While cash aid triggers rapid market circulation, it can induce minor, localised demand-pull inflation if supply chains face structural constraints.
It also carries a latent risk of welfare dependency if the programme lacks clear exit policies.
Financially, the model relies heavily on state revenue, requiring meticulous fiscal balancing despite indirectly bolstering tax revenues through increased economic activity.

Ultimately, cash aid only drives lasting productivity if it is structurally integrated with broader reforms, such as wage restructuring, digital transformation for small businesses, and proactive job placement programmes.
Upward social mobility for the M40
The economic dynamics shift fundamentally when evaluating the potential of expanding cash assistance or fiscal relief to the M40 income group.
Funding the M40 results in a lower immediate economic multiplier but yields a significantly higher long-term return on high-value productivity.
While B40 interventions focus primarily on survival, aid targeted at the M40 drives upward social mobility and formal structural investment.

Because their baseline survival needs are secured, M40 households exhibit a lower MPC and direct surplus funds towards professional education upgrades, debt reduction, healthcare insurance, and domestic tourism.
While this slower velocity of money tempers the immediate multiplier effect, it channels institutional capital into formal consumer sectors that employ a vast segment of the domestic workforce.
As the backbone of the nation’s skilled workforce, reducing cost-of-living pressures on the M40 unlocks high-value labour productivity through two primary channels:

Professional upskilling: M40 individuals are highly likely to utilise financial relief or tax-rebate equivalents to fund professional certifications or postgraduate diplomas. This creates a talent pool capable of anchoring high-value foreign direct investment (FDI).

Mitigating burnout: It eases the intense economic pressures faced by the “squeezed middle” — a demographic often ineligible for heavy subsidies yet highly vulnerable to inflation — thereby stabilising white-collar productivity.
Furthermore, unlike the B40, a portion of the disposable income left with the M40 enters the broader financial ecosystem as productive capital.
These individuals channel surplus funds into unit trusts, voluntary Employees Provident Fund (EPF) contributions, or retail equities, deepening national investment liquidity.
This liquidity also enables M40 professionals to seed side hustles, micro-digital enterprises, and freelance consulting ventures, fostering broader innovation across the digital economy.
Conclusion
Ultimately, the core differences between funding these two socio-economic tiers lie in their macroeconomic outcomes.

While the B40 target impact drives immediate retail consumption, rapid market velocity, and basic labour survival through direct cash transfers, the M40 target impact enables discretionary spending, high-value professional upskilling, and managerial efficiency through delivery mechanisms like tax reliefs, education credits, and housing incentives.
Maximising Malaysia’s economic potential requires a balanced, dual-track approach rather than an adversarial policy debate.
Funding the B40 establishes the vital economic and social floor, ensuring the baseline labour force remains stable, healthy, and participant in the economy.

Conversely, providing targeted relief to the M40 builds the economic ladder, offering the upward momentum necessary to push the workforce out of the middle-income trap and into high-productivity industries.
True economic foresight lies in managing both ends of this continuum simultaneously.
